items.title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
items.summary: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected. Our response We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms. Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below. What customers should do Developer guidance For developers, look beneath the SDK. An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy. Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore. This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment. Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier. Timeline The timeline of events so far is below. Date and Time Event October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment. October 20, 02:00 UTC Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms (except Cloudflare One Agent on iOS, for which app review is still pending). October 20 09:15 UTC Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published. October 20 19:20 UTC CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed. Looking forward The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.
items.summary_html:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should doDeveloper guidance

For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline

The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms (except Cloudflare One Agent on iOS, for which app review is still pending).

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

items.title: Manage all your Microsoft Sentinel data in one place with Unified Data Management (Public Preview)
items.summary: As security teams bring in more data from more sources and use it across SIEM and XDR workflows, decisions about connector health, ingestion volume, and cost optimization get harder. Today, we’re announcing the public preview of Unified Data Management for Microsoft Sentinel, available in the new Data & connectors experience in the Microsoft Defender portal, so you can monitor and manage your data from a single place. What Unified Data Management is and why it matters Unified Data Management brings connectors, tables, and ingestion health together. Instead of moving between separate pages, you can see your full data landscape, spot issues, and act on them from one view. It’s designed to help you quickly answer questions like: Which connectors are configured and which need attention? Which tables are receiving data? Are there ingestion spikes, drops, or stale data patterns? Which tables drive the most ingestion volume? What schema, transformations, and retention settings apply to a table? You’ll find it under Setup & configuration > Data & connectors , organized into three tabs: Overview , Connectors , and Tables . Overview: See health at a glance The Overview tab gives you a workspace-level snapshot of ingestion and health, so you can catch data issues before they impact analytics, detections, investigations, or reporting. It surfaces: Ingestion volume : Daily ingestion split by Analytics tier and Data Lake tier for your selected time range. Connectors that need attention : Connectors with credential errors, ingestion failures, or outages, including error type, failure count, and last successful ingestion. Table ingestion fluctuations : Tables with unexpected volume changes, grouped into spikes and drops. Data ingestion volume by table : Your top ingesting tables, ranked by daily volume. Ingestion latency by table : How long it takes for data to become available after it’s generated. Together, these insights help you troubleshoot connector failures, track down cost spikes, validate that new connectors are flowing, and catch unexpected changes in volume. Figure 1: The Overview tab shows daily ingestion volume by tier alongside data health insights, including connectors that need attention and tables with unexpected volume spikes or drops. Connectors: One inventory for unified and classic connectors The Connectors tab puts unified data connectors and Sentinel classic data connectors side by side, so it’s easier to see which data sources are onboarded and how they're connected. From here, you can: View onboarded connectors with their status, provider, content source, and available updates. Switch between unified connectors and Sentinel classic connectors. Search and filter connectors by provider, data type, and status. Open connector details to review configuration and health. Unified connectors reduce duplication by allowing supported data sources to connect once and feed data across Microsoft security products. Sentinel classic connectors continue to support the broad connector ecosystem, including connectors built with the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) . Figure 2: The Connectors tab brings unified and Sentinel classic connectors into a single inventory, with counts for onboarded and connected connectors, available updates, and filters for provider, data type, and status. Tables: Health, schema, transformations, and retention in one place The Tables tab brings Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft Defender XDR tables together with their health signals, schema, transformations, and retention settings. Key insights now appear right in the grid, so you can compare tables side by side: last data received, average daily ingestion volume, estimated daily ingestion cost, volume anomaly, tier, and retention settings. This makes it easier to spot tables that have gone stale, are growing unexpectedly, or are driving a big share of your ingestion volume. Select any table to open the details panel, which organizes everything about that table into tabs: Details panel tab What it shows Overview Table type, tier, analytics retention, total retention, and other table metadata. Schema Column names, data types, and descriptions, with no KQL query required. Transformations Filter, Split, and Scope Tag transformation rules applied to the table. Retention Analytics retention and total retention settings. Figure 3: The Tables tab opens a details panel for any selected table. The Schema tab is especially useful when you need to understand incoming data, validate table fields, or create transformation logic without first writing schema-discovery queries. Built for everyday data operations in the Microsoft Defender portal Data management touches nearly every part of security operations, from detection and investigation to hunting, retention, and cost optimization. By bringing these tasks into the Microsoft Defender portal, Unified Data Management cuts down on context switching and makes it clearer how connectors, tables, health, transformations, and retention fit together. It’s one more step in Microsoft Sentinel’s investment in a unified security operations experience, where SIEM and XDR data can be managed and used together. Preview availability and prerequisites Unified Data Management is now available in public preview in commercial cloud environments. To experience it, you’ll need: Microsoft Sentinel onboarded to the Microsoft Defender portal. Unified role-based access control (URBAC) enabled in the Microsoft Defender portal. Data (manage) permission in the Data Operations permission group. Workspace permissions equivalent to Log Analytics Contributor , including permissions to write workspace and table settings. Get started Ready to try it? Open the Microsoft Defender portal and go to Setup & configuration > Data & connectors . From there: Start on the Overview tab to check ingestion volume and data health. Use the Connectors tab to view your unified and classic connectors. Explore the Tables tab to review table health, schema, transformations, and retention. For implementation and configuration guidance, see: Manage data in Microsoft Sentinel and Defender Configure data connectors Manage your existing tables and data Monitor the health of your Microsoft Sentinel data connectors Unified connectors overview Microsoft Sentinel data connectors More Microsoft Sentinel data integration news Public Preview: Nested API Support Comes to Microsoft Sentinel CCF Create a pull codeless connector for Microsoft Sentinel Logs Ingestion API in Azure Monitor

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of Unified Data Management for Microsoft Sentinel, available in the new Data & connectors experience in the Microsoft Defender portal, so you can monitor and manage your data from a single place.

What Unified Data Management is and why it matters

Unified Data Management brings connectors, tables, and ingestion health together. Instead of moving between separate pages, you can see your full data landscape, spot issues, and act on them from one view. It’s designed to help you quickly answer questions like:

  • Which connectors are configured and which need attention?
  • Which tables are receiving data?
  • Are there ingestion spikes, drops, or stale data patterns?
  • Which tables drive the most ingestion volume?
  • What schema, transformations, and retention settings apply to a table?

You’ll find it under Setup & configuration > Data & connectors, organized into three tabs: Overview, Connectors, and Tables.

Overview: See health at a glance

The Overview tab gives you a workspace-level snapshot of ingestion and health, so you can catch data issues before they impact analytics, detections, investigations, or reporting. It surfaces:

  • Ingestion volume: Daily ingestion split by Analytics tier and Data Lake tier for your selected time range.
  • Connectors that need attention: Connectors with credential errors, ingestion failures, or outages, including error type, failure count, and last successful ingestion.
  • Table ingestion fluctuations: Tables with unexpected volume changes, grouped into spikes and drops.
  • Data ingestion volume by table: Your top ingesting tables, ranked by daily volume.
  • Ingestion latency by table: How long it takes for data to become available after it’s generated.

Together, these insights help you troubleshoot connector failures, track down cost spikes, validate that new connectors are flowing, and catch unexpected changes in volume.

Figure 1: The Overview tab shows daily ingestion volume by tier alongside data health insights,
including connectors that need attention and tables with unexpected volume spikes or drops.

Connectors: One inventory for unified and classic connectors

The Connectors tab puts unified data connectors and Sentinel classic data connectors side by side, so it’s easier to see which data sources are onboarded and how they're connected. From here, you can:

  • View onboarded connectors with their status, provider, content source, and available updates.
  • Switch between unified connectors and Sentinel classic connectors.
  • Search and filter connectors by provider, data type, and status.
  • Open connector details to review configuration and health.

Unified connectors reduce duplication by allowing supported data sources to connect once and feed data across Microsoft security products. Sentinel classic connectors continue to support the broad connector ecosystem, including connectors built with the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF).

Figure 2: The Connectors tab brings unified and Sentinel classic connectors into a single inventory, with counts
for onboarded and connected connectors, available updates, and filters for provider, data type, and status.

Tables: Health, schema, transformations, and retention in one place

The Tables tab brings Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft Defender XDR tables together with their health signals, schema, transformations, and retention settings.

Key insights now appear right in the grid, so you can compare tables side by side: last data received, average daily ingestion volume, estimated daily ingestion cost, volume anomaly, tier, and retention settings. This makes it easier to spot tables that have gone stale, are growing unexpectedly, or are driving a big share of your ingestion volume.

Select any table to open the details panel, which organizes everything about that table into tabs:

Details panel tab

What it shows

Overview

Table type, tier, analytics retention, total retention, and other table metadata.

Schema

Column names, data types, and descriptions, with no KQL query required.

Transformations

Filter, Split, and Scope Tag transformation rules applied to the table.

Retention

Analytics retention and total retention settings.

 

Figure 3: The Tables tab opens a details panel for any selected table. The Schema tab is especially useful when you need to
understand incoming data, validate table fields, or create transformation logic without first writing schema-discovery queries.

Built for everyday data operations in the Microsoft Defender portal

Data management touches nearly every part of security operations, from detection and investigation to hunting, retention, and cost optimization. By bringing these tasks into the Microsoft Defender portal, Unified Data Management cuts down on context switching and makes it clearer how connectors, tables, health, transformations, and retention fit together.

It’s one more step in Microsoft Sentinel’s investment in a unified security operations experience, where SIEM and XDR data can be managed and used together.

Preview availability and prerequisites

Unified Data Management is now available in public preview in commercial cloud environments. To experience it, you’ll need:

  • Microsoft Sentinel onboarded to the Microsoft Defender portal.
  • Unified role-based access control (URBAC) enabled in the Microsoft Defender portal.
  • Data (manage) permission in the Data Operations permission group.
  • Workspace permissions equivalent to Log Analytics Contributor, including permissions to write workspace and table settings.
Get started

Ready to try it? Open the Microsoft Defender portal and go to Setup & configuration > Data & connectors. From there:

  1. Start on the Overview tab to check ingestion volume and data health.
  2. Use the Connectors tab to view your unified and classic connectors.
  3. Explore the Tables tab to review table health, schema, transformations, and retention.

items.title: The Real Jump Scare Isn’t the Attacker; It’s The Vulnerabilities You’re Focusing On
items.summary: Key Takeaways Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with. Mean time to exploitation is about −7 days. Mean time to remediate sits around +30 days. Qualys research: closures rose from 73M (2022) to 473M (2025) – 6× – while critical findings still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited. A volume-and-CVSS program spends most of its effort on the rest. 15% of organizations that operationalized the pipeline patched before a vulnerability hit the CISA KEV list. October is here, bringing a chill in the air, spooky decorations, and, fittingly, Cybersecurity Awareness Month. It’s a timely reminder for security leaders to revisit and strengthen their strategy. The past 12 months alone show how cyber threats are getting smarter and faster. There’s a haunting paradox that should be top of mind. Security teams are doing more vulnerability remediation than ever before. They’re patching faster, scanning deeper, and closing more tickets than any team in history, yet attackers exploit systems at an alarming rate, faster than ever before. Fortunately, with the right cyber risk management plan, security teams can navigate the dark landscape of AI-driven attackers. But before we talk about defense, let’s outline a few of attackers’ tricks. The Threat Landscape Is Accelerating Ransomware is one of the leading cyber threats, rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year , and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031 . If that projection holds, it will put severe pressure on already strained security teams. AI is escalating the problem rather than easing it. AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. More attacks are coming, and those powered by AI make each breach more expensive to address. The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days . Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached. The Financial Reality Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident , up 12% from last year. The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average . With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise. The Remediation Paradox Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted. The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered. This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time , and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time. The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes. As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process. The Path Forward So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed. When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40% . That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise. In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate? As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact. Scary Stats That Will Keep You Up At Night Ransomware is rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year , and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031 . AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. Mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days . Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident , up 12% from last year. The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average . Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time , and half were weaponized before a patch existed. A: Organizations are closing far more vulnerabilities, Qualys research shows a 6× rise in closures from 2022 to 2025, while a larger share of critical findings remain open at day seven. The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached.

The Financial Reality

Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.

The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.

With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise.

The Remediation Paradox

Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted.

The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered.

This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time.

The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes.

As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process.

The Path Forward

So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed.

When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40%. That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise.

In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate?

As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact.

Scary Stats That Will Keep You Up At Night
  • Ransomware is rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031.
  • AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost.
  • Mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days.
  • Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.
  • The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average.
    • The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.
  • Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%.

  • Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed.

A: Organizations are closing far more vulnerabilities, Qualys research shows a 6× rise in closures from 2022 to 2025, while a larger share of critical findings remain open at day seven. More effort has not produced better coverage of the exposures attackers use.

items.title: Cloud Security Billing, Simplified: Introducing the Defender Workload Unit
items.summary: That's the thinking behind an upcoming improvement to Microsoft Defender for Cloud: the Defender Workload Unit , or DWU. It's a new billing model and product experience that translates workload-specific usage into a common billing unit, with one unit price and one place to estimate and track costs. Why we’re improving our billing model We heard two things consistently: cloud security pricing can be complex, and tracking cost can take real work. DWU simplifies this with one unit price. Workload usage still converts behind the scenes. What changes is that organizations see a single unit and have one place to estimate, track, and explain cloud security spend. How DWU helps: Simplify pricing. Bring multiple workload-specific measures under one common billing model. Simplify onboarding and expansion. Make it easier to enable and extend protection across cloud environments. Match how you evaluate cloud security. Understand protection across your entire cloud environment, rather than workload by workload. Reduce cost-tracking friction. Make costs easier to estimate, track, and explain. One thing we deliberately kept unchanged: billing stays tied to what is used. How it compares DWU translates workload-specific usage into a common billing unit with a consistent per-unit price. Each workload continues to convert into DWUs according to its applicable usage measure. Workloads still count behind the scenes, including servers, databases, storage, containers, posture management, APIs, AI services, app services, Key Vault, and Azure Resource Manager. What changes are what customers see: one unit and one price. Workload-specific usage is converted into DWUs and aggregated across your environment, based on a consistent global per-unit price calculated hourly and billed monthly. Estimation, reporting, and billing use the same DWU framework, making it easier to understand how usage translates into cost. What changes is how customers estimate, buy, manage, and track consumption. DWU brings together changes to the billing model, supporting tools, and management experience. Here is how the new experience compares with the existing model. Existing PAYG model With DWU Estimating cost Manual mapping, plan by plan Signed-in estimator, formula visible. Sizing environment Manual inventory Read-only discovery script; your data stays with you Tracking spend Multiple billing signals Defender portal dashboard, detail in Azure Cost Management Database plans Multiple instance/hour-based plans A single instance/hour-based plan Containers pricing vCore-based pricing Per-node pricing APIs pricing Multiple plans A single plan at a reduced price Plan Management Azure portal only Defender portal only (based on customer scope selection) The benefits of DWU DWU is designed to make Defender for Cloud consumption easier to estimate and track by translating supported workload usage into a common billing unit. Actual consumption and cost will depend on your workload mix, usage, pricing arrangement, and applicable discounts. We are committing to pricing that's easier to understand and manage. Clearer cost planning. As your estate grows, you can watch how costs scale. Transparency you can show your finance team. The new cost estimator requires you to sign in and shows the pricing formula and how your estimate is calculated. The same ways to buy. DWU is available through Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement Enterprise, Cloud Solution Provider, and buy-online channels. Streamlined onboarding . Enable selected Defender for Cloud plans across subscriptions and management scopes through a unified experience. Easier expansion. Extend protection as your cloud environment grows without introducing a new customer-facing pricing construct for every workload. More holistic visibility. Understand protection and consumption across your cloud environment, rather than workload by workload. What's new to help you A cost estimator. Enter resource quantities to receive an immediate list-price estimate. A path from estimate to deployment. The experience follows a simple flow: estimate, deploy, and track. Move directly from your estimate to deployment, then monitor cost through the Defender portal. A dashboard that answers the next question. See total spend, which workloads drive it, and how it trends over time. New pricing models for some workloads. Containers move from vCore-based pricing to per-node. APIs consolidate multiple plans into one with a reduced plan. Database workload protection is consolidated from multiple instance-per-hour plans into one. What stays in your control Simpler doesn't mean less flexible. Choose which workload plans to enable and change them at any time. In the product, tenant-level enablement applies to Azure subscriptions and management groups connected to the Defender portal. You can also enable plans for an individual connected management group or subscription. When you opt into a subscription, its workloads move together. Where to start A 30-day platform trial . Eligible subscriptions that are new to Cloud Security can start a Defender for Cloud trial in the Defender portal. The trial is optional, is granted at the subscription level, and is limited to one trial per subscription. It covers the full platform, including all plans, rather than one capability at a time. After the trial ends, billing begins for the subscription, unless all cloud security plans are disabled before the trial expires. Two questions worth bringing to your next planning review: How clearly can we estimate and explain Defender for Cloud consumption across supported workloads? If we cannot do so clearly, that's the gap DWU can close. When did we last compare our intended protection scope with our current cloud-resource inventory? The read-only discovery script can tell you, with nothing leaving your environment. One common unit and a more consistent way to estimate and track consumption can make it easier to understand and explain what you’re protecting. Learn more and get started Calculate your DWU estimates with the new Cloud Security Cost Estimator . Learn more about DWU and start onboarding . FAQ Does DWU cover multicloud environments? Initial support is focused on Azure, with broader multicloud and hybrid support planned over time. Does DWU cover Security Copilot? No, DWU does not offer coverage for Security Copilot. Can I use the new container and API models through the existing PAYG experience in Azure? No, they are available only through the DWU experience in the Defender portal.
items.summary_html:
That's the thinking behind an upcoming improvement to Microsoft Defender for Cloud: the Defender Workload Unit, or DWU. It's a new billing model and product experience that translates workload-specific usage into a common billing unit, with one unit price and one place to estimate and track costs.

Why we’re improving our billing model

We heard two things consistently: cloud security pricing can be complex, and tracking cost can take real work. DWU simplifies this with one unit price. Workload usage still converts behind the scenes. What changes is that organizations see a single unit and have one place to estimate, track, and explain cloud security spend.

How DWU helps:

  • Simplify pricing. Bring multiple workload-specific measures under one common billing model.
  • Simplify onboarding and expansion. Make it easier to enable and extend protection across cloud environments.
  • Match how you evaluate cloud security. Understand protection across your entire cloud environment, rather than workload by workload.
  • Reduce cost-tracking friction. Make costs easier to estimate, track, and explain.

One thing we deliberately kept unchanged: billing stays tied to what is used.

How it compares

DWU translates workload-specific usage into a common billing unit with a consistent per-unit price. Each workload continues to convert into DWUs according to its applicable usage measure. Workloads still count behind the scenes, including servers, databases, storage, containers, posture management, APIs, AI services, app services, Key Vault, and Azure Resource Manager. What changes are what customers see: one unit and one price.

Workload-specific usage is converted into DWUs and aggregated across your environment, based on a consistent global per-unit price calculated hourly and billed monthly. Estimation, reporting, and billing use the same DWU framework, making it easier to understand how usage translates into cost.

What changes is how customers estimate, buy, manage, and track consumption. DWU brings together changes to the billing model, supporting tools, and management experience. Here is how the new experience compares with the existing model.

 

Existing PAYG model

With DWU

Estimating cost

Manual mapping, plan by plan

Signed-in estimator, formula visible.

Sizing environment

Manual inventory

Read-only discovery script; your data stays with you

Tracking spend

Multiple billing signals

Defender portal dashboard, detail in Azure Cost Management

Database plans

Multiple instance/hour-based plans

A single instance/hour-based plan

Containers pricing

vCore-based pricing

Per-node pricing

APIs pricing

Multiple plans

A single plan at a reduced price

Plan Management

Azure portal only

Defender portal only (based on customer scope selection)

 

The benefits of DWU

DWU is designed to make Defender for Cloud consumption easier to estimate and track by translating supported workload usage into a common billing unit. Actual consumption and cost will depend on your workload mix, usage, pricing arrangement, and applicable discounts. We are committing to pricing that's easier to understand and manage.

Clearer cost planning. As your estate grows, you can watch how costs scale.

Transparency you can show your finance team. The new cost estimator requires you to sign in and shows the pricing formula and how your estimate is calculated.

The same ways to buy. DWU is available through Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement Enterprise, Cloud Solution Provider, and buy-online channels.

Streamlined onboarding. Enable selected Defender for Cloud plans across subscriptions and management scopes through a unified experience.

Easier expansion. Extend protection as your cloud environment grows without introducing a new customer-facing pricing construct for every workload.

More holistic visibility. Understand protection and consumption across your cloud environment, rather than workload by workload.

What's new to help you

A cost estimator. Enter resource quantities to receive an immediate list-price estimate.

A path from estimate to deployment. The experience follows a simple flow: estimate, deploy, and track.

Move directly from your estimate to deployment, then monitor cost through the Defender portal.

A dashboard that answers the next question. See total spend, which workloads drive it, and how it trends over time.

New pricing models for some workloads. Containers move from vCore-based pricing to per-node. APIs consolidate multiple plans into one with a reduced plan. Database workload protection is consolidated from multiple instance-per-hour plans into one.

What stays in your control

Simpler doesn't mean less flexible. Choose which workload plans to enable and change them at any time. In the product, tenant-level enablement applies to Azure subscriptions and management groups connected to the Defender portal. You can also enable plans for an individual connected management group or subscription. When you opt into a subscription, its workloads move together.

Where to start

A 30-day platform trial. Eligible subscriptions that are new to Cloud Security can start a Defender for Cloud trial in the Defender portal. The trial is optional, is granted at the subscription level, and is limited to one trial per subscription. It covers the full platform, including all plans, rather than one capability at a time.

 After the trial ends, billing begins for the subscription, unless all cloud security plans are disabled before the trial expires.

Two questions worth bringing to your next planning review:

  1. How clearly can we estimate and explain Defender for Cloud consumption across supported workloads? If we cannot do so clearly, that's the gap DWU can close.
  2. When did we last compare our intended protection scope with our current cloud-resource inventory? The read-only discovery script can tell you, with nothing leaving your environment.

One common unit and a more consistent way to estimate and track consumption can make it easier to understand and explain what you’re protecting.

Learn more and get started
  • Calculate your DWU estimates with the new Cloud Security Cost Estimator.
  • Learn more about DWU and start onboarding.
FAQ
  • Does DWU cover multicloud environments? Initial support is focused on Azure, with broader multicloud and hybrid support planned over time.
  • Does DWU cover Security Copilot? No, DWU does not offer coverage for Security Copilot.
  • Can I use the new container and API models through the existing PAYG experience in Azure? No, they are available only through the DWU experience in the Defender portal.

eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise Triggers Emergency Action Across Browsers
items.summary: The private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates have been compromised, prompting emergency blocks across major browsers and software platforms. The affected certificates chain to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome, placing clients that still accept them at risk of trusting forged certificates. However, the public disclosures reviewed do not establish that these keys can be cracked in seconds. They confirm that a researcher demonstrated control of the keys, not how they were obtained or how quickly any cryptographic attack could recover them. A researcher identified as Wayne reported the compromise to root program teams on October 17, 2026. To demonstrate access, Wayne signed the message “We have a problem here – Wayne” using each affected intermediate CA private key. The disclosure site , published by Dennis Jackson, provides certificates, public keys, and signatures for independent checks. Researchers can use OpenSSL to extract a certificate’s public key and verify the corresponding signature. This proves signing capability without requiring publication of the private keys themselves. An intermediate certificate authority helps connect a website’s certificate to a trusted root. If its signing key is exposed, an attacker may create certificates that vulnerable clients accept as genuine. Mozilla warned that someone able to intercept a connection could use fraudulent certificates to impersonate websites and potentially read or change traffic. The risk echoes earlier reporting on unauthorized HTTPS certificates obtained through compromised domain registries and misissued TLS certificates affecting the 1.1.1.1 DNS service . Those cases involved different failures, but show why certificate trust is a security concern beyond the browser padlock. Browsers Block Certificates as Software Updates Mozilla received the report at 20:06 UTC on October 17 and completed its OneCRL blocklist rollout by 22:59 UTC. Standard Firefox configurations received protection without requiring a browser update or restart, according to Mozilla’s incident statement . The disclosure site says Chrome also blocked the affected certificates on October 17. Apple followed on October 19, while Microsoft’s protection arrived on October 20. eMudhra has also revoked the compromised intermediate certificates. Revocation alone does not protect every application. Some clients do not receive browser blocklists or check whether a certificate has been revoked. These programs need separate updates to stop accepting the affected certificate chains. Mozilla released Firefox 158.0.1, ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 to cover users whose settings could prevent OneCRL delivery. Its NSS 3.131.1 update also removes the signing root from the trusted certificate list used by other applications. The incident response page lists fixes including Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, Python certifi 2026.10.19, and Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10. Node.js and Composer ca-bundle updates were listed as pending when the page was reviewed. Users should update browsers and operating systems promptly. Developers should also check certificate bundles shipped with applications rather than assume an operating system update covers every runtime. Administrators can use the disclosure site’s test endpoints and certificate chains to assess remaining exposure. A certificate rejection indicates that the tested client refuses the affected chain. Manual root removal should remain an expert measure because it can disrupt legitimate connections. The verified finding is a serious signing key compromise. The available evidence does not establish a seconds-long cracking method or confirm attacks against users. How the keys became exposed remains publicly unconfirmed. An EDR alert reveals an attack. items.title: More Hay On The Haystack: What Our AI Panel Disagreed On
items.summary: When I started in digital forensics in 2002 (I know, I just dated myself), I was told my job was to find the needle in the haystack. AI can throw a lot more hay on that pile, and if you don’t have a strong foundation as an examiner, you may never find the needle. I said that while moderating the AI panel on day two of the SANS DFIR Summit & Training 2026 in Arlington, with three panelists I knew wouldn’t agree on everything. Ovie Carroll is Director of the DOJ Cybercrime Lab and has taught for SANS since 2009 (he was clear his comments were his own, not his employer’s). Ovie is also co-author of FOR500 : Windows Forensic Analysis. Mari DeGrazia is Director at IDX Cyber Response, a Principal Instructor at SANS Institute and the author of FOR563 : Applied AI for Digital Forensics and Incident Response. Raymond DePalma is authoring FOR581: Investigating and Responding to Compromised AI Systems, a new SANS course on what to do when the AI itself is the victim. Lee Crognale, our Curriculum Lead for DFIR, warmed up the room with a few polls, including whose boss has banned AI at work and whose boss requires it. Panels aren’t my favorite format because the best answers get rushed at the end, so I started with closing thoughts first. Never trust, always verify Mari went first. Our industry has always said “trust but verify,” and she thinks AI calls for “never trust, always verify.” Ovie was just as blunt: AI will fail, because all tools fail, and it will hallucinate, lie to you, guess at what you want, and try to please you. Everyone agreed on that much. Where they split was on what verifying looks like, and whether most of us do it at all. Ovie, who has 30 years in this field, doesn’t think most examiners validate the tools they already use. They push the button and move on, often because leadership doesn’t understand forensics well enough to give them time to do more. He also said there has never been such a thing as a full forensic analysis. Hand your best case to the weakest analyst in your office and they’ll find an artifact you missed, because nobody has enough time. Ovie worries AI becomes the super easy button. If we aren’t validating now, he asked, what makes us think AI will suddenly make us start? And if it hands you a mountain of output to check, are you really saving time? He also has a rule of five: the first time you use AI you’re seeing what it’s about, the second time it’s not bad, the third time it’s wow, the fourth time you’re a genius, and from the fifth time on you’ve stopped reading what it puts out. Last month he tried to stage an intervention for a friend of 30 years who now sends him AI-written emails. Ray agreed and disagreed, which he said was to make it spicy. Training is fundamental, he said, because the judgment layer is the one thing we still have that AI doesn’t. But when a model hallucinates, he wants you to ask why. Did it run out of context window, or miss the right knowledge base? Could a script do that step the same way every time? A planned workflow that calls deterministic tools, with an evaluation harness testing the results, holds up better than a one-shot prompt with no examples and no stopping point. Treat AI like an intern, at best Mari’s answer to the validation problem was one of the more practical things I heard at the Summit. She treats AI like an intern. It takes a first pass at the data while she works on other outputs, flags four or five things worth a look, and she validates those. You wouldn’t let an intern hand you a final answer on an important case without checking it, especially with your name going on the report. Use your AI where you would an intern. Keep in mind that not all cases are the same and not all niches of DFIR are the same. Act wisely! Mari also doesn’t ask AI to do a tool’s job. Her agent doesn’t convert timestamps; it calls a conversion tool she has already validated, so the only thing left to check is whether it picked the right tool. Ray learned the same lesson decoding web shells. The AI’s output looked convincing until CyberChef proved it wrong, and now his workflow has the AI call CyberChef instead. Without that check, he said, he could have handed a client incorrect evidence. That only works because you were trained on those tools yourself. Ovie made the same argument from the other side: without a deep understanding of the artifacts, an analyst can’t tell when AI missed something or got it wrong. He named where that depth comes from: FOR500 and FOR508 for Windows, FOR585 for smartphones, FOR577 for Linux, and FOR518 for Mac. Yes, we’re a training company and those are our courses. His point stands anyway. If you don’t know what the artifact should look like, you won’t catch the mistake. Then Ovie put me on the spot and asked how often, in my last multi-murder investigation, I got that gut feeling that something in the data wasn’t right. The honest answer is daily. AI can follow rules, but it doesn’t have the instinct that sends you back to look again. In court, the artifact is what matters One audience question asked whether non-experts can testify about AI findings. Ovie, reminding us he isn’t a lawyer, said no. Testimony rests on reliability under the Daubert standard, and he pointed to the debate over proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 , which would hold machine-generated evidence offered without an expert to the same bar as expert testimony. It’s still a proposal; the federal Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules decided this year to gather more input first. Ray and Ovie then did a decent chatbot impression (“I apologize for the confusion. I made an error in my previous response.”) to make a serious point. That exchange is discoverable, and so are your prompts, the model, how it was trained, and every mistake it made. Ovie added that models will change an answer just to agree with you. He quoted a friend who told him credibility is your most valuable commodity, so spend it wisely. One unchecked AI report in court can burn yours and your agency’s. Mari asked the follow-up I suspect a lot of the room was thinking: what if AI is just a brainstorming partner and you find everything again independently in your forensic tools? Ovie’s answer applies with or without AI. Your report and testimony should be about the artifact itself, the SQLite database or the log record, and tools belong on the last page of the report. Use AI to get to the artifacts faster, like when you’re facing a unified audit log with 20 million records, then validate and write about what you found. I was glad to hear it, since my keynote on the Idaho case the day before showed only the artifacts. Ovie also borrowed a line from Eric Zimmerman for tool developers: when your tool fails, fail spectacularly, not silently in an audit log nobody looks at. A recent tool with AI built on top told his team five times, with high confidence, that the data they wanted wasn’t there. It was sitting in an unencrypted SQLite database the tool just didn’t parse. Ray’s advice is to question AI providers the way we question every other vendor, and he pointed to the EDR Telemetry Project , which shows what endpoint products collect and where the gaps are. Local or cloud: pick the right vehicle Mari admits she’s biased toward local models, since that’s what FOR563 teaches. Her argument is control. About a year ago a major provider pulled a model overnight, and anyone who had tested its tool calling and built a workflow around it lost that workflow the same night. When I started in digital forensics in 2002 (I know, I just dated myself), I was told my job was to find the needle in the haystack. AI can throw a lot more hay on that pile, and if you don’t have a strong foundation as an examiner, you may never find the needle. 

I said that while moderating the AI panel on day two of the SANS DFIR Summit & Training 2026 in Arlington, with three panelists I knew wouldn’t agree on everything. Ovie Carroll is Director of the DOJ Cybercrime Lab and has taught for SANS since 2009 (he was clear his comments were his own, not his employer’s). Ovie is also co-author of FOR500: Windows Forensic Analysis. Mari DeGrazia is Director at IDX Cyber Response, a Principal Instructor at SANS Institute and the author of FOR563: Applied AI for Digital Forensics and Incident Response. Raymond DePalma is authoring FOR581: Investigating and Responding to Compromised AI Systems, a new SANS course on what to do when the AI itself is the victim. 

Lee Crognale, our Curriculum Lead for DFIR, warmed up the room with a few polls, including whose boss has banned AI at work and whose boss requires it. Panels aren’t my favorite format because the best answers get rushed at the end, so I started with closing thoughts first. 

Never trust, always verify 

Mari went first. Our industry has always said “trust but verify,” and she thinks AI calls for “never trust, always verify.” Ovie was just as blunt: AI will fail, because all tools fail, and it will hallucinate, lie to you, guess at what you want, and try to please you. Everyone agreed on that much. Where they split was on what verifying looks like, and whether most of us do it at all. 

Ovie, who has 30 years in this field, doesn’t think most examiners validate the tools they already use. They push the button and move on, often because leadership doesn’t understand forensics well enough to give them time to do more. He also said there has never been such a thing as a full forensic analysis. Hand your best case to the weakest analyst in your office and they’ll find an artifact you missed, because nobody has enough time. 

Ovie worries AI becomes the super easy button. If we aren’t validating now, he asked, what makes us think AI will suddenly make us start? And if it hands you a mountain of output to check, are you really saving time? 

He also has a rule of five: the first time you use AI you’re seeing what it’s about, the second time it’s not bad, the third time it’s wow, the fourth time you’re a genius, and from the fifth time on you’ve stopped reading what it puts out. Last month he tried to stage an intervention for a friend of 30 years who now sends him AI-written emails. 

Ray agreed and disagreed, which he said was to make it spicy. Training is fundamental, he said, because the judgment layer is the one thing we still have that AI doesn’t. But when a model hallucinates, he wants you to ask why. Did it run out of context window, or miss the right knowledge base? Could a script do that step the same way every time? A planned workflow that calls deterministic tools, with an evaluation harness testing the results, holds up better than a one-shot prompt with no examples and no stopping point. 

Treat AI like an intern, at best 

Mari’s answer to the validation problem was one of the more practical things I heard at the Summit. She treats AI like an intern. It takes a first pass at the data while she works on other outputs, flags four or five things worth a look, and she validates those. You wouldn’t let an intern hand you a final answer on an important case without checking it, especially with your name going on the report. Use your AI where you would an intern. Keep in mind that not all cases are the same and not all niches of DFIR are the same. Act wisely! 

Mari also doesn’t ask AI to do a tool’s job. Her agent doesn’t convert timestamps; it calls a conversion tool she has already validated, so the only thing left to check is whether it picked the right tool. Ray learned the same lesson decoding web shells. The AI’s output looked convincing until CyberChef proved it wrong, and now his workflow has the AI call CyberChef instead. That only works because you were trained on those tools yourself. Ovie made the same argument from the other side: without a deep understanding of the artifacts, an analyst can’t tell when AI missed something or got it wrong. He named where that depth comes from: FOR500 and FOR508 for Windows, FOR585 for smartphones, FOR577 for Linux, and FOR518 for Mac. Yes, we’re a training company and those are our courses. His point stands anyway. If you don’t know what the artifact should look like, you won’t catch the mistake. 

Then Ovie put me on the spot and asked how often, in my last multi-murder investigation, I got that gut feeling that something in the data wasn’t right. The honest answer is daily. AI can follow rules, but it doesn’t have the instinct that sends you back to look again.

items.title: Expanded cross-tenant delegated access in Microsoft Defender is generally available
items.summary: Security operations rarely stop at a single tenant boundary. Managed security service providers (MSSPs) protect many customer environments, and central security teams often operate across a tenant estate spanning business units, regions, or subsidiaries. In both cases, teams need to delegate security work without granting broad access or managing permissions one analyst at a time. Today, we’re announcing the general availability of cross-tenant delegated administration in Microsoft Defender, built on the same governance relationship model as Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance . Organizations can now use a consistent governance model to establish cross-tenant relationships, delegate access to partner or central security teams, and enforce least-privilege permissions across their tenant estate. We’re also extending delegated access to support Microsoft Sentinel resources and enabling granular permissions for delegated users through Defender unified RBAC, reducing the need for separate access models across identity and security. With the consistent access model, MSSPs partners (non-CSP) and multitenant organizations can run security operations across tenants, while each customer or governed tenant decides exactly what access to grant. Govern access across your tenant estate Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance helps organizations establish least-privilege governance relationships across related tenants. The same governance relationship model now extends into Microsoft Defender and Sentinel, enabling MSSPs and central security teams to manage security operations across governed environments without requiring separate local administrator identities in each tenant. This model helps organizations: Scale without multiplying identities. Analysts use their home-tenant accounts instead of requiring local administrator or Microsoft Entra B2B guest accounts in every governed tenant. Apply least privilege. Each governed tenant controls the roles and resource scopes assigned to remote tenant groups. Simplify ongoing administration. The partner or central team keeps access current by managing membership in its own security groups rather than maintaining individual assignments across customer tenants. Support integrated security operations. MSSPs and multitenant organizations can use a consistent governance relationship to support delegated operations across Microsoft Defender and Sentinel. Bring identity and security access together. Use a consistent governance relationship model across Microsoft Entra, Defender, and Sentinel, reducing the need for separate delegated-access arrangements. One relationship, two controls A governance relationship is a directional connection between two Microsoft Entra tenants: The governing tenant is where the MSSP or central security team manages its analysts and security groups. The governed tenant is the customer or organizational tenant that grants delegated access. After the relationship is approved, selected security groups from the governing tenant are represented in the governed tenant as remote tenant groups. The governed tenant can then assign the supported roles and resource scopes those groups need, while the governing tenant continues to manage group membership. This creates a clear separation of responsibilities: tenant administrators set the access boundaries in the governed tenant, and partners or central security teams manage their analysts within those boundaries. How the relationship works The governance relationship is established through a three-step, consent-based handshake: The governed tenant sends an invitation. A customer or organizational administrator enables governance invitations in Microsoft Defender and invites the governing tenant. The governing tenant sends the relationship request. The MSSP or central security team creates an access template containing the relevant security groups and Microsoft Entra role assignments, then sends the governance relationship request. The governed tenant approves the request and assigns roles and resource scopes. The governed tenant explicitly approves the governance relationship and configures the Defender and Sentinel roles and resource scopes granted to the remote tenant groups. With approval and permissions in place, the governance relationship is ready to be used. Figure 1: The governed tenant reviews the requested role assignments and retains final approval over delegated access. The relationship provides the cross-tenant foundation. Governed-tenant administrators then apply the workload and resource permissions required for the intended security operations: For Microsoft Defender: Administrators can assign supported Microsoft Defender unified RBAC roles to remote tenant groups, including custom roles with the permissions and scopes required for the work. For Microsoft Sentinel: Customers can manage delegated access using Defender unified RBAC or Azure RBAC, assigning remote tenant groups the permissions needed to operate customer environments with least privilege. Figure 2: Assign custom roles to a remote tenant group using Defender unified RBAC. This distinction allows each governed tenant to approve the relationship and right-size access for its own environment while the governing tenant manages the analysts who perform the work. What partners are saying Partners are seeing how expanded support for delegated access can simplify cross-tenant operations and help them deliver managed security services with least privilege. “The ability to assign Azure RBAC and Defender Unified RBAC to remote tenant groups over GDAP will allow us to securely and efficiently configure and access customer environments at scale. Historically, we would need to configure a range of different access methods to access all the different services, but now we can use GDAP to access everything we need to provide managed SOC services.” — Riley Boon, Senior Capability Engineer, CyberCX “Microsoft's investments in its partner programs pay off in real outcomes for the products BlueVoyant and our customers rely on every day. Over the past several months, Microsoft has worked alongside BlueVoyant to address limitations in Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) and deliver new capabilities, including support for assigning GDAP security groups to Sentinel workspace roles and Unified Role-Based Access Control (URBAC) support for GDAP remote tenant groups. These improvements let us manage customer environments with least-privilege access. That is what customers have been asking for and Microsoft listened.” — Ryan Sturm, Senior Manager – Microsoft Security Engineering, BlueVoyant Whether you’re onboarding your first customer tenant or consolidating access across dozens, the same model applies: tenant administrators set the boundaries, and your team works within them. Get started Start with the work your partner or central security team needs to do. Identify the eligible security groups, establish the governance relationship, and assign only the workload roles and scopes that work requires. Configure delegated access with governance relationships for multitenant organizations Manage unified role-based access control in multitenant management Create custom roles with Microsoft Defender unified RBAC Additional resources Microsoft Entra tenant governance documentation
