October 20, 2026: This post was republished to reflect the new migration capability from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP) or the Identity Center directory, now available in IAM Identity Center.

September 2, 2026: This post was republished to include Active Directory migration strategies and automation for permission sets.

AWS IAM Identity Center manages user access to Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources, including both AWS accounts and applications. You can use IAM Identity Center to create and manage user identities within the Identity Center identity store or to connect to other identity sources.

Organizations that are switching identity providers (IdPs), consolidating identity infrastructure, adopting new single sign-on capabilities, or migrating off legacy on-premises systems may need to change the identity source in IAM Identity Center. Previously, migrations from Active Directory to another identity source deleted users, groups, memberships, and assignments at the moment of cutover. Now, migrations away from Active Directory preserve your users, groups, memberships, and assignments, just as transitions between an external IdP and the Identity Center directory already do. Only switching to Active Directory still removes users, groups, and assignments. Because the change applies to the entire Identity Center instance at once, test validation and a dress rehearsal are strongly recommended.

This post walks you through the migration process and provides sample code to assist the transition. It includes architectural guidance and a step-by-step runbook for switching from Active Directory to Okta. This guide helps AWS administrators, identity engineers, and project teams switch identity sources safely.

Note: This walkthrough uses Okta as a representative example of a SAML 2.0 identity provider. The inclusion of Okta in this example does not constitute an endorsement of any specific identity provider.

Identity source options in IAM Identity Center

The identity source is the definitive system of record: it determines which directory holds the primary copy of user identities and group memberships used for AWS access.

Each IAM Identity Center instance connects to one identity source at a time. IAM Identity Center supports three main identity sources:

  • Identity Center directory – The default identity store. Users and groups are created and managed directly within IAM Identity Center, with no dependency on an external provider. Suitable for organizations without an existing enterprise directory or those wanting a setup that uses only AWS services.
  • Active Directory – Integration with an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory or AWS Managed Microsoft AD through AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. This lets organizations reuse their existing AD identities, group memberships, and access policies.
  • External IdP – Integration with third-party providers that support SAML 2.0, including Okta Universal Directory, Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), Ping Identity, and others. This is the approach covered in the migration runbook that follows.

For example, migrating from Active Directory to an external IdP carries your existing users and groups over to the new identity source. IAM Identity Center keeps the same identity store, user IDs, and group IDs, and SCIM updates only the external identifier (externalId) to reflect the new source.

How access flows to AWS resources

IAM Identity Center grants access to AWS resources in two ways, as shown in Figure 1:

  • Permission set assignments – Users or groups are assigned permission sets within specific AWS accounts. This enables assume-role access, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles (named AWSReservedSSO_...) are automatically created in each account to back these assignments.
  • Application assignments – Users or groups are granted access to AWS-managed applications (such as Amazon SageMaker Studio, Amazon OpenSearch Service and so on) and customer-managed applications integrated with IAM Identity Center.

Figure 1: Granting access to AWS resources for users and groups managed by an identity source in IAM Identity Center

When you change the identity source, the downstream impact on these assignments depends heavily on which sources you’re switching from and to. In some transitions, assignments remain intact.

When you switch the identity source from Active Directory to an external IdP or to the Identity Center directory, users, groups, user and group IDs, group memberships, and their associated assignments are preserved. Users keep their access to AWS accounts and applications after the new identity source takes over. Switching to Active Directory from any source removes users, groups, and assignments at the moment of cutover, so pre-migration backup and post-migration restoration are still essential in that scenario.

What changes when switching identity source in IAM Identity Center

Migrations away from Active Directory, and transitions between an external IdP and the Identity Center directory, now preserve users, groups, memberships, and assignments. Transitions to Active Directory removes users, groups, and assignments permanently from IAM Identity Center at the moment of cutover, as shown in the following table. For more information, see Considerations for changing your identity source.

IAM Identity Center item Status upon switch from AD to external IdP or Identity Center directory Status upon switch from external IdP or Identity Center directory to AD Users and groups in Identity Center Preserved (same user and group IDs; the externalId changes as the new source takes over) Deleted (must be re-provisioned from AD) Account assignments Preserved Deleted (must be recreated) Application assignments Preserved* Deleted (must be recreated)

Note: *Test each application in a non-production environment before you migrate. Also inventory any assignments that live inside an application itself, because those sit outside IAM Identity Center.

Before you start: common blockers
  • Matching attribute – Confirm which attribute your target IdP uses to find an existing user (sometimes called matching precedence or existing resource lookup). The IdP must take over each existing Identity Center user and group rather than create a duplicate. Test this in a non-production environment.
  • Required attributes – Every user must have a username, first name, last name, and display name. If any required attribute is missing, that user silently fails to provision. If you send email, it must be unique and single-valued.
  • Username and NameID – Each user’s IdP userName must exactly match the existing Identity Center username, and the SAML NameID must map to the same value. Decide your sign-in identifier (for example, a legacy sAMAccountName or a UPN) before cutover.
  • Groups – Confirm that your IdP supports group provisioning through SCIM (for example, Google Workspace provisions users only). Group names must be unique, and renaming a group can cause it to be treated as new, which strands its assignments. Depending on the external Identity provider, users who belong to a group only through a nested group are not provisioned and lose group-based access. Inventory nested groups and directly assign the child groups that contain those users before cutover.
  • Emergency access – Set up a break-glass administrative access path that does not depend on AWS Identity Center.
Sample deployment

The following five-step summary (expanded into seven phases in the runbook that follows) applies to an identity source transition in IAM Identity Center from Active Directory to Okta, focusing on permission set assignments. The AD-to-Okta runbook in the next section expands each of these steps with specific instructions and commands. To assist users, you can also use the Identity Center migration tool script, which provides a structured workflow for Identity Center migrations with commands for precheck, cutover, validation, and cleanup. Because assignments are now preserved, the restore command is used only for manual rollback. The sample scripts and detailed steps are available on GitHub.

Note: This solution is available in the GitHub aws-samples repository. You can report bugs or make feature requests through GitHub Issues. The builders of this solution can help with GitHub issues. Enterprise Support customers can reach out to their Technical Account Manager (TAM) for further questions or feature requests.

Prerequisites

Before you start this walkthrough, make sure you have the following prerequisites in place:

  • Python 3.10 or later
  • AWS credentials configured using environment variables, an AWS configuration file, or a named AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) profile (specified with --profile)
  • An active IAM Identity Center instance in the target account
  • Okta Global Admin access
  • Install the migration tool as described in the README file
Basic solution walkthrough

The following steps summarize the migration process. The next section expands each step with detailed Okta-specific instructions and commands.

Step 1: Back up users, groups, and assignments – Before making any changes, export your current identity data such as users, groups, and all assignments. This backup protects you if something goes wrong during migration. Store them in a secure, access-controlled location. The runbook includes a script that exports all current IAM Identity Center assignments and principals to a CSV file, then validates referential integrity.

Step 2: Prepare and validate users and groups in the target identity source – Before switching the IAM Identity Center identity source, confirm that your users and groups exist in the new authoritative source. Verify usernames, display names, email addresses, group names, group memberships and other required attributes. Each user’s userName in the new source must exactly match the existing Identity Center username, because this is how the new source usually takes over the user. In a test environment, confirm that an existing user is matched, not duplicated.

Step 3: Switch IAM Identity Center to the new identity source, and configure sign-in – Update IAM Identity Center to point to the new identity source. For external IdPs, upload the SAML metadata and configure the Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) and issuer URLs in your IdP. Before enabling SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management), confirm that a pilot user can sign in.

WARNING: The identity source change applies to the entire Identity Center instance. After you confirm it, Active Directory sync and authentication stop, and users can’t sign in until SAML sign-in works with the new IdP. Users, groups, memberships, and assignments are preserved.

Step 4: Enable SCIM provisioning and verify takeover – Enable automatic provisioning and assign users and groups to the IAM Identity Center application in your IdP. The IdP takes over each existing user and group. Then run the validate command to compare the live assignments against your backup and find any missing or extra assignments.

If drift is found, the script writes a drift_report.csv file with MISSING and EXTRA entries.

Step 5: Validate access – Test access for a sample of users across different roles and permission levels before declaring the migration complete. Confirm that users can authenticate through the new identity source, access their expected AWS accounts, and assume the correct IAM roles. Confirm that the identity source shows your external IdP, that users and groups keep the same IDs, and that no duplicates were created.

Detailed runbook for Okta migration

This runbook covers one of the most common identity source transitions: migrating from an Active Directory to Okta as a SAML 2.0 identity provider.

The sample deployment describes what happens during a transition. It walks through seven phases: stakeholder alignment and pre-migration inventory, pre-cutover validation, the identity source switch itself, takeover verification, post-migration testing, ongoing cleanup and monitoring, and a documented manual rollback procedure for when things don’t go to plan.

If you’re migrating to Active Directory, which still removes users, groups, memberships and assignments, you can adapt the backup and restore scripts from this guide.

Phase 1: Plan your pre-migration activities

Pre-migration planning has four components: stakeholder engagement, inventory, scheduling, and access verification. Complete all four before you schedule the cutover.

1.1 – Document relevant stakeholders:

Fill out this table with actual contact information. You’ll need to reach these people during the cutover window.

Stakeholder Org Name Email Phone Active Directory administrator Your organization AWS administrator Your organization Identity provider (IdP) administrator Your organization Identity Center team/AWS Organizations administrator AWS account team Application owners AWS account team Identity provider (IdP) solutions architect AWS account team

1.2 – Inventory current state:

Before any changes are made, document the complete current state of your IAM Identity Center configuration. Capture a baseline of all three assignment layers: the users and groups assigned to the IAM Identity Center application in your IdP, the account and application assignments in IAM Identity Center, and any assignments inside the applications themselves:

Run the precheck script to export all current Identity Center assignments and principals to CSV.

```bash 
python -m idc_migration_tool precheck --output-dir ./export 
```

This will produce the following artifacts:

  • assignments.csv – One row per account, permission-set, and principal assignment
  • principals.csv – All users and groups from the identity store

1.3 – Define the cutover window:

Schedule the migration during a low-usage period to minimize user impact. Size the maintenance window using timings from a full-dress rehearsal in a test environment. SCIM provisioning is rate-limited, so for large directories, sync users in batches. Identify a maintenance window of sufficient length to complete all phases, including time for validation and potential manual rollback (described in Phase 7) if needed. Notify all affected users in advance of the potential temporary disruption to single-sign-on access.

1.4 – Confirm access requirements:

Verify that the following access is confirmed and tested before the cutover window:

  • AWS Administrator access to IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
  • Identity provider (IdP) administrator access (for example, Okta) to configure the IAM Identity Center application, create the SCIM integration, and assign users to the AWS app.
  • A break-glass or emergency administrative access path that does not depend on the identity source you are migrating.
Phase 2: Complete final pre-cutover steps

Before starting the cutover, complete the final validation, access, and communication checks described in this phase.

2.1 – Export IAM Identity Center configuration:

Validate that the backup files generated in Step 1.2 are present and non-empty before proceeding.

2.2 – Communicate impact to users:

Send advance notice to all affected users covering:

  • The migration timeline and expected impact window.
  • That users can’t sign in between the identity source change and the new IdP’s sign-in going live, but that their access and assignments are unchanged.
  • The new sign-in process. After migration, users sign in through your IdP (for example, the Okta My Apps dashboard) or the AWS access portal, depending on the sign-in flow you choose.
  • Whether the new sign-in flow is IdP-initiated (through Okta) or SP-initiated (through the AWS access portal), and any differences in the user experience.
  • After migration, the d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start access portal URL is no longer supported, and the console shows the supported dual-stack regional URL (https://ssoins-.portal..app.aws) instead, so you must communicate the new URL and update bookmarks/allow-lists.
  • That the custom access portal alias (friendly URL) isn’t supported after migrating away from Active Directory. If a proxy or bookmark relies on redirect flows, plan to update it.

Prepare a user guide for the new sign-in process and an FAQ for common issues. Schedule a training session to demonstrate how to access AWS through Okta. Ensure your support team is briefed and ready to handle an influx of access issues during and immediately after the cutover.

2.3 – Validate Okta-to-IAM Identity Center sync (pre-cutover testing):

Using a sandbox or test environment if available, perform the following validation steps before executing against production:

  • Run the full migration in a test instance that mirrors your production AD configuration and applications and confirm that existing test users are matched by Okta and not duplicated.
  • Use the AWS Management Console for IAM Identity Center to verify that groups and users appear in Users & Groups with the correct attributes.
  • Test the complete end-to-end sign-in flow for a test user. Authenticate through Okta, access the AWS portal, and assume a role in a test account. Confirm that the user keeps access to their assigned accounts, permission sets, and applications.
Phase 3: Complete the cutover

You’re ready to configure Okta, switch the IAM Identity Center identity source, and complete the production cutover.

Important: Downtime begins when you confirm the identity source change in Step 3.2 and ends when SAML sign-in works through Okta. Have the Okta application, SAML metadata, and signing certificate ready before you start. Users, groups, memberships, and assignments are preserved.

3.1 – Configure the Okta application:

  1. Sign in to Okta as an administrator.
  2. Navigate to Applications and then to Browse App Catalog.
  3. Search for AWS IAM Identity Center and choose Add Integration. Choose Done.
  4. Choose the newly created app and select the Sign On tab.
  5. Locate the Metadata URL (it will look like: https:///app//sso/saml/metadata). Open this URL in a new browser tab.
  6. An XML file will render in the browser. Save this file. This is your SAML metadata file, which will be uploaded to IAM Identity Center.
  7. Download and save the SAML signing certificate from the Sign On tab.

3.2 – Switch the identity source in IAM Identity Center:

  1. In the IAM Identity Center console navigation pane, choose Settings.
  2. Choose Actions and select Change Identity Source.

    Important: This change applies to the entire Identity Center instance. On the confirmation screen, you must enter ACCEPT to confirm. During this step and before SCIM provisioning is enabled, if the change could not be completed by Identity Center you will see a clear error message in the console to retry changing identity providers. It is safe to retry.

  3. Select External Identity Provider.
  4. Upload the XML metadata file and the SAML signing certificate downloaded from Okta.
  5. Confirm the change. IAM Identity Center will display progress updates as it migrates to the new identity provider.
  6. Don’t enable automatic provisioning yet. Complete Step 3.3 and confirm pilot sign-in in Step 3.4 first.

3.3 – Configure the ACS and issuer URLs in Okta:

  1. In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings and then Actions. Select Manage Authentication.
  2. Copy the IAM Identity Center Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL and the IAM Identity Center Issuer URL.
  3. Return to Okta and choose Applications and select IAM Identity Center app. Select the Sign On tab and choose Edit.
  4. Under Advanced Sign On Settings, paste the ACS URL and Issuer URL into the corresponding fields.
  5. Choose Save.

3.4 – Confirm pilot sign-in:

Before you enable SCIM provisioning, assign an existing pilot user to the IAM Identity Center application in Okta and confirm they can sign in through the AWS access portal. The SAML NameID that Okta sends must exactly match the user’s existing Identity Center username. If sign-in fails, fix the mapping now before proceeding to the next step.

3.5 – Enable automatic provisioning (console) and connect SCIM in Okta:

  1. In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings, then choose Enable Automatic Provisioning. Copy and securely record the SCIM endpoint URL and access token.
  2. Return to the IAM Identity Center app in Okta. Choose the Provisioning tab.
  3. Choose Configure API Integration.
  4. Paste the SCIM Endpoint URL into the Base URL field.
  5. Paste the Access Token into the API Token field.
  6. Choose Test API Credentials. You should receive confirmation that the credentials are valid.
  7. Choose Save.
  8. On the Provisioning page, choose Edit and under To App enable all three provisioning options (Create Users, Update User Attributes, and Deactivate Users). Choose Save. (The To App settings control how Okta provisions users to IAM Identity Center. All three options are required for the migration to work correctly.)
  9. On the Push Groups tab, push the groups that are assigned to the AWS application. Group names must exactly match the existing group names in IAM Identity Center.
  10. In the attribute mappings, confirm that userName maps to the existing Identity Center username and that first name, last name, display name, and a single email address are populated.

3.6 – Test SCIM takeover:

Before you assign all users, verify that Okta takes over existing users correctly:

  1. In Okta, select an existing pilot user who already exists in IAM Identity Center (People).
  2. Open the user and navigate to the Applications tab.
  3. Assign the AWS IAM Identity Center app to this test user.
  4. Wait 5–10 minutes for SCIM sync to run.
  5. In the IAM Identity Center console, select Users and confirm that the pilot user still has the same user ID, that no duplicate user was created, and that the user’s assignments still work.

    Note: If the user is duplicated or doesn’t update after 10 minutes, check the Okta System Log for SCIM provisioning errors and verify the SCIM endpoint URL and token are correctly configured.

  6. After the pilot user is taken over successfully, assign the remaining users and groups to the application in Okta. For large directories, assign them in batches.
Phase 4: Verify takeover

Now that you’ve completed cutover, verify that Okta has taken over all users and groups and that the preserved assignments match your pre-migration baseline.

4.1 – Verify SCIM takeover:

Confirm that all production users and groups are provisioned from Okta, that they keep the same user and group IDs, and that no duplicates were created. Check the Okta provisioning logs for errors such as “Refused to create a new, duplicate resource.”

4.2 – Check for assignment drift: Compare the live assignments against the pre-migration CSV

```bash 
python -m idc_migration_tool validate --csv ./export/assignments.csv --output-dir ./export 
```

If drift is found, the script writes a drift_report.csv file with MISSING and EXTRA entries. Because assignments are preserved, investigate any entries before you continue.

Phase 5: Post-migration validation

After the cutover, validate end-to-end access for representative user roles and confirm that assignments were preserved.

5.1 – Test end-to-end access:

Using a test Okta user account, complete the following validation steps:

  1. Sign in to the Okta Dashboard.
  2. Choose the AWS IAM Identity Center tile under My Apps.
  3. Select an assigned AWS account from the portal.
  4. Confirm that you can assume a role and access the AWS console.
  5. Test role switching within the console to validate permission boundaries.

5.2 – Spot-check multiple user types:

Validate access for a representative sample of users across different access levels, including Administrator, Developer, Read-Only or Audit, and any other standard roles defined in your environment. Confirm that permission sets are correctly mapped and that no unintended access has been granted or denied.

For each application, confirm that user-specific data and settings are intact and that any assignments inside the application still work.

Phase 6: Post-migration cleanup and monitoring

After confirming the migration is stable, shift focus to ongoing monitoring of provisioning and authentication, and update your operational documentation.

6.1 – Decommission AD only when stable:

  • Don’t decommission the Active Directory domain controllers until you’re confident the migration is stable and rollback is no longer needed. Keep AD online as a fallback. Deleting the AD directory removes the manual rollback option and the AD-based access portal endpoint.
  • The following command will identify disabled users, empty groups, and unassigned permission sets. 
    ```bash 
# Report only 
python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup 
 
# Report and prompt for deletion 
python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup --delete 
```

6.2 – Monitor SCIM sync:

  • Confirm that SCIM provisioning continues to run without errors in the days following migration.
  • Monitor new user onboarding from Okta to verify that newly created Okta users are automatically provisioned into IAM Identity Center.
  • Review IAM Identity Center and AWS CloudTrail logs for failed sign-in attempts or unexpected authentication errors.

6.3 – Update documentation:

Update all internal documentation to reflect the new identity architecture:

  • Record the SCIM integration details, SAML metadata links, and new group-to-permission-set mappings.
  • Update internal SOPs and onboarding guides to reflect the new Okta-based login process.
  • Document troubleshooting procedures for the most common failure modes.

6.4 – Post-migration checklist:

Before closing the migration project, confirm all of the following:

  • Users can authenticate successfully through Okta.
  • Permission sets are correctly assigned to the correct users and groups.
  • Account assignments are working correctly across accounts.
  • Monitoring and logging are configured and alerting on anomalies.
  • Internal documentation and SOPs are updated.
  • Support team is trained on the new login process.
  • Rollback procedures have been reviewed and are ready if needed.
  • Active Directory integration cleanup is scheduled (do not rush decommission).
Phase 7: Rollback (if needed)

Rollback requires manually switching the identity source back to Active Directory, which deletes users, groups, memberships and assignments, and then rebuilding assignments from the pre-migration backup files, as described in the following steps.

Note: Define in advance what counts as a failure, who makes the rollback decision, and the acceptable discrepancy threshold. Only initiate rollback if the Okta migration has failed and cannot be recovered within the migration window. Rollback is a manual, time-consuming process. There is no single-button undo for an identity source switch.

7.1 – Switch identity source back to Active Directory:

  1. Navigate to IAM Identity Center and choose Settings, then Actions, and then Change Identity Source.
  2. Select Active Directory as the identity source.
  3. Select your existing AD domain. Ensure AD is still running and reachable before confirming.
  4. Accept the conditions and confirm the switch. Identity Center will display progress updates.
  5. When complete, choose Resume Sync, then choose Start Guided Setup.
  6. Confirm the attribute mappings and select the users and groups to sync.
  7. Review and save the configuration.

7.2 – Wait for AD users and groups to repopulate:

After completing the guided setup, AD users and groups will begin to reappear in IAM Identity Center through the directory sync. This might take several minutes depending on the size of your directory.

7.3 – Recreate account assignments:

Recreate the assignments from the pre-migration CSV file. This will resolve each principal name in identity store, create the assignment, and poll until completion, and produce a summary of succeeded, failed, and skipped counts.

```bash 
python -m idc_migration_tool cutover --csv ./export/assignments.csv 
```

7.4 – Validate access:

Confirm users can authenticate using the original AD-based AWS access portal URL and can access their expected AWS accounts and roles. Test key role types (such as Admin, Developer, and Audit) before declaring rollback complete.

Troubleshooting the cutover

The identity source change in Step 3.2 runs as a sequence of steps: stopping Active Directory sync, disconnecting the directory, and deleting the AD sync profile. If a step after “Stopping Active Directory sync” fails, the Confirm change screen reports which steps failed and offers a Retry failed steps button. You will see one of two error messages, both safe to retry:

  1. “The identity source change could not be completed. Please try again.” — AD sync was stopped but the directory wasn’t disconnected, so new users and changes are not currently syncing from Active Directory. Choose Retry failed steps to complete the transition. If instead you want to stay on Active Directory, choose Start guided setup in the Settings page to reconfigure the sync.
  2. “The identity source change could not be completed. Your identity source has been reverted to Active Directory. Please try again.” — IAM Identity Center automatically rolled back to a healthy AD-connected state, and a banner confirms that AD sync resumed. You don’t need to reconfigure the sync; choose Retry failed steps when you’re ready to try again.

Important: In both cases, choose Retry failed steps on the Confirm change screen. If you navigate away from this screen, you can no longer retry the failed steps and will need to restart the identity source change.

For troubleshooting tips, see Troubleshooting IAM Identity Center issues.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

Conclusion

This post covered how to migrate your IAM Identity Center identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (Okta), including backing up existing assignments, validating your target identity source, performing the cutover, verifying that the new identity source took over your users and groups with their assignments intact, validating access, and rolling back if needed.

For the backup and restore scripts referenced in this guide, see the aws-samples GitHub repository. For more information about IAM Identity Center configuration and permission set management, visit the AWS Security Blog and the AWS IAM Identity Center documentation.

Xiaoxue Xu

Xiaoxue is a Solutions Architect for AWS based in Toronto. She primarily works with Financial Services customers to help secure their workload and design scalable solutions on the AWS Cloud.

Kanwar is a Principal Technical Account Manager at AWS who works with customers to optimize their use of AWS services and achieve their business objectives.

Richard Merritt

items.title: Free Helpline for Victims of Online Crime Pilots in South Africa
items.summary: South Africans who fall victim to cybercrime now have more support available. MiDO Academy, The Cyber Helpline (UK) and Amazon Web Services (AWS) launched the pilot of The Cyber Helpline in South Africa , a free, confidential service providing practical guidance and compassionate support to individuals affected by online fraud, investment and employment scams, hacked accounts, phishing and smishing, social media fake profiles, sextortion, online harassment, identity theft, malware and ransomware incidents.

Breaking More Encrypted USB Drives with AI
items.summary: Earlier this year, I showed how to break encrypted USB drives with time-travel debugging ( slides ) at RE//verse . After having a lot of recent success with AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research, I wanted to see how well AI could handle the same tasks. Not surprisingly, it exceeded my expectations. In one case, it reproduced my research in seven minutes using static analysis. I then asked it to analyze two products I had not considered in my original research, and it tore those apart just as easily. Breaking NetacFileLock again I started with NetacFileLock , which I had previously analyzed using time-travel debugging (TTD) to trace the ciphertext back to its AES key. I only did one prompt: This is a file encryption utility. Analyze its crypto system and see if it is secure. You can use Binary Ninja MCP to help you. Within seven minutes, Codex reached the main flaw: the program initialized AES-256 with a fixed 32-byte key embedded in the executable. The user password was checked separately and did not determine the encryption key. This means anyone can decrypt the file without knowing the user password. During those seven minutes, the agent also made the following findings, some of which were not discussed in my talk: NetacFileLock wrote the user’s password into diagnostic logs. It encrypted independent 16-byte blocks without an IV or chaining, giving it ECB-style behavior. It used MD5 for password verification. It used an unkeyed MD5 digest as a file “signature.” Its SM4 option used another fixed key. One open question in my research was why only one-third of my test file was encrypted. That is now solved too: the behavior is not limited to PDF files; it applies to any file over 1,024 bytes when fast mode is enabled. Fast mode covers the following file formats: PNG, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, DWG, PSD, PST, DBX, Office, MDB, WPD, PDF, ZIP, RAR, WAV, AVI, RAM, RM, MPEG, MOV, ASF, and MIDI I did not bother asking AI why anyone would choose to do this. I had mixed feelings after this. On the one hand, I was surprised and even a bit worried that AI could do it so quickly. On the other hand, this is an excellent time to become much more productive with AI’s help. KakaSoft USB Copy Protection From there, I wanted to test AI against something new. After a little searching, I found a seemingly promising product category: “copy-protected” USB drives. The vendors claim that files copied onto these drives can be viewed only through their software and cannot be extracted from the device. I was immediately suspicious. If a client can display a file, it must decrypt that file; when the user controls the computer doing the decryption, preventing extraction is extremely difficult. I started with KakaSoft USB Copy Protection 5.6.0.299. I was working on macOS, while the tool runs only on Windows. This was hardly a problem: I asked the AI to handle the installer and analyze the extracted Windows binaries. The program offered three security strengths: Normal: “Hide and Lock Files.” This does not encrypt the file. High: “Scramble and encrypt file headers.” The program XORs at most the first 16,385 bytes with a byte-sized key derived from the password. There are only 256 possible keys, known file signatures reveal the key immediately, and everything after the scrambled prefix remains plaintext. Highest: “256-bit Blowfish Encryption.” This was the safest-looking option and the one I selected. The first two were obviously insecure. What caught my eye was the AI’s suggestion that it might recover a file encrypted at the Highest level without the password. When I asked for details, however, it appeared uncertain. To confirm the weakness, I ran the software and let it protect a small text file. When I inserted the protected drive, it appeared to contain only USBCopyProtect.exe , which was required to view the file. This did not bother the AI. It first located the protected data, which KakaSoft had hidden inside an unusual directory tree on the exFAT volume. Parsing the raw directory entries produced this tree: USB root └── HPSafeBox [hidden + system] ├── desktop.ini [hidden + system] ├── con.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652} └── Important Folder └── Com1.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652} └── \x7f\x7f\uE347.. [unusual UTF-16 name] ├── Info.bd ├── Daily.db └── NLLastF [hidden + system] └── test.txt.txt [667 bytes] HPSafeBox and NLLastF had the exFAT hidden and system attributes. The Com1.{...} component combines the reserved Windows device name COM1 with a shell CLSID-style suffix. The next directory’s on-disk name begins with two 0x7f DEL characters, followed by the private-use Unicode character U+E347 and two dots. These names confuse normal Windows path handling and help keep the tree out of Explorer. Here is a shortened hexdump of the hidden 667-byte test.txt.txt : 00000000: a0 ea 96 ca 0e 03 f0 98 0b 3e ad 18 99 a7 e3 9d .........>...... 00000010: 08 b2 f6 55 b7 2f 47 3c 0e 66 2b a9 1f 82 97 c8 ...U./G<.f+..... 00000020: b5 47 c4 22 09 08 30 2c 7a 65 9b b8 b3 1e 87 25 .G."..0,ze.....% 00000030: 45 35 49 a4 58 1c 63 5b 4e e3 ee 0a 05 48 b3 56 E5I.X.c[N....H.V ... 00000250: 20 32 34 31 38 35 36 35 37 33 31 34 32 41 44 38 241856573142AD8 00000260: 38 32 30 36 43 45 31 42 46 38 33 35 46 41 38 46 8206CE1BF835FA8F 00000270: 37 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 7............... 00000280: 00 00 00 0e 6b 61 6b 61 65 6e 63 72 79 70 74 69 ....kakaencrypti 00000290: 6f 6e 08 42 6c 6f 77 46 69 73 68 on.BlowFish The first eight bytes are a random salt, the next eight are the Blowfish CBC IV, and the ciphertext begins at offset 0x10 . The final 75 bytes start at 0x250 . This trailer contains a 32-character verifier followed by the readable strings kakaencryption and BlowFish : 8-byte salt | 8-byte IV | Blowfish ciphertext | 75-byte trailer The client was a 32-bit Delphi program. The AI followed its TBlowfishEncryption class to learn how those bytes were decrypted. Each file had its own salt and IV. The fatal problem was how the key was derived: internal password = modified MD5 of an embedded seed file key = RIPEMD-128(salt || internal password) plaintext = Blowfish-CBC-Decrypt(file key, IV, ciphertext) The first hash was recognizably based on MD5, but it was not standard MD5. Here are the first eight operations of the third round in a vanilla implementation: HH ( a , b , c , d , x [ 5 ], 4 , 0xfffa3942 ); HH ( d , a , b , c , x [ 8 ], 11 , 0x8771f681 ); HH ( c , d , a , b , x [ 11 ], 16 , 0x6d9d6122 ); HH ( b , c , d , a , x [ 14 ], 23 , 0xfde5380c ); HH ( a , b , c , d , x [ 1 ], 4 , 0xa4beea44 ); HH ( d , a , b , c , x [ 4 ], 11 , 0x4bdecfa9 ); HH ( c , d , a , b , x [ 7 ], 16 , 0xf6bb4b60 ); HH ( b , c , d , a , x [ 10 ], 23 , 0xbebfbc70 ); The rotation counts repeat 4, 11, 16, 23 . KakaSoft kept the same constants and message order, but its corresponding calls use 4, 11, 16, 16, 4, 11, 11, 4 . The changed arguments are visible in the decompiled client: Vanilla digest rendering normally looks like this: static const char hex [] = "0123456789ABCDEF" ; out [ i * 2 ] = hex [ digest [ i ] >> 4 ]; out [ i * 2 + 1 ] = hex [ digest [ i ] & 0x0f ]; KakaSoft performs the same lookup with 1903642857ACBEDF instead: This second change is only character substitution; the altered rotations are what make the raw digest differ from standard MD5. Rather than reimplementing this custom hash by hand, the AI emulated the relevant code in the client and produced the fixed internal password: AEF33093...DA1E With this value, it decrypted the file with Blowfish and restored its original bytes. In other words, the product not only failed to prevent copying; its files could be recovered without knowing the password. The static work took about two minutes to unpack the installer and another seven minutes to analyze its cryptography, requiring two prompts from me. Once I supplied the protected drive, the AI needed about 26 minutes and six short prompts–mostly confirmations about the mounted drive, test password, and analysis direction–to extract the hidden file, recover KakaSoft’s modified MD5 construction, and prove passwordless decryption. Nexcopy The second new target was Nexcopy Copy Secure , provisioned with Drive Wizard 1.0.81. The drive included both Windows and macOS viewers. The Mac viewer retained useful Objective-C method names, making its design particularly easy to follow. After plugging the protected drive into my Mac, those two viewers were all Finder showed: The protected content was encrypted this time with three-key Triple-DES in CBC mode. The problem was again how the key was stored. The drive contained an encrypted configuration file. The viewer opened it with this fixed 32-byte certificate embedded in the application: 83E89F19...A56F Both the 324-byte configuration and the 140-byte protected test.txt began with the same 36-byte ASCII marker. Here is the complete encrypted test.txt container: 00000000: 31 42 46 37 41 38 41 30 2d 36 45 42 46 2d 34 36 1BF7A8A0-6EBF-46 00000010: 42 38 2d 38 46 31 44 2d 35 35 41 44 42 36 41 46 B8-8F1D-55ADB6AF 00000020: 42 35 44 32 3b 2f 7e af c0 8f 84 c4 7f 45 fc d6 B5D2;/~......E.. 00000030: f8 68 27 bc 73 7a 3b 7a 33 c7 9e f0 46 da 70 04 .h'.sz;z3...F.p. 00000040: 53 44 46 4e 61 aa ea b9 aa d4 75 19 e8 32 b7 06 SDFNa.....u..2.. 00000050: 29 d0 3c f8 04 d7 af da c3 ab ae 46 87 a1 68 fd ).<........F..h. 00000060: 1e 9c 04 18 3c be 27 51 72 82 de 8b 5d 5c 49 98 ....<.'Qr...]\I. 00000070: c3 97 97 91 d0 10 b0 01 e1 1c 38 49 9a fc e2 6b ..........8I...k 00000080: 72 8d 45 8b 58 48 8f e6 9b 4f f6 02 r.E.XH...O.. The first 36 bytes are the marker; the remaining 104 bytes are padded 3DES-CBC ciphertext. The encrypted configuration used the same marker followed by 288 ciphertext bytes. Decrypting it with the embedded certificate produced: vid=FA6E pid="8598" prefix="7015A1496E" error_msg="Please contact [company information here] for an XXXXXXX." key="6CF96891F31A329CED2B33171D6518740AD1212B687CDACE892962F7C59F7172" password="123456" start=\Mac Viewer.app\Data The key field was the content certificate: a 24-byte 3DES key followed by an 8-byte IV. The password was a separate UI setting. fixed value in viewer ↓ encrypted configuration ↓ content key + IV ──→ protected-file decryption UI password ──→ string comparison in the viewer USB identifiers ──→ software device check The password and device checks only controlled whether the official viewer continued. They were not inputs to the file key. In fact, the Mac viewer retrieved the stored password and compared it directly with the entered text using isEqualToString: . With the content key and IV, the AI decrypted the ciphertext and restored its original contents. Nexcopy also attempted to enforce copy protection in the viewers. The code enumerated processes, intercepted screenshot-related keys, used clipboard APIs, and looked for applications such as ScreenFlow, Camtasia, Debut, Grab, and QuickTime. Those checks may discourage casual copying, but they do not protect the content key from someone who can inspect the viewer and reproduce its decryption. Altogether, the AI took about ten minutes and five prompts from me to unpack the installer, trace the cryptography, and identify the key-management failure. Conclusion KakaSoft and Nexcopy failed at two levels. They did not keep their copy-protection promise, and they did not even encrypt the files securely. In both cases, an attacker can recover and decrypt the protected files without knowing the user-chosen password. AI is improving rapidly, and in my experience it has already accelerated reverse engineering and vulnerability research significantly. These three examples show that, with minimal prompting, AI can independently produce valuable research results in remarkably little time. I am especially impressed by how quickly it locates the relevant code–a task that often consumes a substantial part of a human reverse engineer’s time. If you have not tried this workflow, you should. One easy way to get started is to download Binary Ninja Free and set up its MCP server –or ask your AI agent to do it for you!

00000280: 00 00 00 0e 6b 61 6b 61 65 6e 63 72 79 70 74 69  ....kakaencrypti
00000290: 6f 6e 08 42 6c 6f 77 46 69 73 68                 on.BlowFish

The first eight bytes are a random salt, the next eight are the Blowfish CBC IV, and the ciphertext begins at offset 0x10. The final 75 bytes start at 0x250. This trailer contains a 32-character verifier followed by the readable strings kakaencryption and BlowFish:

8-byte salt | 8-byte IV | Blowfish ciphertext | 75-byte trailer

The client was a 32-bit Delphi program. The AI followed its TBlowfishEncryption class to learn how those bytes were decrypted. Each file had its own salt and IV. The fatal problem was how the key was derived:

internal password = modified MD5 of an embedded seed
file key          = RIPEMD-128(salt || internal password)
plaintext         = Blowfish-CBC-Decrypt(file key, IV, ciphertext)

The first hash was recognizably based on MD5, but it was not standard MD5. Here are the first eight operations of the third round in a vanilla implementation:

HH(a, b, c, d, x[ 5],  4, 0xfffa3942);
HH(d, a, b, c, x[ 8], 11, 0x8771f681);
HH(c, d, a, b, x[11], 16, 0x6d9d6122);
HH(b, c, d, a, x[14], 23, 0xfde5380c);
HH(a, b, c, d, x[ 1],  4, 0xa4beea44);
HH(d, a, b, c, x[ 4], 11, 0x4bdecfa9);
HH(c, d, a, b, x[ 7], 16, 0xf6bb4b60);
HH(b, c, d, a, x[10], 23, 0xbebfbc70);

The rotation counts repeat 4, 11, 16, 23. KakaSoft kept the same constants and message order, but its corresponding calls use 4, 11, 16, 16, 4, 11, 11, 4. The changed arguments are visible in the decompiled client:

Vanilla digest rendering normally looks like this:

static const char hex[] = "0123456789ABCDEF";
out[i * 2]     = hex[digest[i] >> 4];
out[i * 2 + 1] = hex[digest[i] & 0x0f];

KakaSoft performs the same lookup with 1903642857ACBEDF instead:

This second change is only character substitution; the altered rotations are what make the raw digest differ from standard MD5.

Rather than reimplementing this custom hash by hand, the AI emulated the relevant code in the client and produced the fixed internal password:

AEF33093...DA1E

With this value, it decrypted the file with Blowfish and restored its original bytes. In other words, the product not only failed to prevent copying; its files could be recovered without knowing the password.

The static work took about two minutes to unpack the installer and another seven minutes to analyze its cryptography, requiring two prompts from me. Once I supplied the protected drive, the AI needed about 26 minutes and six short prompts–mostly confirmations about the mounted drive, test password, and analysis direction–to extract the hidden file, recover KakaSoft’s modified MD5 construction, and prove passwordless decryption.

Nexcopy

The second new target was Nexcopy Copy Secure, provisioned with Drive Wizard 1.0.81. The drive included both Windows and macOS viewers. The Mac viewer retained useful Objective-C method names, making its design particularly easy to follow.

After plugging the protected drive into my Mac, those two viewers were all Finder showed:

The protected content was encrypted this time with three-key Triple-DES in CBC mode. The problem was again how the key was stored.

The drive contained an encrypted configuration file. The viewer opened it with this fixed 32-byte certificate embedded in the application:

83E89F19...A56F

Both the 324-byte configuration and the 140-byte protected test.txt began with the same 36-byte ASCII marker. Here is the complete encrypted test.txt container:

00000000: 31 42 46 37 41 38 41 30 2d 36 45 42 46 2d 34 36  1BF7A8A0-6EBF-46
00000010: 42 38 2d 38 46 31 44 2d 35 35 41 44 42 36 41 46  B8-8F1D-55ADB6AF
00000020: 42 35 44 32 3b 2f 7e af c0 8f 84 c4 7f 45 fc d6  B5D2;/~......E..
00000030: f8 68 27 bc 73 7a 3b 7a 33 c7 9e f0 46 da 70 04  .h'.sz;z3...F.p.
00000040: 53 44 46 4e 61 aa ea b9 aa d4 75 19 e8 32 b7 06  SDFNa.....u..2..
00000050: 29 d0 3c f8 04 d7 af da c3 ab ae 46 87 a1 68 fd  ).<........F..h.
00000060: 1e 9c 04 18 3c be 27 51 72 82 de 8b 5d 5c 49 98  ....<.'Qr...]\I.
00000070: c3 97 97 91 d0 10 b0 01 e1 1c 38 49 9a fc e2 6b  ..........8I...k
00000080: 72 8d 45 8b 58 48 8f e6 9b 4f f6 02              r.E.XH...O..

The first 36 bytes are the marker; the remaining 104 bytes are padded 3DES-CBC ciphertext. The encrypted configuration used the same marker followed by 288 ciphertext bytes. Decrypting it with the embedded certificate produced:

vid=FA6E
pid="8598"
prefix="7015A1496E"
error_msg="Please contact [company information here] for an XXXXXXX."
key="6CF96891F31A329CED2B33171D6518740AD1212B687CDACE892962F7C59F7172"
password="123456"
start=\Mac Viewer.app\Data

The key field was the content certificate: a 24-byte 3DES key followed by an 8-byte IV. The password was a separate UI setting.

fixed value in viewer
        ↓
encrypted configuration
        ↓
content key + IV ──→ protected-file decryption
UI password       ──→ string comparison in the viewer
USB identifiers   ──→ software device check

The password and device checks only controlled whether the official viewer continued. They were not inputs to the file key. In fact, the Mac viewer retrieved the stored password and compared it directly with the entered text using isEqualToString:.

With the content key and IV, the AI decrypted the ciphertext and restored its original contents.

Nexcopy also attempted to enforce copy protection in the viewers. The code enumerated processes, intercepted screenshot-related keys, used clipboard APIs, and looked for applications such as ScreenFlow, Camtasia, Debut, Grab, and QuickTime. Those checks may discourage casual copying, but they do not protect the content key from someone who can inspect the viewer and reproduce its decryption.

Altogether, the AI took about ten minutes and five prompts from me to unpack the installer, trace the cryptography, and identify the key-management failure.

Conclusion

KakaSoft and Nexcopy failed at two levels. They did not keep their copy-protection promise, and they did not even encrypt the files securely. In both cases, an attacker can recover and decrypt the protected files without knowing the user-chosen password.

AI is improving rapidly, and in my experience it has already accelerated reverse engineering and vulnerability research significantly. These three examples show that, with minimal prompting, AI can independently produce valuable research results in remarkably little time. I am especially impressed by how quickly it locates the relevant code–a task that often consumes a substantial part of a human reverse engineer’s time.

If you have not tried this workflow, you should. One easy way to get started is to download Binary Ninja Free and set up its MCP server–or ask your AI agent to do it for you!

items.title: FBI Suspects Cybersecurity Executive Helped ShinyHunters Run Extortion Website
items.summary: Federal investigators suspect an executive at a United States consulting firm helped ShinyHunters operate a website used to pressure hacked companies into paying ransom demands. The allegation raises questions about whether trusted ransomware advisers crossed from helping victims into supporting the criminals demanding payment for stolen data. The suspected website operator has not been publicly named or charged. Separately, the FBI arrested Edward Dubrovsky, a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive , on October 8 in Pennsylvania. Reporting does not establish that Dubrovsky operated the website, and allegations against him remain unproven as the federal investigation continues into his conduct. The website, shinywire[.]com, reportedly operated from approximately May 3 through October 16, 2026. It listed nearly 100 organizations targeted by ShinyHunters. Each listing encouraged the victim to contact the group, discuss payment terms, and avoid the release of stolen information, according to sources familiar with the continuing federal investigation. Shinywire Turned Stolen Files Into Payment Pressure Victim pages displayed samples of stolen files to support the demands. Organizations that did not engage within seven days reportedly faced publication of their data on a separate ShinyHunters leak site accessible through Tor. This setup used public exposure and deadlines to push companies toward negotiations with the hacking group. KrebsOnSecurity cited two sources who said investigators believe an executive at a large American consulting firm actively helped run Shinywire. The publication withheld the executive’s identity and the company’s name because no charges had been filed. It described the firm as having more than 1,000 associates across its consulting business. Dubrovsky’s arrest forms another part of the investigation. As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report , he faces allegations involving a conspiracy to threaten the release of confidential information for money and interference with commerce through threats. The sealed complaint limits public scrutiny of the conduct prosecutors attribute to the Canadian executive. The public court docket records his arrest and subsequent commitment to the Eastern District of Texas. It also shows that federal defenders were appointed and detention was ordered pending a hearing in the charging district. Those procedural records do not establish guilt or reveal the full evidence behind the allegations against him. Investigators reportedly gained leads after Dutch police arrested ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in September. Sources told KrebsOnSecurity that officers accessed recent Signal conversations while he was logged in. Those messages allegedly revealed frequent contact with Dubrovsky and an executive at the unnamed American firm now under scrutiny. According to the reporting, some exchanges suggested the executives knew details about new ShinyHunters victims before those organizations discovered their breaches. Another allegation is that Dubrovsky knew sensitive FBI information had been stolen before the group publicly threatened its release. These claims come from sources, not publicly tested court evidence. The investigation gained urgency after ShinyHunters targeted the FBI’s recruitment website in September. Reportedly stolen records included Social Security numbers, home addresses, medical information, and details about employee assignments. The sensitivity of those files increased the stakes beyond a standard corporate breach and placed additional pressure on investigators pursuing suspects. ShinyHunters commonly steals credentials through phishing and uses compromised accounts to take data from cloud services. It then threatens publication unless victims pay. This is extortion based on stolen information, which does not require encrypting a victim’s computers. According to KrebsOnSecurity, the FBI attributes more than $70 million in 2026 payments to the group. The case also highlights the risks of trusting promises to delete stolen records. In the PowerSchool breach and extortion case , a payment of approximately $2.85 million did not prevent later demands targeting affected school districts. Subsequent attempts used information from the same breach, showing how stolen records can remain a continuing source of pressure. KrebsOnSecurity also reported concerns about negotiators whose fees rise with the final ransom payment. CyberAcuView chief executive Mark Camillo said that arrangement creates conflicting interests because the adviser benefits from a larger payment. He called for greater transparency around fees, cryptocurrency costs, and the financial interests involved in settling demands. The FBI’s May 15 ShinyHunters advisory warned that attackers may combine stolen information with threatening messages, calls, and harassment. It advised people contacted directly not to pay or respond to demands. The bureau also urged victims to preserve communications and report suspected activity through IC3 or an FBI field office. For now, the website allegation remains a reported investigative finding involving an unnamed executive, while Dubrovsky faces separate criminal proceedings. Neither should be presented as a conviction. Public filings and further evidence will be needed to establish who supported ShinyHunters, what they did, and whether their actions broke the law. items.title: Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services to Test Stolen Credentials Without Paying a Cent
items.summary: Criminals have found a way to use open banking as a low-cost checking service for stolen bank and card details. In a campaign described by Group-IB, fraudsters abused a spend-management platform’s account-linking process to check whether credentials worked and whether linked accounts held funds. The platform did not lose money through stolen funds, but it unknowingly paid for the checks through its open-banking provider. The scheme also used the platform’s email and payment notices to send phishing messages. These claimed that a sale through the online marketplace Poshmark was waiting for verification and urged recipients to follow a link. Poshmark was impersonated and was not involved in the activity; Group-IB also said its systems had not been compromised. Analysts from Group-IB identified the activity while investigating abuse of a client’s fraud-protection environment. They assessed it as consistent with Classiscam, a scam-as-a-service operation, and described two linked uses of the platform: sending phishing messages and testing stolen credentials. This was a fraud campaign—not a report of malware infecting the platform. Group-IB’s findings are detailed in its report on the checker scheme. Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services Rather than send every message directly, the criminals used the platform’s own notification system. They added recipients to accounts and triggered messages that appeared to be genuine payment alerts. The emails borrowed the credibility of a real business service, while the message pretended that a Poshmark sale could not be completed until the recipient verified an account. The link led to a fake page designed to collect personal and payment details. Group-IB says the form could request names, card details, phone numbers, email addresses, billing addresses, one-time passcodes and card balances. Mock-up of a phishing message delivered through the platform’s own notification system (Source – Group-IB) Some versions also sought payment-wallet or online-banking details. A countdown added pressure by suggesting that the recipient had little time to claim the money. This use of trusted service messages echoes other cases where criminals abuse real platform notifications to deliver phishing content. Account linking served as a credential checker The second part of the scheme took place when an account tried to connect a bank account or card. Some spend-management services let users link a bank through an open-banking aggregator. With the user’s permission, this login-based process can return account details such as a balance and transaction history. That can help a legitimate user manage spending, but it can also confirm to a criminal that stolen credentials are valid and the account is active. The key detail is who pays. Group-IB says the platform may be billed by its aggregator for successful links, while the fraudster uses the result without paying that fee. The criminal gets a useful signal; the platform absorbs the service cost. In its estimate, a successful verification may cost about USD 0.30 to USD 1.00. For one million billable links a year, if 0.5% to 1% were checker activity, the illustrative annual cost would be about USD 2,500 to USD 5,000, using USD 0.50 per link. Group-IB observed the phishing and checking activity happening in parallel. That meant one-time codes stolen from victims could be used quickly during an account-link attempt. The same devices were linked to accounts sending phishing messages and accounts testing cards. On 27 April, device identity [496-] was associated with two accounts of each type; on 28 April, identity [524-] was associated with six of each. These links helped investigators connect activity that might otherwise look like separate incidents. Phishing form used to collect personal and payment data (Source – Group-IB) Many fraud teams look for losses on their own company’s records: unauthorised purchases, false reimbursements or account takeovers. Here, the platform was being used as infrastructure rather than directly robbed. The victims could be marketplace sellers or cardholders who were not even customers of the platform, and the cost could appear on an aggregator invoice rather than as a clear fraud loss. items.summary_html:
Criminals have found a way to use open banking as a low-cost checking service for stolen bank and card details. In a campaign described by Group-IB, fraudsters abused a spend-management platform’s account-linking process to check whether credentials worked and whether linked accounts held funds.

The platform did not lose money through stolen funds, but it unknowingly paid for the checks through its open-banking provider. The scheme also used the platform’s email and payment notices to send phishing messages.

These claimed that a sale through the online marketplace Poshmark was waiting for verification and urged recipients to follow a link. Poshmark was impersonated and was not involved in the activity; Group-IB also said its systems had not been compromised.

Analysts from Group-IB identified the activity while investigating abuse of a client’s fraud-protection environment.

They assessed it as consistent with Classiscam, a scam-as-a-service operation, and described two linked uses of the platform: sending phishing messages and testing stolen credentials.

This was a fraud campaign—not a report of malware infecting the platform. Group-IB’s findings are detailed in its report on the checker scheme.

Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services

Rather than send every message directly, the criminals used the platform’s own notification system. They added recipients to accounts and triggered messages that appeared to be genuine payment alerts.

The emails borrowed the credibility of a real business service, while the message pretended that a Poshmark sale could not be completed until the recipient verified an account.

The link led to a fake page designed to collect personal and payment details. Group-IB says the form could request names, card details, phone numbers, email addresses, billing addresses, one-time passcodes and card balances.

Mock-up of a phishing message delivered through the platform’s own notification system (Source – Group-IB)

Some versions also sought payment-wallet or online-banking details. A countdown added pressure by suggesting that the recipient had little time to claim the money.

This use of trusted service messages echoes other cases where criminals abuse real platform notifications to deliver phishing content.

Account linking served as a credential checker

The second part of the scheme took place when an account tried to connect a bank account or card. Some spend-management services let users link a bank through an open-banking aggregator.

With the user’s permission, this login-based process can return account details such as a balance and transaction history. That can help a legitimate user manage spending, but it can also confirm to a criminal that stolen credentials are valid and the account is active.

The key detail is who pays. Group-IB says the platform may be billed by its aggregator for successful links, while the fraudster uses the result without paying that fee.

The criminal gets a useful signal; the platform absorbs the service cost. In its estimate, a successful verification may cost about USD 0.30 to USD 1.00.

For one million billable links a year, if 0.5% to 1% were checker activity, the illustrative annual cost would be about USD 2,500 to USD 5,000, using USD 0.50 per link.

Group-IB observed the phishing and checking activity happening in parallel. That meant one-time codes stolen from victims could be used quickly during an account-link attempt.

The same devices were linked to accounts sending phishing messages and accounts testing cards. On 27 April, device identity [496-] was associated with two accounts of each type; on 28 April, identity [524-] was associated with six of each. These links helped investigators connect activity that might otherwise look like separate incidents.

Phishing form used to collect personal and payment data (Source – Group-IB)

Many fraud teams look for losses on their own company’s records: unauthorised purchases, false reimbursements or account takeovers. Here, the platform was being used as infrastructure rather than directly robbed. The victims could be marketplace sellers or cardholders who were not even customers of the platform, and the cost could appear on an aggregator invoice rather than as a clear fraud loss.

The observed activity also included disposable email addresses and a mix of hosting services, VPNs, data-centre networks, proxies and residential IP addresses. Group-IB found that accounts created from different device identities could share device and location fingerprints.

This helps explain why blocking a single IP address, or relying only on simple rate limits, may not be enough. Criminals also use automated Classiscam phishing sites to create convincing pages that collect financial information.

Group-IB recommends watching for suspicious activity at three points: account creation, the first outbound messages and the first bank or card link.

Signals may include disposable email use, repeated device or location fingerprints, rapid messages to unfamiliar recipients and account links soon after sign-up.

Reviewing these events together can help teams spot connected behaviour rather than treating each action as an isolated case.

Platforms can also set limits or extra checks for new or low-trust accounts, scan links before messages go out and review unusual spikes in account-linking volume. Finance teams can compare aggregator invoices and link counts against normal customer demand.

Group-IB reports that after its team became involved, a client reduced the time to block fraudulent accounts from several hours to under a minute, and stopped more than 230 accounts in May 2026.

items.title: Best Cybersecurity Thought Leadership Agencies
items.summary: The best cybersecurity thought leadership agencies help organisations turn expert insight into credible executive content, original research and influential industry commentary. For technical, practitioner-led thought leadership: Bora combines cybersecurity content expertise with a team that includes former security practitioners. For research-led programmes: CyberEdge Group and 10Fold offer examples of turning cybersecurity data into substantial reports and media stories. For audience intelligence and search visibility: CyberTheory focuses on understanding security decision-makers, while Content Visit and First Page Sage connect expert content with organic discovery. For media visibility and storytelling: Eskenzi PR and Code Red offer specialist cybersecurity communications; Merritt Group combines cybersecurity and government-market expertise; Column Five brings brand storytelling and visual content capabilities. Entries are listed in no particular order. This guide compares agencies that deliver thought leadership services, rather than individual cybersecurity influencers. What is a cybersecurity thought leadership agency? A cybersecurity thought leadership agency helps a business develop and communicate informed perspectives on security challenges, technologies and industry developments. The work can include executive ghostwriting, cybersecurity bylines, original research, white papers, interviews and expert commentary. Its defining feature is the substance behind the content: a useful argument, a distinctive interpretation or evidence that helps readers make better decisions. A cybersecurity PR agency typically focuses on reputation, media relationships and communications. A cybersecurity content marketing agency may support a wider range of educational and commercial material. Either can deliver thought leadership when it has the expertise and processes to develop original insights. For example, a basic article explaining ransomware is educational content. A research-backed argument about how organisations should rethink ransomware recovery can become thought leadership. The format may be similar, but the contribution is different. For buyers, the question is whether an agency can extract expertise, challenge familiar assumptions and turn that work into a sustained programme. How we selected these agencies Agencies were assessed through their first-party service descriptions, published research, client references and case studies. To qualify, an agency needed to demonstrate cybersecurity expertise or an established cybersecurity practice; services relevant to thought leadership, such as expert writing, research or earned editorial; and publicly identifiable client work or a substantive published research asset. The selection includes cybersecurity specialists and broader agencies with relevant experience. Their different levels of cybersecurity focus are identified in the comparison table. Agencies without demonstrable cybersecurity work, providers offering only routine content production, and individual influencers were excluded. Directory appearances alone were not treated as sufficient evidence. Entries are listed in no particular order. “Best for” labels are editorial assessments of likely fit, rather than performance rankings. Agency-reported results are attributed accordingly and have not been independently audited. Historical case studies demonstrate experience, rather than necessarily confirming a current client relationship. The guide will be reviewed annually to check services, supporting evidence and continued relevance. Best cybersecurity thought leadership agencies in 2026 The right shortlist depends on the work you need: original research, technically credible writing, executive visibility, search discovery or international communications. Agency Cyber focus Best for Named clients or public references Illustrative work or research Bora Cybersecurity specialist Technical, practitioner-led content Fortra, Thales, Tenable, Pentest-Tools.com Expert-led content programmes CyberEdge Group Cybersecurity specialist Research-led thought leadership Google Cloud Security: report sponsor Cyberthreat Defense Report Content Visit Cybersecurity specialist SEO and AI-search visibility IBM/Randori, Morphisec IBM red-teaming content programme CyberTheory Cybersecurity specialist within ISMG CISO audience intelligence Client cases anonymised; research partner Cyentia Institute CISO Engagement and Decision Drivers Study Merritt Group Dedicated cybersecurity practice Commercial and government markets Wandera; security references include Telos and Checkmarx Wandera media programme 10Fold Cybersecurity practice within deep-tech PR Research-driven earned media ForgeRock, AttackIQ ForgeRock Consumer Breach Report Eskenzi PR Cybersecurity specialist Expert commentary and media visibility Bridewell, Armis, Huntress, KnowBe4 Bridewell thought leadership campaign Code Red Cybersecurity specialist network Multi-region PR and research BlackFog Cross-border research and commentary First Page Sage Cybersecurity vertical within a broader agency Search-led thought leadership Cyberfort and Okta listed as client experience; Cadence case study Cadence technical content programme, outside cybersecurity Column Five Cybersecurity experience within a broader agency Brand storytelling and visual content HackerOne Cyberstrength campaign The profiles below explain the evidence behind these examples. Bora Best for: Technical, expert-led thought leadership informed by former security practitioners. Bora focuses on cybersecurity marketing and thought leadership. Its staffing differentiator is explicit: the team includes former cybersecurity practitioners alongside journalists, writers, marketers and PR professionals. Bora describes its combined cybersecurity experience as 150 years. Named work includes Fortra, Thales, Tenable and Pentest-Tools.com. Its published examples describe interviewing subject-matter experts, creating technical guides and developing market narratives from offensive security expertise. Bora also reports producing seven of Thales’s ten leading globally deployed content pieces in 2025. Its long-running Thales and Fortra relationships illustrate ongoing editorial support, including expert interviews and content development. The fit is strongest where writers need to understand technical detail while making an organisation’s expertise useful to buyers. CyberEdge Group Best for: Syndicated research assets and data-driven thought leadership. CyberEdge Group combines cybersecurity research, content and marketing services. Its offering includes custom research reports and competitive sales tools designed to support thought leadership and commercial conversations. Its flagship asset is the annual Cyberthreat Defense Report . The 2026 edition draws on responses from 1,200 IT security professionals across 17 countries and 19 industries. Google Cloud Security identifies itself as a sponsor, providing a named example of the report’s industry relationships. Source: 2026 Cyberthreat Defense Report, CyberEdge Group, LLC. CyberEdge is worth considering when a programme needs a substantial evidence base. Buyers should distinguish between sponsoring an existing study and commissioning proprietary research: these offer different levels of ownership, differentiation and flexibility. Content Visit Best for: Connecting technical cybersecurity content with SEO and AI-search visibility. items.title: WP2Shell Attack Lets Hackers Create WordPress Admin Accounts and Install Web Shells Without Login
items.summary: WP2Shell combines two WordPress Core flaws to move from an unauthenticated request to server-side code execution. It can let an attacker create an administrator account and install a plugin-based web shell. Seqrite’s October 16 analysis lists affected releases, but does not establish widespread live exploitation. The report says the flaws were disclosed in July 2026. The chain matters because it removes the login step. A public site running an affected release may be exposed before an owner sees a suspicious account or plugin. Analysts at Seqrite identified and documented WP2Shell, combining CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 into a route from a public REST API request to code execution. Their technical breakdown of WP2Shell explains the sequence and host artifacts. CVE-2026-63030 affects the REST API batch controller at /wp-json/batch/v1 , which processes several API requests in one submission. Seqrite says nested requests can confuse route handling and reach functionality that should require authentication. This flaw alone does not execute code; it provides a path to the second weakness. CVE-2026-60137 is an SQL injection flaw in the posts endpoint. The public author_exclude parameter maps to author__not_in in WP_Query . WP2Shell Attack According to Seqrite, poorly handled input can affect the database query. Chained with the route flaw, it lets an unauthenticated request reach the vulnerable query. The proof of concept then establishes an administrator-level foothold and remote code execution. In simple terms, SQL injection lets input affect a database query in an unintended way. Here, the first flaw helps an unauthenticated request reach that vulnerable query; the second supplies the database weakness. The chain’s impact comes from how the two issues work together, not from either flaw being described as a direct web shell by itself. Once code runs on the server, an attacker may have a way to make further changes beyond the WordPress dashboard. The demonstrated steps matter to defenders. The chain can create an unexpected administrator account, stage a ZIP archive in uploads, unpack PHP files, and move a plugin directory into wp-content/plugins . Wp2shell Exploit Flow (Source – SEQRITE) The plugin acts as a web shell, an interface for running server commands. Cybersecurity News has covered a separate WordPress account creation vulnerability and recent Comment2Shell vulnerability coverage , where different flaws also lead to account or shell risks. Seqrite describes temporary write checks under wp-content , followed by archive staging in wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ and extraction under wp-content/upgrade/ . Sample archive The sample archive is wp2shell_4e9b3641.zip ; extracted files and plugin folders use a wp2shell_ pattern. The report says httpd.exe may perform file writes, as it can during normal plugin operations. That process name alone is not proof of compromise. More useful signs are the WP2Shell filenames, new PHP files, and unexpected administrators. A WordPress poisoned plugin supply-chain incident also involved a web shell, but used a different delivery method. The report lists WordPress 6.9.0–6.9.4 and 7.0.0–7.0.1 as vulnerable to the full chain. Versions 6.8.0–6.8.5 are affected by CVE-2026-60137. It lists 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed. Upgrade to the appropriate fixed release or a later supported version, and verify the update completed. Restricting unauthenticated access to sensitive REST API features may reduce exposure where practical, but does not replace patching. After updating, review accounts for unfamiliar administrators, inspect plugin and cache folders for new or changed PHP files, and check logs for suspicious batch-endpoint requests. Look for temp-write-test-* files, wp2shell_*.zip archives, and wp2shell_ plugin folders. If found, preserve evidence, disable suspicious plugins, reset affected credentials, and investigate persistence. A patched version number alone does not prove an earlier compromise has been removed. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator from source Notes Endpoint /wp-json/batch/v1 REST API batch endpoint File pattern temp-write-test-* Temporary files under wp-content/ Archive example wp2shell_4e9b3641.zip Sample in wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ Directory pattern wp2shell_ Seen under upgrade and plugins directories PHP file pattern wp2shell_ .php Example extracted filename File activity New or changed .php files in plugins or cache folders Compare with expected site activity Account Unexpected administrator Check creation time Detection HTTP/CVE-2026-63030!DP.50405 Quick Heal network detection Detection HTTP/CVE-2026-63030!SP.50370 Quick Heal network detection Detection SL_A WP2Shell Suspicious PHP File Modification in WordPress Plugins Behavioral detection Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears.
