items.title: Hackers Use Generative AI to Build Custom Malware and Bypass Traditional Security Detection
items.summary: Hackers are using generative AI to build custom malware, rewrite harmful scripts, and make phishing messages harder to spot. The shift puts pressure on security tools that mainly depend on known file signatures, while helping ransomware operators move faster from their first foothold to data theft and encryption. The danger is not that every AI-generated program escapes detection. Instead, attackers can produce unfamiliar code more quickly, reducing the value of rules built around older samples. At the same time, better language support helps their fake emails and websites blend into normal business activity, making familiar warning signs less dependable. Researchers from Zscaler noted these changes in an analysis of AI-enabled ransomware published on October 16, 2026. Written by principal information security researcher Phil Hagen, the report describes how attackers use AI across social engineering, data discovery, and malware development. It examines broader methods rather than identifying a newly named malware family or a single confirmed campaign. Hackers Use Generative AI Traditional security products often compare files and network traffic against known patterns. These signatures remain useful for spotting familiar threats, but their limits become clearer when attackers keep changing the code that produces the same harmful result. Zscaler says generative AI makes those changes faster and easier to produce. Attackers can also build their own tools instead of relying on widely used programs that defenders already track. Related reporting on AI agents automating cyberattacks describes how code generation and repeated rebuilding can shorten attack workflows. For defenders, unfamiliar tooling means fewer dependable matches against previously collected samples. This also complicates efforts to identify who carried out an attack. Custom malware once suggested access to skilled developers or substantial funding. Zscaler warns that readily available language models now give smaller ransomware groups similar development options, making unique tools a weaker clue when assessing an attacker’s resources or identity. The distinction between AI-assisted development and malware that uses AI while running matters. Zscaler describes rapid script creation and revision, not proof that every payload independently rewrites itself. Coverage of malware that rewrites itself explores that separate development, where changing code can further weaken checks based on fixed file patterns. Better Phishing and Faster Data Theft The attack often begins before any custom malware runs. Generative AI can help criminals write clear emails, create convincing websites, and communicate naturally in a target’s language. This reduces obvious spelling and grammar mistakes that many employees have been trained to treat as signs of phishing. Zscaler also describes phishing messages that persuade users to run remote monitoring and management software. These tools have legitimate business uses, but attackers can abuse the access they provide to control a victim’s computer and potentially reach other systems. The initial trick can therefore open a path beyond one device. Web content creates another challenge. Research covered in GenAI-generated malicious web pages shows how code created after a page loads can change what users encounter. That browser-based technique is separate from Zscaler’s analysis, but it illustrates why reviewing only a page’s initial content may miss harmful behavior that appears later. Once inside a network, attackers can use AI to search and classify large amounts of accessible information. Zscaler says this helps them locate valuable material for theft or encryption faster than traditional scripts and playbooks. Finding sensitive data sooner can increase pressure on victims facing ransom demands or threatened public disclosure. The central issue is a shorter response window. Faster discovery and custom script development leave defenders less time to connect suspicious activity before files are stolen or encrypted. Detection therefore needs to consider what a program does, not simply whether its file matches a known malicious sample. Zscaler points to AI-based detection, combined security data, and faster investigation as defensive measures. Its report describes controls aimed at phishing sites, attacker command infrastructure, suspicious browser content, and ransomware response. These are vendor-described capabilities, not evidence that one product can stop every AI-assisted attack. items.summary: TL;DR: Financial institutions need to demonstrate that security controls are effective in production and that security investments reduce business risk. Across regulatory frameworks including NYDFS, OSFI, DORA, MAS and APRA, verified control evidence helps institutions demonstrate resilience and support accountable risk decisions. Thousands of Android Phones Ship With Hidden Malware That Disables Google Play Protections
items.summary: Thousands of Android phones across more than 150 countries have been found running malware planted in their firmware before purchase. The campaign, called Midnight Mimosa, targets low-cost devices and gives attackers system access without requiring owners to download a harmful app or click a suspicious link. The malware can secretly install and remove apps, load new code, and generate fake advertising activity. Before installing extra payloads, it temporarily disables the Google Play Store package, then restores it. Researchers assess this behavior as an attempt to avoid Google Play Protect detection, rather than proof that every protection remains permanently disabled. Researchers from PolySwarm noted the malware’s firmware-level access in their Midnight Mimosa research report, published October 19. Their analysis draws on Bitdefender’s investigation, which observed thousands of infected devices over roughly two years. Mexico, France, and Italy had the highest observed counts, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil, and Spain. Those figures describe observed infections, not confirmed targeting. Thousands of Android Phones Ship With Hidden Malware The infection starts with a malicious system application signed with an Android platform certificate. This trusted position lets it install packages, remove applications, grant permissions, and change protected settings. Earlier cases of preinstalled Android phone malware show why checking downloaded apps alone cannot address threats already embedded in a device’s software. The component hides its main functions inside a native library. When loaded, that library uses RC4 encryption to unpack a concealed Java framework. The framework then contacts command-and-control servers, receives settings, and downloads DEX or JAR plugins. These are Android code modules that let operators change the malware’s behavior without replacing the original system application. Different plugins handle advertising fraud and silent app installation. Some generate fake ad views, clicks, and conversion events through hidden windows and automated actions. The activity appears to come from ordinary tools, including weather apps, app lockers, text scanners, and file managers. Bitdefender identified at least 32 disguised applications within the wider payload network. How the Malware Evades Checks Temporarily disabling the Play Store creates a window for installing additional software while attempting to avoid detection. Some malicious apps also falsely list Google Play as their installer, despite lacking the signature block applied through Play distribution. That mismatch can help investigators distinguish a claimed installation source from evidence of how an app actually arrived. The technique adds detail to earlier Midnight Mimosa firmware findings , which described how the hidden component survives while visible payloads change. Separately, researchers found 13 related ad-fraud apps distributed through Google Play. These shared malware markers and infrastructure, but did not have the same privileged access as the firmware-installed component. The enabler also includes functions linked to Accessibility, Notification Access, and SMS permissions, including ways to enable sensitive access automatically. Researchers did not observe these permissions being used for theft. However, the ability to fetch new code means the campaign’s future behavior cannot be judged only from the advertising modules already examined. Another payload contains proxy software capable of registering a device and opening two-way TCP tunnels. This could allow outside traffic to pass through an infected phone’s internet connection. The distinction matters: researchers confirmed the underlying capability, but did not observe actual traffic relaying during their documented test. An initially reported control endpoint was also later identified as a sinkhole. The wider risk resembles the abuse described in reporting on malicious residential proxy networks , where compromised consumer devices provide network access for other users. That comparison does not establish a link between operations. For Midnight Mimosa, proxy functionality could expose homes or workplaces to traffic they did not authorize. Affected devices included inexpensive MediaTek-based phones, counterfeit flagship models, and devices reporting identifiers associated with Doogee and Cubot products. Some firmware certificates carried identifiers associated with Shenzhen Zediel. Researchers could not determine where the malware entered the supply chain or establish that the certificate owner knowingly participated. Connections to Joker, Phantom, and Click malware likewise do not prove a shared operator. Removing a visible app may leave the firmware enabler able to install replacements. Cleanup therefore requires attention to the underlying firmware, not just individual payloads. Google explains that its app safety checks examine applications during installation and scan devices periodically, but this case shows why trusted system components also need scrutiny. items.title: NIS2 Explained: Requirements, Deadlines, and LogTotal Use Cases Across Europe
items.summary: What Is NIS2? NIS2 is Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the EU’s baseline cybersecurity law for organizations that keep energy grids, water systems, hospitals, logistics chains, food supply and digital infrastructure running. It replaced the original NIS Directive (EU) 2016/1148 and turned a loosely applied, sector-by-sector regime into a single framework with common obligations, common reporting timelines and real enforcement powers. So, what is NIS2 in practical terms for a security team? Three things. First, it defines who is in scope through size thresholds and two sector annexes, splitting covered organizations into essential and important entities. Second, it prescribes a minimum set of risk-management controls in Article 21, from incident handling and logging to supply chain security and cryptography. Third, it imposes a staged incident notification process in Article 23, with the first signal due to the national CSIRT or competent authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident. Because NIS2 is a directive rather than a regulation, every Member State writes its own national law. The core obligations are shared, but registration portals, supervisory authorities and reporting forms differ from Rome to Warsaw, which is exactly why a country-level view matters. Try LogTotal, free NIS2 Release Date and the Road to Compliance The directive was published in the Official Journal on 27 December 2022 and entered into force on 16 January 2023. Member States had until 17 October 2024 to transpose it, with national measures applying from 18 October 2024. Few made it: Italy and Belgium were among the handful that had laws in force on time. The Commission responded with letters of formal notice in November 2024, reasoned opinions in May 2025 and, on 8 July 2026, referrals to the Court of Justice of the EU for the remaining laggards. According to the nisd2.eu transposition tracker , as of 16 October 2026 a national law is in force in 24 of the 27 Member States. France, Ireland and Spain are still without one. For NIS2 compliance, the takeaway is that the clock is national, not European. Germany’s BSIG amendments have applied since 6 December 2025, Poland’s amended KSC Act since 3 April 2026, the Dutch Cyberbeveiligingswet since 15 August 2026 and Austria’s NISG 2026 since 1 October 2026. Each brings its own registration window, so a multi-country operator can be compliant in Milan while already late in Gdańsk. What the NIS2 Directive Requires The NIS2 Directive puts obligations into three buckets: governance, technical controls and reporting. Governance sits in Article 20. Management bodies must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures, oversee their implementation and complete regular training. Accountability no longer stops at the CISO. Technical controls sit in Article 21(2), which lists ten minimum measures: risk analysis and information system security policies; incident handling; business continuity, backup and crisis management; supply chain security; secure acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling; assessment of control effectiveness; cyber hygiene and training; cryptography; HR security, access control and asset management; and MFA plus secured communications. For digital infrastructure and ICT service providers, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 spells these out in detail, including explicit monitoring and logging requirements. Reporting sits in Article 23, and this is where SOC teams feel the pressure: 24 hours: early warning, including whether the incident is suspected to be malicious or to have cross-border impact 72 hours: incident notification with an initial severity and impact assessment and available indicators of compromise One month: final report with root cause, mitigation and cross-border impact A 24-hour early warning is only credible if the team can actually read its logs within hours, not days. Why the EU Replaced NIS1 with NIS2 NIS1 failed on consistency. Each Member State decided for itself which companies counted as operators of essential services, so two hospitals of the same size in neighbouring countries could face completely different obligations. Penalties were low and rarely applied, and incident reporting thresholds varied so widely that cross-border situational awareness barely existed. The threat picture moved faster than the law. Between the Commission’s December 2020 proposal and the final text, Europe saw ransomware take down hospital IT, the SolarWinds and Kaseya supply chain compromises reach thousands of downstream customers, and the February 2022 attack on Viasat’s KA-SAT network cut remote monitoring for around 5,800 Enercon wind turbines in Germany. That last case made one point very clear: an attack on an IT service provider can produce physical, OT-level consequences in a different sector and a different country. NIS2 answers with a wider scope, harmonised minimum controls, explicit supply chain duties, personal accountability for management and a common incident clock. It also formalises cooperation through EU-CyCLONe and the CSIRTs network, so a significant incident in Lyon is no longer a purely French problem. NIS2 Fines and Management Liability Article 34 sets the ceilings that national laws must reach at minimum: Entity type Maximum administrative fine Supervision model Essential At least €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Ex ante: audits, on-site inspections, security scans Important At least €7 million or 1.4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Ex post: triggered by evidence or an incident The turnover reference is the whole undertaking, not the local subsidiary, which is why group-level CFOs now read NIS2 briefings. Money is only part of the exposure. For essential entities, Article 32 allows authorities to suspend certifications or authorisations and to temporarily bar a CEO or legal representative from managerial functions until deficiencies are fixed. Authorities can also order an entity to publicly disclose its non-compliance. In practice, regulators look for evidence. An organization that can show when it detected an incident, which logs it examined and how it reached its 24-hour and 72-hour conclusions is in a far stronger position than one that reconstructs the timeline after the fact. What Is NIS2?

NIS2 is Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the EU’s baseline cybersecurity law for organizations that keep energy grids, water systems, hospitals, logistics chains, food supply and digital infrastructure running. It replaced the original NIS Directive (EU) 2016/1148 and turned a loosely applied, sector-by-sector regime into a single framework with common obligations, common reporting timelines and real enforcement powers.

So, what is NIS2 in practical terms for a security team? Three things. First, it defines who is in scope through size thresholds and two sector annexes, splitting covered organizations into essential and important entities. Second, it prescribes a minimum set of risk-management controls in Article 21, from incident handling and logging to supply chain security and cryptography. Third, it imposes a staged incident notification process in Article 23, with the first signal due to the national CSIRT or competent authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident.

Because NIS2 is a directive rather than a regulation, every Member State writes its own national law. The core obligations are shared, but registration portals, supervisory authorities and reporting forms differ from Rome to Warsaw, which is exactly why a country-level view matters.

NIS2 Release Date and the Road to Compliance

The directive was published in the Official Journal on 27 December 2022 and entered into force on 16 January 2023. Member States had until 17 October 2024 to transpose it, with national measures applying from 18 October 2024. Few made it: Italy and Belgium were among the handful that had laws in force on time.

The Commission responded with letters of formal notice in November 2024, reasoned opinions in May 2025 and, on 8 July 2026, referrals to the Court of Justice of the EU for the remaining laggards. According to the nisd2.eu transposition tracker, as of 16 October 2026 a national law is in force in 24 of the 27 Member States. France, Ireland and Spain are still without one.

Germany’s BSIG amendments have applied since 6 December 2025, Poland’s amended KSC Act since 3 April 2026, the Dutch Cyberbeveiligingswet since 15 August 2026 and Austria’s NISG 2026 since 1 October 2026. The NIS2 Directive puts obligations into three buckets: governance, technical controls and reporting.

Governance sits in Article 20. Management bodies must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures, oversee their implementation and complete regular training. Accountability no longer stops at the CISO.

Technical controls sit in Article 21(2), which lists ten minimum measures: risk analysis and information system security policies; incident handling; business continuity, backup and crisis management; supply chain security; secure acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling; assessment of control effectiveness; cyber hygiene and training; cryptography; HR security, access control and asset management; and MFA plus secured communications. For digital infrastructure and ICT service providers, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 spells these out in detail, including explicit monitoring and logging requirements.

Reporting sits in Article 23, and this is where SOC teams feel the pressure:

  • 24 hours: early warning, including whether the incident is suspected to be malicious or to have cross-border impact
  • 72 hours: incident notification with an initial severity and impact assessment and available indicators of compromise
  • One month: final report with root cause, mitigation and cross-border impact

A 24-hour early warning is only credible if the team can actually read its logs within hours, not days.

NIS1 failed on consistency. Each Member State decided for itself which companies counted as operators of essential services, so two hospitals of the same size in neighbouring countries could face completely different obligations. Penalties were low and rarely applied, and incident reporting thresholds varied so widely that cross-border situational awareness barely existed.

The threat picture moved faster than the law. Between the Commission’s December 2020 proposal and the final text, Europe saw ransomware take down hospital IT, the SolarWinds and Kaseya supply chain compromises reach thousands of downstream customers, and the February 2022 attack on Viasat’s KA-SAT network cut remote monitoring for around 5,800 Enercon wind turbines in Germany. items.title: How to keep your architecture intact when agents write the code
items.summary: AI agents are generating code at a pace that far outstrips any human's ability to review it. That shift moves the engineer’s job upward, away from typing lines in an IDE to governing overall structure. Agents can write a working function, but the bigger issue is whether the system that function joins still holds together six months from now. Matt Erman, Senior Software Engineer at Blackboard and author of the Manning book “Grokking Software Architecture,” joined Tom Howlett on episode 6 of The Next Commit. The discussion centered around a problem Matt has been working on from the architect's chair. His conclusion: the fundamentals of good software engineering still hold, but the way teams practice them has to change. What follows is his playbook for keeping architecture intact while agents scale output, and why verification has to carry the load that human review no longer can. Why an agent's intelligence is the problem, not the solution The common complaint about coding agents is that they are dumb. Matt turned this notion on its head, saying "[part] of the problem with AI agents is that they're too smart," and continued, "They know the entire internet. Everything that you could possibly know about architecture, the AI agent can know or knows." That breadth is exactly the risk. An agent with every architectural pattern in its training data, handed a vague task, will reach for all of them at once. "If you don't constrain it, it will essentially take a hodgepodge of all these different architectures or ideas and patterns and just mix them together," Matt said, "because it doesn't know what you're actually trying to accomplish." Most engineering organizations adopting AI tooling have discovered a powerful structural insight: constraint is actually the key to success. The more you narrow the solution space with architectural boundaries, the more an agent's knowledge becomes an asset instead of a source of entropy. "The more you can constrain it architecturally, the more you can constrain it with boundaries, the better your results are gonna be," Matt said, "because it won't allow the agent to go outside of those. Or if it does, it will fail the build and the agent will have to retry it." Human review cannot scale, so stop trying to scale it From Matt’s perspective, human code review has hit a wall. "AI agents are putting out so much code that human review is becoming almost impossible because you can't scale it," he said. "Even if you had ten people reviewing the code, all they'd be doing is reviewing code and not doing anything else." Add more reviewers and you add more failure modes. People get tired. They take vacation. They have a bad day and rubber-stamp a diff they should have questioned. Multiply that across the volume agents now generate, and human review becomes the weakest link in the system. Matt’s answer to these challenges is a shift in where you invest. "You don't optimize the code, you optimize the feedback loop," Matt said. "You basically scale the verification process around the agent instead of scaling the manual review process. Because that's what ultimately we'll be able to scale." The safety net shifts from human attention to automated, independent code verification . The loop runs the same way every time, at machine speed, across every change. It catches what a distracted reviewer misses, and it does not get tired. Fitness functions: the mechanism that holds architecture in place The load-bearing piece of Matt's verification layer is architectural fitness functions. They test something unit and integration tests cannot reach: the structural rules of the system itself. "You can write all the unit tests you want," Matt said. "Those will check your code... but they don’t necessarily check the architectural bounds." A fitness function does. It verifies that a controller stays clean, that a component respects its dependency direction, that nothing reaches into the database when it should go through the proper service. The reason this matters is cost. An architectural violation might not cause any visible problem for months. Then it compounds. "Over the course of time, your architecture continues to degrade until you hit a point where it just fails completely," Matt said. "When that happens, that becomes much more expensive to fix than fixing a random code bug, because those are foundational components that need to be redone and re-architected." A bug has a small blast radius, whereas architectural rot can take down the whole application. Fitness functions earn their keep twice. After implementation, they reject violations and force the agent to retry the right way. Before implementation, they act as an executable specification. Matt bakes them into the engineering guidelines his agent reads before planning, which also describe the target architecture. “So when it designs the plan, it already has [everything] planned out based on how the architecture should look." The agent arrives at the plan already constrained, so it rarely goes off track in the first place. When something does escape, Matt fixes it and then locks it down. "The one thing that is extremely important is that you not only fix it, but you also create regression tests around it," Matt said. Each defect that slips through becomes a regression test, a durable record that both the team and the agent can learn from. Break the work into phases you can actually verify Letting an agent run an entire feature in one shot creates a debugging nightmare. If tests fail at the end, you have no idea which part broke it. "You could have done something in phase three that directly caused a regression in phase one," Matt said. "You have no idea where you're starting from." His process splits every feature into phases, each one a clean commit boundary. Each phase has to meet the same bar as the full feature. “All the tests have to pass, there can be no regressions from the previous phase," he said. A passing phase gets committed as a baseline checkpoint before the next begins. The payoff is containment. When a regression appears at phase seven and the earlier phases are green, the cause is confined to the latest increment. "If something goes wrong during that phase, you don't have to worry," Matt said. "You just go back, pull the last git commit and start over." This is the same discipline that has always defined good incremental development, now applied to keep agent output verifiable at every step. Architecture is a scope, not a job title One of Matt's most compelling ideas is that anyone who changes a system—regardless of their title—is, in effect, making architectural decisions. "Every time you make a change to a class or decide what table goes into a database or what service calls are made, those are all architectural decisions at the end of the day," he said. "The difference is just at what scope they're being made." A software developer makes decisions at the component boundary. A senior engineer works at the application boundary. An architect looks at the whole system. Same kind of decision, different scope. That framing matters even more in the agentic era, because the engineer’s value is moving up the chain. "Instead of the engineer writing code at a lower level, the value of the engineer actually moves up into the architectural judgment," Matt said. He described architectural growth as three stages: Awareness comes first: understanding how a change ripples through the system, who the downstream consumers are, what happens when something gets called. Alignment follows, as your work starts fitting the system's intent and you understand how things are done and why. Accountability is earned last. "As you start building the trust, eventually they'll start giving you more accountability," Matt said. "It's something that you earn over time." That trust, critically, does not extend to the agent. "You don't trust the AI agent blindly, but you trust the verification system you build around the agent," Matt said. "If you don't trust the verification system that you've built, then it's probably not good enough." The engineer owns the intent, the constraints, and the evidence. The agent operates inside them. The takeaway Matt built his entire control system by hand, one skill file and fitness function at a time. That works for a disciplined engineer tending a single codebase. It does not scale to an organization running multiple agents across dozens of projects, where the architecture has to hold to one standard regardless of which tool wrote the code. This is where his hard-won practice meets what code verification needs to become at scale. SonarQube is the independent verification layer for all code, and it works across all three loops. In the agentic loop, it feeds architectural context to coding agents as they plan and write, so the constraints are in place before the first line is generated. In the CI verification loop, it enforces the structure you intend in the quality gates your team already uses, and flags deviations as issues before they merge. In the code maintenance loop, it discovers your real architecture across the whole codebase, so it catches drift that builds up over months, not just the violation in today’s diff. Every change is held to one zero-trust, multilayered standard with an industry-leading low false-positive rate, whichever tool wrote it, so the engineer keeps the judgment while the verification layer carries the volume. Agents write the code now. You still own the architecture. The teams that encode that ownership into an independent, enforceable standard are the ones whose systems will still hold together a year from now. Listen to the full conversation with Matt Erman on The Next Commit .

Add more reviewers and you add more failure modes. People get tired. They take vacation. They have a bad day and rubber-stamp a diff they should have questioned. Multiply that across the volume agents now generate, and human review becomes the weakest link in the system.

Matt’s answer to these challenges is a shift in where you invest. "You don't optimize the code, you optimize the feedback loop," Matt said. "You basically scale the verification process around the agent instead of scaling the manual review process. Because that's what ultimately we'll be able to scale."

The safety net shifts from human attention to automated, independent code verification. The loop runs the same way every time, at machine speed, across every change. It catches what a distracted reviewer misses, and it does not get tired.

Fitness functions: the mechanism that holds architecture in place

The load-bearing piece of Matt's verification layer is architectural fitness functions. They test something unit and integration tests cannot reach: the structural rules of the system itself.

"You can write all the unit tests you want," Matt said. "Those will check your code... but they don’t necessarily check the architectural bounds." A fitness function does. It verifies that a controller stays clean, that a component respects its dependency direction, that nothing reaches into the database when it should go through the proper service.

The reason this matters is cost. An architectural violation might not cause any visible problem for months. Then it compounds. "Over the course of time, your architecture continues to degrade until you hit a point where it just fails completely," Matt said. "When that happens, that becomes much more expensive to fix than fixing a random code bug, because those are foundational components that need to be redone and re-architected." A bug has a small blast radius, whereas architectural rot can take down the whole application.

Fitness functions earn their keep twice. After implementation, they reject violations and force the agent to retry the right way. Before implementation, they act as an executable specification. Matt bakes them into the engineering guidelines his agent reads before planning, which also describe the target architecture. “So when it designs the plan, it already has [everything] planned out based on how the architecture should look." The agent arrives at the plan already constrained, so it rarely goes off track in the first place.

When something does escape, Matt fixes it and then locks it down. "The one thing that is extremely important is that you not only fix it, but you also create regression tests around it," Matt said. Each defect that slips through becomes a regression test, a durable record that both the team and the agent can learn from.

Break the work into phases you can actually verify

Letting an agent run an entire feature in one shot creates a debugging nightmare. If tests fail at the end, you have no idea which part broke it. "You could have done something in phase three that directly caused a regression in phase one," Matt said. "You have no idea where you're starting from."

His process splits every feature into phases, each one a clean commit boundary. Each phase has to meet the same bar as the full feature. “All the tests have to pass, there can be no regressions from the previous phase," he said. A passing phase gets committed as a baseline checkpoint before the next begins.

The payoff is containment. When a regression appears at phase seven and the earlier phases are green, the cause is confined to the latest increment. "If something goes wrong during that phase, you don't have to worry," Matt said. "You just go back, pull the last git commit and start over." This is the same discipline that has always defined good incremental development, now applied to keep agent output verifiable at every step.

Architecture is a scope, not a job title

One of Matt's most compelling ideas is that anyone who changes a system—regardless of their title—is, in effect, making architectural decisions. "Every time you make a change to a class or decide what table goes into a database or what service calls are made, those are all architectural decisions at the end of the day," he said. "The difference is just at what scope they're being made."

A software developer makes decisions at the component boundary. A senior engineer works at the application boundary. An architect looks at the whole system. Same kind of decision, different scope. That framing matters even more in the agentic era, because the engineer’s value is moving up the chain. "Instead of the engineer writing code at a lower level, the value of the engineer actually moves up into the architectural judgment," Matt said.

He described architectural growth as three stages: 

  1. Awareness comes first: understanding how a change ripples through the system, who the downstream consumers are, what happens when something gets called. 
  2. Alignment follows, as your work starts fitting the system's intent and you understand how things are done and why. 
  3. Accountability is earned last. "As you start building the trust, eventually they'll start giving you more accountability," Matt said. "It's something that you earn over time."

That trust, critically, does not extend to the agent. "You don't trust the AI agent blindly, but you trust the verification system you build around the agent," Matt said. "If you don't trust the verification system that you've built, then it's probably not good enough." The engineer owns the intent, the constraints, and the evidence. The agent operates inside them.

The takeaway

Matt built his entire control system by hand, one skill file and fitness function at a time. That works for a disciplined engineer tending a single codebase. It does not scale to an organization running multiple agents across dozens of projects, where the architecture has to hold to one standard regardless of which tool wrote the code.

This is where his hard-won practice meets what code verification needs to become at scale. SonarQube is the independent verification layer for all code, and it works across all three loops. In the agentic loop, it feeds architectural context to coding agents as they plan and write, so the constraints are in place before the first line is generated. In the CI verification loop, it enforces the structure you intend in the quality gates your team already uses, and flags deviations as issues before they merge. In the code maintenance loop, it discovers your real architecture across the whole codebase, so it catches drift that builds up over months, not just the violation in today’s diff. Every change is held to one zero-trust, multilayered standard with an industry-leading low false-positive rate, whichever tool wrote it, so the engineer keeps the judgment while the verification layer carries the volume.

Agents write the code now. You still own the architecture. The teams that encode that ownership into an independent, enforceable standard are the ones whose systems will still hold together a year from now.

Listen to the full conversation with Matt Erman on The Next Commit.

items.title: Google Gemini 4 Argon: An evaluation
items.summary: Gemini 4 Argon passes 85.66% of the tasks it is tested on. In our evaluation, it also produces more blocker vulnerabilities than blocker bugs. Passing tests and being safe to ship are different questions, and this model shows the gap clearly. Most of its findings are maintainability issues. Most of its severe findings are security issues. How was Gemini 4 Argon evaluated? Model: Gemini 4 Argon, high reasoning effort Language: Java Benchmark: the same Java benchmark we use for every model, covering HumanEval, MBPP and ComplexCodeEval. The run records 4,444 tasks. All of them are analyzed for code quality and security, which is where every density figure below comes from. Of those, 544 of them ship with executable tests, and the pass rate covers only those. Analyzer: SonarQube systematic code analysis. Complexity and code smell densities are per 1,000 lines of code (kLOC). Bug and vulnerability densities, and all category breakdowns, are per million lines (mLOC). Three terms worth defining first: Cyclomatic complexity: counts independent paths through a function. Cognitive complexity: a SonarQube metric that weights nested and deeply branched logic more heavily, reflecting how hard the code is for a human to read. Severity: the impact level a finding carries, inherited from the rule that raised it. It describes how much a finding affects the software qualities Sonar measures. It is not a prediction of how likely that code is to reach production. Gemini 4 Argon key metrics at a glance Metric Gemini 4 Argon Lines of code (total) 619,852 Functions 85,245 Comments density (% of LOC) 4.6% Cyclomatic complexity per kLOC 244.39 Cognitive complexity per kLOC 148.97 Bugs 347 Vulnerabilities 193 Code smells 9,626 All findings 10,166 Overall issue density per kLOC 16.40 Functional skill (pass rate) 85.66% Missing completions 1.55% What is Gemini 4 Argon's functional pass rate? The pass rate is 85.66% across the 544 test-backed tasks, which is 466 solutions passing and 78 not. Roughly one in seven fails its tests. Of all 4,444 tasks, 69 returned no usable code at all, which is 1.55%. That matters because 33 of them fall inside the 544 test-backed tasks, the same set the pass rate is drawn from. A task with no completion produces nothing to analyze and nothing to run, so it is not a failed attempt so much as an absent one. If you are planning around this model, treat the pass rate and the completion rate as two separate questions. How much code does Gemini 4 Argon generate? Gemini 4 Argon generated 619,852 lines across the benchmark, spread over 85,245 functions and 22,656 classes. That function count is the number to notice. It works out at 7.3 lines per function and about 3 statements each, with roughly 27 lines per class. This is code built from many small pieces rather than a few large ones. Fine-grained functions are generally easier to read and test one at a time. The trade is that following a single operation can mean moving through more of them, so reviewers spend more time on call paths and less on any individual body. Comment lines total 30,029, which is 4.6% of output. There is a reasonable amount of inline context for anyone picking the code up later. How complex is Gemini 4 Argon's generated code? Cyclomatic complexity is 244.39 per kLOC and cognitive complexity is 148.97 per kLOC. Read those two together rather than separately. Cyclomatic counts decision points. Cognitive weights the nested ones more heavily. Cognitive sitting well below cyclomatic says the branching is frequent but mostly flat, so there are many decisions and comparatively little logic buried inside other logic. Combined with 7.3 lines per function, that is a consistent picture: short functions, plenty of branches, shallow nesting. Neither figure tells you whether the code works, but both indicate how much a reviewer has to hold in their head at once, and shallow beats deep on that measure. What bugs does Gemini 4 Argon generate? It produced 347 bugs across the benchmark, a density of 560 per mLOC. Reliability severity Per mLOC BLOCKER 34 CRITICAL 34 MAJOR 310 MINOR 182 The severity profile is weighted toward the middle. Blocker and critical together are 42 findings, or 12% of all bugs, and major carries more than half the total on its own. For a team triaging reliability work, most of it sits in the tier that wants fixing without stopping the release. Bug category Per mLOC Concurrency / threading 94 Performance / structure 92 Exception handling 77 Type safety / casts 76 API contract violation 63 Resource / stream leaks 58 Null / data value 55 Pattern / regex 34 Control flow mistake 6 Uncategorized 3 Data structure 2 No single bug category dominates, and that has a practical consequence. The largest, concurrency and threading, is 58 findings, or 17% of the total. The next six all land between 34 and 57. Seven categories therefore cover 319 of the 347 bugs with no single one carrying the group. The consequence is that there is no single lever for bug remediation here. A team that fixes every concurrency finding has cleared 17% of the reliability work and left six other categories largely untouched. Concurrency findings still deserve attention disproportionate to their count. They are among the harder bugs to catch in review and to reproduce once they ship, because they depend on timing and on the environment they run in. The rules that flag them are narrow and specific: double-checked locking, a lock not released on every path out of a method, synchronizing on a field that gets reassigned, a counter incremented on a volatile field, and calls to wait or notify made without holding the lock. What security vulnerabilities does Gemini 4 Argon generate in code? Gemini 4 Argon produced 193 vulnerabilities, a density of 311 per mLOC. This is the smallest group of findings by volume and the most severe by profile. Security severity Per mLOC BLOCKER 35 CRITICAL 213 MAJOR 15 MINOR 48 Blocker and critical together are 154 of the 193 findings. Four out of five security findings sit at critical or above, which is the inverse of the bug profile, where the same two tiers were 12%. The blocker row is the one to sit with. There are 22 blocker vulnerabilities here, which is more than the 21 blocker bugs, even though there are 347 bugs and only 193 vulnerabilities. Put across the whole run, vulnerabilities are 1.9% of all findings and 28% of the blocker-level ones. Security is a small share of the work and a large share of the risk. Vulnerability category Per mLOC Cryptography misconfiguration 127 Insecure system resource handling 81 Inadequate error handling (I/O) 26 XML external entity (XXE) 23 Uncategorized 19 Injection attack 15 Hard coded credentials 11 Certificate validation omissions 5 Web API security misconfiguration 3 Path traversal injection 2 Where the bugs were spread thin, the vulnerabilities concentrate. Cryptography misconfiguration and insecure system resource handling together are 129 of the 193 findings, so two categories hold two thirds of the security surface. Both are well covered by automated analysis. Where reliability review has to stay broad, security review can be narrowed to two categories and still cover most of it. Crypto misconfiguration covers weak algorithms, insecure key sizes, and random number generators used in ways they should not be. The long tail is short but worth naming because the categories are specific. Hard coded credentials appears 7 times and path traversal once. These are small numbers, and they are the kind of finding where one instance reaching a production branch is the problem rather than the volume. How maintainable is Gemini 4 Argon-generated code? The run produced 9,626 code smells, a density of 15.53 per kLOC. This is 95% of all findings by volume. Maintainability severity Per mLOC BLOCKER 58 CRITICAL 2,691 MAJOR 6,321 MINOR 5,814 INFO 645 Major and minor carry 7,522 of the 9,626 findings between them, and blocker is 36. The volume is real but it sits low on the severity scale. The 1,668 critical findings, 17% of the total, are the part to prioritize. Code smell category Per mLOC Collection / generics parameter type 3,896 Design / framework best practices 2,559 Regex / pattern / string format 1,881 Cognitive computational complexity 1,721 Naming / style / documentation 1,497 Dead / unused / redundant code 1,366 Assignment / field / scope visibility 1,144 Control / conditional logic 994 Deprecation / obsolete API 329 Uncategorized 137 Structure / architecture 5 Collection and generics is the largest category at 25% of all smells. One caveat on reading any row in this table: each category groups a lot of rules, 17 Java rules in the case of collection and generics, and they are not all the same kind of problem. That row spans raw types and missing type parameters, redundant casts, and collection handling that could be simpler, so the total does not tell you how much of it is any one of those. How many tokens does Gemini 4 Argon use? Tokens Gemini 4 Argon Input 1,517,336 Output 6,362,719 Reasoning 11,886,018 Total 19,766,073 One accounting note before reading these. In this run, reasoning tokens are reported separately from output tokens rather than inside them, and the three figures add to the total. Not every provider reports it this way, so this is not a number to set against a reasoning figure from another model without checking first. The headline is the ratio. Gemini 4 Argon spent 11.9 million tokens reasoning and 6.4 million producing code, which is about 1.9 thinking tokens for every token written. Reasoning alone is 60% of the total spend. Per line of generated Java that works out at roughly 10 output tokens and 19 reasoning tokens. This is a model that deliberates, which is consistent with the high reasoning effort setting this run used. If you are budgeting for it, the reasoning side is the larger line item by a wide margin. What are the biggest risks of using Gemini 4 Argon-generated code in production? Three places to point verification effort. Security is first, and it is first by severity rather than by volume. There are 22 blocker vulnerabilities and 132 critical ones, in a group that is under 2% of all findings. Two categories hold two thirds of it, and both are well covered by automated analysis, so of the three risks here this is the one that narrows down cleanly. The spread of the bugs is second. With 347 bugs spread across seven categories of roughly the same size, reliability review cannot be narrowed to one or two rule groups. Clearing the largest category, concurrency, addresses 58 findings and leaves 289. Plan for breadth. Missing completions are third. In total, 69 tasks returned nothing, and 33 of those sit in the test-backed subset. This is not a code quality measure at all, which is exactly why it is easy to miss. A task that produces no code produces no findings and no test result, so it looks clean in every table in this article. Three takeaways: Most findings are maintainability issues. Security findings are the most severe. Code smells are 95% of the 10,166 findings. Vulnerabilities are 1.9% of them, but 80% of those are blocker or critical, against 12% of bugs and 18% of code smells. Bug remediation has no single lever. The largest bug category is 17% of the total, and seven categories are all roughly the same size. Reliability review has to stay broad. It spends more on reasoning than on writing. It used 11.9 million reasoning tokens against 6.4 million output tokens, and 19.8 million in total. The total is about two and a half times the GPT-6 runs we have published, which used medium effort where this run used high. If you are estimating spend, start from the reasoning figure rather than the amount of code you expect back. What to do next If you adopt Gemini 4 Argon, point automated checks at cryptography misconfiguration and insecure resource handling first. Together they hold two thirds of its security findings. Keep reliability review broad, because no single bug category carries the load. And track missing completions separately, because a task that returns no code never shows up as a finding. SonarQube flags the first two through algorithmic analysis on every change, at the speed the model writes code. Full evaluation results for Gemini 4 Argon, along with every other model we have measured, are on the Sonar LLM Leaderboard .

Gemini 4 Argon passes 85.66% of the tasks it is tested on. In our evaluation, it also produces more blocker vulnerabilities than blocker bugs. Passing tests and being safe to ship are different questions, and this model shows the gap clearly.  Most of its findings are maintainability issues. Most of its severe findings are security issues.

How was Gemini 4 Argon evaluated?

Model: Gemini 4 Argon, high reasoning effort

Language: Java

Benchmark: the same Java benchmark we use for every model, covering HumanEval, MBPP and ComplexCodeEval. The run records 4,444 tasks. All of them are analyzed for code quality and security, which is where every density figure below comes from. Of those, 544 of them ship with executable tests, and the pass rate covers only those.

Three terms worth defining first:

  • Cyclomatic complexity: counts independent paths through a function.
  • Cognitive complexity: a SonarQube metric that weights nested and deeply branched logic more heavily, reflecting how hard the code is for a human to read.
  • Severity: the impact level a finding carries, inherited from the rule that raised it. It describes how much a finding affects the software qualities Sonar measures. It is not a prediction of how likely that code is to reach production.

What is Gemini 4 Argon's functional pass rate?

The pass rate is 85.66% across the 544 test-backed tasks, which is 466 solutions passing and 78 not. Roughly one in seven fails its tests. Of all 4,444 tasks, 69  returned no usable code at all, which is 1.55%. 

That matters because 33 of them fall inside the 544 test-backed tasks, the same set the pass rate is drawn from. A task with no completion produces nothing to analyze and nothing to run, so it is not a failed attempt so much as an absent one. If you are planning around this model, treat the pass rate and the completion rate as two separate questions.

How much code does Gemini 4 Argon generate?

Gemini 4 Argon generated 619,852 lines across the benchmark,  spread over 85,245 functions and 22,656 classes.

That function count is the number to notice. It works out at 7.3 lines per function and about 3 statements each, with roughly 27 lines per class. This is code built from many small pieces rather than a few large ones.

Fine-grained functions are generally easier to read and test one at a time. The trade is that following a single operation can mean moving through more of them, so reviewers spend more time on call paths and less on any individual body.

Comment lines total 30,029, which is 4.6% of output. There is a reasonable amount of inline context for anyone picking the code up later.

How complex is Gemini 4 Argon's generated code?

Cyclomatic complexity is 244.39 per kLOC and cognitive complexity is 148.97 per kLOC.

Read those two together rather than separately. Cyclomatic counts decision points. Cognitive weights the nested ones more heavily. Cognitive sitting well below cyclomatic says the branching is frequent but mostly flat, so there are many decisions and comparatively little logic buried inside other logic.

Combined with 7.3 lines per function, that is a consistent picture: short functions, plenty of branches, shallow nesting. Neither figure tells you whether the code works, but both indicate how much a reviewer has to hold in their head at once, and shallow beats deep on that measure.

What bugs does Gemini 4 Argon generate?

The consequence is that there is no single lever for bug remediation here. A team that fixes every concurrency finding has cleared 17% of the reliability work and left six other categories largely untouched. 

Concurrency findings still deserve attention disproportionate to their count. They are among the harder bugs to catch in review and to reproduce once they ship, because they depend on timing and on the environment they run in. The rules that flag them are narrow and specific: double-checked locking, a lock not released on every path out of a method, synchronizing on a field that gets reassigned, a counter incremented on a volatile field, and calls to wait or notify made without holding the lock.

The long tail is short but worth naming because the categories are specific. Hard coded credentials appears 7 times and path traversal once. These are small numbers, and they are the kind of finding where one instance reaching a production branch is the problem rather than the volume.

How maintainable is Gemini 4 Argon-generated code?

One caveat on reading any row in this table: each category groups a lot of rules, 17 Java rules in the case of collection and generics, and they are not all the same kind of problem. That row spans raw types and missing type parameters, redundant casts, and collection handling that could be simpler, so the total does not tell you how much of it is any one of those.

One accounting note before reading these. In this run, reasoning tokens are reported separately from output tokens rather than inside them, and the three figures add to the total. Not every provider reports it this way, so this is not a number to set against a reasoning figure from another model without checking first.

The headline is the ratio. Gemini 4 Argon spent 11.9 million tokens reasoning and 6.4 million producing code, which is about 1.9 thinking tokens for every token written. Reasoning alone is 60% of the total spend.

Per line of generated Java that works out at roughly 10 output tokens and 19 reasoning tokens. This is a model that deliberates, which is consistent with the high reasoning effort setting this run used. If you are budgeting for it, the reasoning side is the larger line item by a wide margin.

What are the biggest risks of using Gemini 4 Argon-generated code in production?

Three places to point verification effort.

Security is first, and it is first by severity rather than by volume. There are 22 blocker vulnerabilities and 132 critical ones, in a group that is under 2% of all findings. Two categories hold two thirds of it, and both are well covered by automated analysis, so of the three risks here this is the one that narrows down cleanly.

The spread of the bugs is second. With 347 bugs spread across seven categories of  roughly the same size, reliability review cannot be narrowed to one or two rule groups. Clearing the largest category, concurrency, addresses 58 findings and leaves 289. Plan for breadth.

Missing completions are third. In total, 69 tasks returned nothing, and 33 of those sit in the test-backed subset. This is not a code quality measure at all, which is exactly why it is easy to miss. A task that produces no code produces no findings and no test result, so it looks clean in every table in this article.

  • Most findings are maintainability issues. Security findings are the most severe. Code smells are 95% of the 10,166 findings. Vulnerabilities are 1.9% of them, but 80% of those are blocker or critical, against 12% of bugs and 18% of code smells.
  • Bug remediation has no single lever. The largest bug category is 17% of the total, and seven categories are all roughly the same size. Reliability review has to stay broad.
  • It spends more on reasoning than on writing. It used 11.9 million reasoning tokens against 6.4 million output tokens, and 19.8 million in total. The total is about two and a half times the GPT-6 runs we have published, which used medium effort where this run used high. If you are estimating spend, start from the reasoning figure rather than the amount of code you expect back.

What to do next

If you adopt Gemini 4 Argon, point automated checks at cryptography misconfiguration and insecure resource handling first. Together they hold two thirds of its security findings. Keep reliability review broad, because no single bug category carries the load. And track missing completions separately, because a task that returns no code never shows up as a finding. SonarQube flags the first two through algorithmic analysis on every change, at the speed the model writes code.

items.title: Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
items.summary: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain . Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. Performance and memory improvements Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers: As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs , and we’re hoping to find more. You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration. By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster: Try tsrs TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm: npm install tsrs npx tsrs Why now? We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript. Why Rust? You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix. We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins. Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release. What’s next? Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint. Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc . We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

items.title: Google may add your number to all your accounts: How to stop it
items.summary: As Android Central reports , users have received unexpected emails telling them their phone number has been verified for secondary Google accounts. Like me and many others, you may have one Google account for everyday use, another for work, and a third for things you would rather keep separate. But if you’re using an Android phone, those accounts may have something in common that you didn’t intend or even know about: your phone number. Google’s own documentation confirms that phone number verification is on by default and adds your number to all Google accounts signed in on the device. This applies to both existing accounts and any you add later. Google says phone number verification helps support features such as signing in, account recovery, Rich Communications Services (RCS) messaging, and finding or securing a lost device. But it also means that a number you intended to use with your main account can become associated with a secondary account simply because both are signed in on the same Android device. If you deliberately left your phone number off a secondary account, this links it to your real identity without you knowingly making that connection. Your number doesn’t automatically become public, but Google gains another way to connect accounts you wanted to keep separate. This reminded me of an article I wrote about unexpected Google account connections: “ Google Play sign-ins can be abused to track another person’s movements .” Signing in to Google Play on one phone allowed me to see its movements in Google Maps Timeline. “After some digging I learned that my Google account was added to my wife’s phone’s accounts when I logged in on the Play Store, but was not removed when I logged out after noticing the tracking issue.” While that particular issue should be solved by Google’s move toward device-based Timeline storage, unwanted phone number associations need to be removed manually. How to remove your number from separate accounts Phone manufacturers arrange their settings differently, so there may be some differences in menu names and locations. We tried to make sure everyone can follow these instructions, but there might be makes and models where you get stuck. Feel free to ask in the comments and maybe others with the same phone can help you. Step 1: Turn off automatic phone number verification This needs to be done on the Android phone itself: Open the phone’s Settings app. Tap Google . On some phones, this may be called Google services or Google services and preferences . Open All services . Under Privacy & security , tap Phone number verification . Turn off Verify phone numbers automatically , or the equivalent verification switch shown on your phone. Turning this off does not remove numbers already added to your accounts. Step 2: Check which accounts already have your number This step can be done in a browser, so should be the same for everyone. Open a browser and type myaccount.google.com into the address bar. Check the account picture or initial in the top-right corner. Make sure you are looking at the account you want to inspect. Select Personal info . Find Contact info , then select Phone . Depending on the layout, you may see Phone directly. Select any number listed to review its details and how it is used. To remove the number from that account, select the delete icon and follow the on-screen instructions. Repeat for each account you want to check. Step 3: Check for other uses of the number There’s a wrinkle. Google says changing a number in your Google Account only affects some services. Other services, such as 2-Step Verification , may use the number separately and may not all appear on the Phone page. On each account you are cleaning up: Check the number’s Usage section on the Phone page to see which services are listed. Visit Security or Security & sign-in and review your recovery phone and 2-Step Verification settings. If you use another Google service that has its own phone number settings, check those settings too. If your goal is to remove the number entirely from a particular account, don’t assume deleting it from Personal info has removed every separate use. Check those security settings as well, but make sure to keep a working alternative sign-in and recovery method before removing the number. Android Central reports that some users say automatic verification switches itself back on after they disable it. Those are user reports, not confirmation that this happens on every phone. But if you’re concerned, check the setting again later. Scammers know more about you than you think. Malwarebytes Mobile Security protects you from phishing , scam texts, malicious sites, and more. We tried to make sure everyone can follow these instructions, but there might be makes and models where you get stuck. Feel free to ask in the comments and maybe others with the same phone can help you.

  • Tap Google. On some phones, this may be called Google services or Google services and preferences.
  • Open All services.
  • Under Privacy & security, tap Phone number verification.

items.title: CVE-2026-110936: Siemens Software Center Flaw Exploited in ClickFix Attacks
items.summary: Siemens has confirmed active exploitation of a high-severity DLL side-loading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center, a desktop application used to download, install, activate, and update Siemens software. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936 and rated 8.4 under CVSS v4.0, the flaw stems from an uncontrolled DLL search path and can lead to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application. The vulnerability has already been weaponized in ClickFix activity linked by Siemens to the Romulus delivery platform. In observed attacks, threat actors paired a legitimate, digitally signed copy of Siemens Software Center with attacker-controlled DLL files rather than modifying the Siemens executable itself. Siemens stressed that its systems, products, and official update channels were not breached. Security teams looking for CVE-2026-110936 detection content can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation, DLL side-loading, suspicious process execution, and related post-compromise behavior. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunt for emerging malicious activity. To Detect CVE-2026-110936 exploitation and related attack patterns, defenders should prioritize behavior-based analytics instead of relying exclusively on hashes of the signed Siemens executable. SOC Prime detections can be applied across multiple SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake technologies and aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK® framework. Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect and Uncoder AI capabilities to transform fresh threat intelligence and indicators into hunting queries, refine detection logic, and accelerate detection engineering workflows. Contact Sales CVE-2026-110936 Analysis CVE-2026-110936 affects Siemens Software Center versions earlier than 4.0.9.8. Siemens classifies the vulnerability as CWE-427, Uncontrolled Search Path Element. The affected application can search an insufficiently restricted location for DLL files, potentially allowing an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted library in a searched directory and execute code with the privileges of Siemens Software Center. The active campaign demonstrates how this weakness can be incorporated into a social-engineering-driven malware chain. Attackers distributed a genuine Siemens Software Center executable carrying a valid digital signature together with malicious DLL files. Siemens said version 3.5.8.7, the latest release at the time of the observed attacks, loaded helper files located alongside the executable without validating them first. As a result, the legitimate Siemens executable itself was not modified. Instead, malicious functionality resided inside attacker-supplied DLL files that were loaded when Software Center started. This approach lets adversaries abuse the trust associated with a legitimately signed application while executing attacker-controlled code. The Hacker News reports that the attack chain used msiexec.exe to launch AllMyBasic.msi, which subsequently executed SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe. Siemens identified archive.dll as one of the malicious components associated with the campaign. Siemens has attributed the activity to Romulus, a multi-platform ClickFix delivery operation. ClickFix attacks typically present victims with deceptive prompts, such as fake CAPTCHA or verification instructions, that persuade users to copy and execute malicious commands themselves. Related Romulus activity has also been observed delivering LegionLoader and abusing legitimate signed applications from other vendors for DLL side-loading. The supplied reports do not describe a public CVE-2026-110936 PoC. However, proof-of-concept availability is less important in this case because Siemens has already confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks. CVE-2026-110936 IOCs published by Siemens include 96.62.218[.]59, used for payload hosting and command-and-control; wizardexpensive[.]com, also associated with payload hosting and C2; and 2.27.248[.]127, which was used to distribute the malicious AllMyBasic.msi package. The published details for CVE-2026-110936 also highlight several host artifacts that can help defenders identify compromised systems. These include SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe executing from AppData\Local\Programs, an SM Software Provisioning Service folder, files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB beside the executable, and an FTSuite directory containing ftc.uml under AppData\Local. Because the Siemens binary used by the attackers is genuine and digitally signed, traditional file reputation alone may fail to expose the attack. Security teams should instead correlate the executable’s location, parent process, adjacent DLL files, persistence artifacts, and outbound network connections. CVE-2026-110936 Mitigation Siemens addressed the vulnerability in Software Center version 4.0.9.8. All earlier versions are considered affected, and existing installations are designed to receive the patched release automatically when the application is started. Organizations should verify that deployed endpoints are running version 4.0.9.8 or newer rather than assuming the automatic update has already been completed. Organizations should also ensure that Siemens software is obtained exclusively through official Siemens sources. The company states that the malicious bundle involved in the campaign was distributed outside its official infrastructure and that no Siemens product or update channel was compromised. Security teams should block the known malicious infrastructure at DNS resolvers, proxies, and firewalls and retrospectively search endpoint and network telemetry for previous connections. Defenders should specifically hunt for SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe executing from AppData\Local\Programs, particularly when launched through msiexec.exe, and inspect for unexpected DLL files placed beside Siemens executables outside normal installation directories. Hash-based monitoring of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe alone is insufficient because the file abused by the attackers is legitimate. Detection logic should instead focus on anomalous execution paths, suspicious child or parent processes, unexpected adjacent DLLs, persistence mechanisms, and communications with known malicious infrastructure. If indicators of compromise are identified, isolate the affected endpoint, terminate the malicious process, remove unauthorized startup entries or scheduled tasks, and reset potentially exposed passwords. Siemens also recommends reviewing historical logs for connections to both active and previously used campaign infrastructure. FAQ What is CVE-2026-110936 and how does it work? CVE-2026-110936 is a high-severity DLL side-loading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center. The application can load DLLs from an uncontrolled search path, potentially allowing a locally authenticated attacker to place a crafted DLL in a searched directory and execute malicious code with the privileges of the affected application. In observed ClickFix attacks, threat actors packaged a legitimate signed Siemens executable together with malicious DLLs so the trusted application would load attacker-controlled code. When was CVE-2026-110936 first discovered? The supplied sources do not provide the exact date on which the vulnerability was initially discovered. Siemens publicly disclosed the flaw through advisory SSA-580366 on October 15, 2026, and credited Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon with reporting it. Siemens subsequently confirmed active exploitation on October 19, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-110936 on systems? Successful exploitation can result in arbitrary code execution with the privileges of Siemens Software Center. In the observed campaign, attackers were able to abuse a trusted, digitally signed application as a carrier for malicious DLL execution, making malicious activity more difficult to distinguish from legitimate software behavior. Can CVE-2026-110936 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Siemens Software Center versions earlier than 4.0.9.8 remain vulnerable. The risk is particularly significant because active exploitation has already been confirmed and attackers have demonstrated that the legitimate Siemens executable can be incorporated into ClickFix-driven malware delivery chains. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-110936? Update Siemens Software Center to version 4.0.9.8 or later and verify that the patched version is actually installed. Download Siemens software only from official sources, block the published malicious infrastructure, and hunt for suspicious execution of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe from user-writable directories. Organizations should also inspect neighboring DLL files, unusual msiexec.exe activity, unexpected persistence artifacts, and historical network connections. If compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint and follow established incident response procedures.
