CVE-2026-110936 affects Siemens Software Center versions earlier than 4.0.9.8. Siemens classifies the vulnerability as CWE-427, Uncontrolled Search Path Element. The affected application can search an insufficiently restricted location for DLL files, potentially allowing an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted library in a searched directory and execute code with the privileges of Siemens Software Center.

The active campaign demonstrates how this weakness can be incorporated into a social-engineering-driven malware chain. Attackers distributed a genuine Siemens Software Center executable carrying a valid digital signature together with malicious DLL files. Siemens said version 3.5.8.7, the latest release at the time of the observed attacks, loaded helper files located alongside the executable without validating them first.

As a result, the legitimate Siemens executable itself was not modified. Instead, malicious functionality resided inside attacker-supplied DLL files that were loaded when Software Center started. This approach lets adversaries abuse the trust associated with a legitimately signed application while executing attacker-controlled code.

The Hacker News reports that the attack chain used msiexec.exe to launch AllMyBasic.msi, which subsequently executed SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe. Siemens identified archive.dll as one of the malicious components associated with the campaign.

Siemens has attributed the activity to Romulus, a multi-platform ClickFix delivery operation. ClickFix attacks typically present victims with deceptive prompts, such as fake CAPTCHA or verification instructions, that persuade users to copy and execute malicious commands themselves. Related Romulus activity has also been observed delivering LegionLoader and abusing legitimate signed applications from other vendors for DLL side-loading.

The supplied reports do not describe a public CVE-2026-110936 PoC. However, proof-of-concept availability is less important in this case because Siemens has already confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks.

CVE-2026-110936 IOCs published by Siemens include 96.62.218[.]59, used for payload hosting and command-and-control; wizardexpensive[.]com, also associated with payload hosting and C2; and 2.27.248[.]127, which was used to distribute the malicious AllMyBasic.msi package.

The published details for CVE-2026-110936 also highlight several host artifacts that can help defenders identify compromised systems. These include SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe executing from AppData\Local\Programs, an SM Software Provisioning Service folder, files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB beside the executable, and an FTSuite directory containing ftc.uml under AppData\Local.

Because the Siemens binary used by the attackers is genuine and digitally signed, traditional file reputation alone may fail to expose the attack. Security teams should instead correlate the executable’s location, parent process, adjacent DLL files, persistence artifacts, and outbound network connections.

CVE-2026-110936 Mitigation

Siemens addressed the vulnerability in Software Center version 4.0.9.8. All earlier versions are considered affected, and existing installations are designed to receive the patched release automatically when the application is started. Organizations should verify that deployed endpoints are running version 4.0.9.8 or newer rather than assuming the automatic update has already been completed.

Organizations should also ensure that Siemens software is obtained exclusively through official Siemens sources. The company states that the malicious bundle involved in the campaign was distributed outside its official infrastructure and that no Siemens product or update channel was compromised.

Security teams should block the known malicious infrastructure at DNS resolvers, proxies, and firewalls and retrospectively search endpoint and network telemetry for previous connections. Defenders should specifically hunt for SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe executing from AppData\Local\Programs, particularly when launched through msiexec.exe, and inspect for unexpected DLL files placed beside Siemens executables outside normal installation directories.

Hash-based monitoring of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe alone is insufficient because the file abused by the attackers is legitimate. Detection logic should instead focus on anomalous execution paths, suspicious child or parent processes, unexpected adjacent DLLs, persistence mechanisms, and communications with known malicious infrastructure.

If indicators of compromise are identified, isolate the affected endpoint, terminate the malicious process, remove unauthorized startup entries or scheduled tasks, and reset potentially exposed passwords. Siemens also recommends reviewing historical logs for connections to both active and previously used campaign infrastructure.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-110936 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-110936 is a high-severity DLL side-loading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center. The application can load DLLs from an uncontrolled search path, potentially allowing a locally authenticated attacker to place a crafted DLL in a searched directory and execute malicious code with the privileges of the affected application. In observed ClickFix attacks, threat actors packaged a legitimate signed Siemens executable together with malicious DLLs so the trusted application would load attacker-controlled code.

When was CVE-2026-110936 first discovered?

The supplied sources do not provide the exact date on which the vulnerability was initially discovered. Siemens publicly disclosed the flaw through advisory SSA-580366 on October 15, 2026, and credited Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon with reporting it. Siemens subsequently confirmed active exploitation on October 19, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-110936 on systems?

Successful exploitation can result in arbitrary code execution with the privileges of Siemens Software Center. In the observed campaign, attackers were able to abuse a trusted, digitally signed application as a carrier for malicious DLL execution, making malicious activity more difficult to distinguish from legitimate software behavior.

Can CVE-2026-110936 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Siemens Software Center versions earlier than 4.0.9.8 remain vulnerable. The risk is particularly significant because active exploitation has already been confirmed and attackers have demonstrated that the legitimate Siemens executable can be incorporated into ClickFix-driven malware delivery chains.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-110936?

Update Siemens Software Center to version 4.0.9.8 or later and verify that the patched version is actually installed. Download Siemens software only from official sources, block the published malicious infrastructure, and hunt for suspicious execution of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe from user-writable directories. Organizations should also inspect neighboring DLL files, unusual msiexec.exe activity, unexpected persistence artifacts, and historical network connections. If compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint and follow established incident response procedures.

items.title: ownCloud at OSS EU 2026 and Why Community Matters
items.summary: Why community engagement is so important We had the privilege of joining the Linux Foundation’s Open Source Summit Europe in Prague earlier this month (7 to 9 October) as a sponsor. First, a big thank you to everyone involved for a wonderful experience! We also weren’t alone. The booth was staffed by a mix of folks from ownCloud and Kiteworks, plus people from our partners Collabora , B1 Systems and Cesnet . Having everyone in one place meant almost any question, from “how do I run this at home” to “how would this fit our infrastructure”, could be answered by someone who actually works with it every day. Our main goals were to re-engage with the community, (re-)introduce people to oCIS and ownCloud, and to listen. And oh boy, were we not disappointed. “I thought you were dead!” and “I’m so glad you’re still here!” were some of the things we most often heard from folks at the conferences and meetups we’ve attended this year, which makes sense, because unfortunately we dropped the ball in community engagement since the end of 2024, and we’ve apologized to the community and our partners for it. We let people down and working in a seemingly black box is the opposite of what Open Source stands for. So, for the record: yes, we’re still alive. But “not dead” is a pretty low bar, and being back in the same room as you reminded me why I fell for open source in the first place. But it only works well when people show up, talk to each other, and occasionally tell you you’re doing it wrong. (We got a bit of all three – and we sincerely thank you for that!) Here’s how the week went, starting a day before the summit with a room full of fellow OSPO nerds – and I say that with love. Starting with OSPOlogy Our week actually started the day before the summit, at OpenChain x OSPOlogy Prague . It was a full-day community event for people who work on open source management, supply chain trust and OSPOs, and it was a great fit for us. We launched the Kiteworks/ownCloud Open Source Program Office (OSPO) earlier this year, so it felt like being among our own people. David Walter, who leads our OSPO, gave a session there called “Two Forks and a CLA-to-DCO Rewrite: What Actually Rebuilds Community Trust”. Honest conversations about forks, governance and trust are rarely comfortable, but they’re the ones that matter most for a project with our history. We enjoyed the rest of the day just as much. Nithya Ruff’s keynote on OSPOs and open technology was a highlight, and so were the hands-on sessions. Dawn Foster’s roundtable on improving your OSPO with CHAOSS made the case for “strategy before metrics”, and one theme stuck with me: metrics need a narrator, because the same dashboard can lead two people to completely different conclusions. Ana Jiménez’s demo on using AI agents with CHAOSS security metrics gave us an interesting look into how she built AI tooling geared towards OSPOs. If you missed it, the presentations and roundtable notes are collected in the OSPOlogy GitHub discussion (because of course they’re open – the day was centered around OSPOs and our love of Open Source!) What we learned A lot of people think we’re a cloud hosting company. Given the name, that’s understandable, and we heard it often enough that eventually we stopped being surprised. Many people assumed we’d try to sell them a public cloud service and we need to fix that. One idea I’m toying with is a tagline like “Bring your own storage, create your ownCloud”. Nothing is final, so tell me what you think. Most people know ownCloud Classic, the PHP version. Plenty of folks were still running it in their homelabs and were happy to find out the project is alive. Somewhere out there is a quietly humming box in a closet that has been faithfully syncing files this whole time, and I love that. But most of them had no idea oCIS exists – another thing to work on. oCIS is fully open source written in Go, with no gated features. This is the one that surprised people most. ownCloud Classic followed an open-core model, so many people assumed oCIS would too. It doesn’t and everything is open and not gated. This is definitely something we need to put front and center, because this was the selling point for a lot of folks. (The fact that it is cloud-native and doesn’t need a database to run, also left quite a few people eager to try it) People were willing to try it. Many of those who hadn’t heard of oCIS were keen to spin it up and try it out. That was probably the most encouraging part of the week. (You can use the same ownCloud demo site we used to try out ownCloud and Collabora right now) People want to know what’s coming. Questions about the future of ownCloud Classic, where oCIS is headed, and where to find the public roadmap came up a lot. That’s fair, and it’s an area where we can and want to be more transparent. Lean or robust, your call One question came up a lot: how big is this thing, really? oCIS is as lean as you want it to be, or as robust as you need. Its modular, extension-based architecture keeps the core simple, so a small setup stays small and an enterprise can build up from there without the core getting complicated. Think of it as a very well-organized toolbox rather than a Swiss Army knife that never closes properly. That’s deliberate. ownCloud focuses on file sync and share, and we’d rather pair that with best-in-class integrations (document editing with Collabora is a good example) than try to build everything ourselves. Doing one thing well, and playing nicely with others who do the same, is pretty much the open source spirit. If you want to see how the extension side works, we wrote about the new ownCloud Marketplace, where Git is the app store . “So what’s your business model?” Once people hear that nothing is gated, the next question is almost always the same, and I love it. If the software is fully open, how does this work? The project itself is not productized. Rather we have funding through organizations that need enterprise-level support that we maintain and build the features they need, which then land in the open codebase for everybody. These are ongoing contracts from the ownCloud Classic era who have now migrated to oCIS. Kiteworks also backs the project as a corporate sponsor (they are our parent company now after all). For people with needs we can’t serve directly, we point to our partner ecosystem, which is one more reason we were so glad to have partners like Collabora, B1 Systems and Cesnet at the booth. There’s a bigger reason I care about this, too: digital sovereignty. With an open license, organizations know the code can outlive any single vendor, whatever happens to that vendor. For a lot of people we know that matters a lot. If you want the longer story of how we got here (the forks, the acquisition, and what we’re changing), I covered it in my FrOSCon talk, Bringing back the Open in Open Source: (Re-)Building Community after forks and acquisition . It’s a case study, and not always a flattering one (and that’s maybe the point). ownCloud Contribution spotlight Contributing doesn’t mean only writing code. Documentation, tutorials, extensions, forum help, bug reports and feature requests all count, and you can bundle several smaller contributions into one entry (a lone typo fix is lovely, but it won’t make the spotlight on its own. Typo fixers, we still love you). The ownCloud Contribution Spotlight is our way of saying thank you to the people who make ownCloud better. Entries for The Launch edition are open until December 1 and we’ll announce the winner at the Monthly Public Community Sprint review on December 18 who gets a ticket to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2027 in Barcelona. Afterwards, from January 2027, this will be a program where we feature and reward a new contribution/contributor every month. If you’ve contributed, or you know someone who has, join in. Highlights from the team For all of us, the best part was getting to interact with the community: hearing how people use ownCloud, what they want more of, and what they honestly think of the company and the product. The keynote conversation between Linus Torvalds and Dirk Hohndel on the last morning was also great, as was the OSPOlogy day. A few other things the team took away: The event felt community driven, not sales driven. Nobody was trying to push a subscription, and if someone wanted help with their own setup, they could get it right at the booth. Some of us were surprised by how many people already know ownCloud. It’s good to see how well the project is regarded in the open source world. Talking with customers and partners left the team convinced that investing in open source is the right call. Explaining things to others is a very efficient way to learn them. Some of us arrived knowing less about ownCloud than we do now. Most visitors seemed genuinely interested in talking to the people behind the products. Long days on your feet at a booth are exhausting, though we get better prepared each time. (Comfortable shoes: the real open source infrastructure.) And one more thank you, because it deserves its own line: Thank you to the Linux Foundation, the events team and all the volunteers for a great event and a wonderful sponsor experience. Everything ran smoothly, and the people we met were great. Come join us If we met in Prague, thank you. You reminded us why we do this. If we didn’t, there’s still a seat for you, and here’s how to grab it: Subscribe to our community newsletter: com/community-events/#newsletter Join the community at owncloud.com Try out a demo of ownCloud and Collabora : owncloud.com Join our monthly public community reviews , where we share what’s happening and listen to what you want next: com/community-events Join the contribution spotlight and let us thank you properly: read how it works Learn more about how the Kiteworks/ownCloud OSPO approaches open source: kiteworks.com/open-source Open source is only as strong as the people who show up for it. Come show up and engage with us.

A lot of people think we’re a cloud hosting company.
Given the name, that’s understandable, and we heard it often enough that eventually we stopped being surprised. Many people assumed we’d try to sell them a public cloud service and we need to fix that. One idea I’m toying with is a tagline like “Bring your own storage, create your ownCloud”.
Nothing is final, so tell me what you think.

Most people know ownCloud Classic, the PHP version.
Plenty of folks were still running it in their homelabs and were happy to find out the project is alive. Somewhere out there is a quietly humming box in a closet that has been faithfully syncing files this whole time, and I love that. But most of them had no idea oCIS exists – another thing to work on.

oCIS is fully open source written in Go, with no gated features.
This is the one that surprised people most. ownCloud Classic followed an open-core model, so many people assumed oCIS would too. It doesn’t and everything is open and not gated. This is definitely something we need to put front and center, because this was the selling point for a lot of folks. (The fact that it is cloud-native and doesn’t need a database to run, also left quite a few people eager to try it)

People were willing to try it.
Many of those who hadn’t heard of oCIS were keen to spin it up and try it out. That was probably the most encouraging part of the week. (You can use the same ownCloud demo site we used to try out ownCloud and Collabora right now)

People want to know what’s coming.
Questions about the future of ownCloud Classic, where oCIS is headed, and where to find the public roadmap came up a lot. That’s fair, and it’s an area where we can and want to be more transparent.

Lean or robust, your call

One question came up a lot: how big is this thing, really?
oCIS is as lean as you want it to be, or as robust as you need. Its modular, extension-based architecture keeps the core simple, so a small setup stays small and an enterprise can build up from there without the core getting complicated. Think of it as a very well-organized toolbox rather than a Swiss Army knife that never closes properly.

That’s deliberate. ownCloud focuses on file sync and share, and we’d rather pair that with best-in-class integrations (document editing with Collabora is a good example) than try to build everything ourselves. Doing one thing well, and playing nicely with others who do the same, is pretty much the open source spirit.
If you want to see how the extension side works, we wrote about the new ownCloud Marketplace, where Git is the app store.

“So what’s your business model?”

Once people hear that nothing is gated, the next question is almost always the same, and I love it. If the software is fully open, how does this work?

The project itself is not productized. Rather we have funding through organizations that need enterprise-level support that we maintain and build the features they need, which then land in the open codebase for everybody. These are ongoing contracts from the ownCloud Classic era who have now migrated to oCIS.
Kiteworks also backs the project as a corporate sponsor (they are our parent company now after all).
For people with needs we can’t serve directly, we point to our partner ecosystem, which is one more reason we were so glad to have partners like Collabora, B1 Systems and Cesnet at the booth.

There’s a bigger reason I care about this, too: digital sovereignty. With an open license, organizations know the code can outlive any single vendor, whatever happens to that vendor. For a lot of people we know that matters a lot.

If you want the longer story of how we got here (the forks, the acquisition, and what we’re changing), I covered it in my FrOSCon talk, Bringing back the Open in Open Source: (Re-)Building Community after forks and acquisition. It’s a case study, and not always a flattering one (and that’s maybe the point).

ownCloud Contribution spotlight

Contributing doesn’t mean only writing code. Documentation, tutorials, extensions, forum help, bug reports and feature requests all count, and you can bundle several smaller contributions into one entry (a lone typo fix is lovely, but it won’t make the spotlight on its own. Typo fixers, we still love you).
The ownCloud Contribution Spotlight is our way of saying thank you to the people who make ownCloud better.
Entries for The Launch edition are open until December 1 and we’ll announce the winner at the Monthly Public Community Sprint review on December 18 who gets a ticket to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2027 in Barcelona. Afterwards, from January 2027, this will be a program where we feature and reward a new contribution/contributor every month.
If you’ve contributed, or you know someone who has, join in.

Highlights from the team

For all of us, the best part was getting to interact with the community: hearing how people use ownCloud, what they want more of, and what they honestly think of the company and the product. The keynote conversation between Linus Torvalds and Dirk Hohndel on the last morning was also great, as was the OSPOlogy day.

A few other things the team took away:

  • The event felt community driven, not sales driven. Nobody was trying to push a subscription, and if someone wanted help with their own setup, they could get it right at the booth.
  • Some of us were surprised by how many people already know ownCloud. It’s good to see how well the project is regarded in the open source world.
  • Talking with customers and partners left the team convinced that investing in open source is the right call.
  • Explaining things to others is a very efficient way to learn them. Some of us arrived knowing less about ownCloud than we do now.
  • Most visitors seemed genuinely interested in talking to the people behind the products.
  • Long days on your feet at a booth are exhausting, though we get better prepared each time. (Comfortable shoes: the real open source infrastructure.)

And one more thank you, because it deserves its own line:
Thank you to the Linux Foundation, the events team and all the volunteers for a great event and a wonderful sponsor experience. Everything ran smoothly, and the people we met were great.

Come join us

If we met in Prague, thank you. You reminded us why we do this. If we didn’t, there’s still a seat for you, and here’s how to grab it:

  • Subscribe to our community newsletter: com/community-events/#newsletter
  • Join the community at owncloud.com
  • Try out a demo of ownCloud and Collabora: owncloud.com
  • Join our monthly public community reviews, where we share what’s happening and listen to what you want next: com/community-events
  • Join the contribution spotlight and let us thank you properly: read how it works
  • Learn more about how the Kiteworks/ownCloud OSPO approaches open source: kiteworks.com/open-source

Open source is only as strong as the people who show up for it. Come show up and engage with us.

items.title: Hackers Hijack 790 GitHub Repositories to Steal Cloud Credentials and AI API Keys
items.summary: A campaign called GhostAction has placed malicious GitHub Actions workflows in 790 repositories, putting cloud credentials, software-publishing tokens, and AI service keys at risk. The total is OpenSourceMalware’s count of publicly recoverable, validated repositories through October 9, 2026; it is not a claim that every repository leaked credentials or suffered confirmed misuse. The campaign abuses trusted developer accounts. Once an attacker can write to a maintainer’s repositories, they can add a workflow that runs when code is pushed or when someone starts it manually. This can expose secrets available to the workflow, turning a stolen account into a route toward cloud systems, package registries, and other projects. Researchers from OpenSourceMalware identified this latest stage while investigating a malicious PyPI package called claudecord and helping its maintainer respond. They found the malicious workflow and traced related activity across hundreds of repositories. Hackers Hijack 790 GitHub Repositories The newer workflow does more than read selected GitHub Actions secrets. It searches files in the repository for strings that resemble credentials, including AWS access keys and tokens for GitHub, GitLab, Google, Slack, SendGrid, OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter. It also scans reachable Git history, where a key removed from the current version of a file may still appear in an older commit. To obtain that history, the workflow uses fetch-depth: 0 . It then looks for credential-like patterns and, in some cases, gathers nearby lines around AWS key IDs. Those lines may contain useful context, such as a matching secret key or details about an account or service. The same collection steps can therefore expose more than a standalone key string. The workflow sends the collected data to attacker-controlled infrastructure over plain HTTP. Because the transfer occurs from a CI runner, it can resemble routine build activity unless defenders inspect workflow changes and outbound network traffic. For background on a previous GhostAction wave, see Cyber Security News’ GhostAction supply chain campaign report . The number reflects a campaign that has grown over time. GitGuardian reported 772 affected repositories between August 31 and September 30, 2026. OpenSourceMalware’s later review recovered 790 through October 9, including repositories that may not remain publicly visible. In a separate October 8 burst, Socket and StepSecurity reported activity across 346 repositories tied to two compromised accounts. These figures cover different periods and evidence sets, so they should not be added together. That burst included repositories owned by the kitao and henrywoo accounts, as well as Uber’s uber/athenadriver . The activity reached active projects, forks, and repositories that had been dormant for years, suggesting automated discovery of repositories the compromised accounts could change. The report says some workflows ran successfully, but it had not found malicious PyPI or crates.io releases linked to this latest burst as of October 9. Why removing the workflow is not enough A successful workflow run may expose credentials even if the file is later deleted. Removing it does not revoke a stolen GitHub token, invalidate cloud or publishing keys, or remove credentials from old commits. Teams should preserve relevant workflow files, run logs, commits, and audit records, then revoke the account credentials that enabled the changes and rotate every secret the workflow could access. They should also check package releases, deployments, and cloud activity from the affected period. For related context, Cyber Security News has covered GitHub Actions PyPI token theft and the financial risk of stolen AI service keys . GitHub’s secure use guidance for Actions recommends least-privilege access, review of workflow code, and rotation of exposed secrets. Requiring approval for sensitive workflow changes and limiting runner network access can add further checks. OpenSourceMalware also identified my-github[.]com , which resolves to the campaign’s current collection IP, as a high-priority indicator. The report says the domain is suspicious, but does not prove that the GhostAction operator registered it. A similarly named GitLab domain is listed only as a watch item, not confirmed campaign infrastructure. Defenders should preserve that distinction when creating alerts. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Context SHA-256 7fbd40446a82c77b23432c6ab73bd8595c98e90e4f4a473198b4d1256f3e8c4b claudecord version 0.3.2 artifact IP address 193.32.204[.]199 Current collection and scanning infrastructure URL http://193.32.204[.]199/?c=monami Newer workflow’s reported collection endpoint URL http://193.32.204[.]199:3000/api/workflow/receive?inj= Variant endpoint reported in seven repositories Domain my-github[.]com Suspicious domain resolving to the current IP; attribution not proven Domain pattern *.my-github[.]com Wildcard DNS; individual subdomains need corroboration Domain my-gitlab[.]com Watchlist only; not attributed to GhostAction Historical IPs/domains 170.39.218[.]2 ; 45.139.104[.]115 ; bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk[.]page ; objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk[.]page ; carte-avantage[.]com ; *.oast[.]fun Earlier campaign infrastructure Workflow paths .github/workflows/github_actions_security.yml ; .github/workflows/security-check.yml ; .github/workflows/security-audit.yml Reported malicious workflow paths; verify file contents and behavior Text markers AKIA_CTX_START ; AKIA_CTX_END ; send-secrets ; Prepare Cache Busting ; git log -p --all 2>/dev/null \| head -200000 ; curl -s -m 20 -X POST --data-binary Payload and collection markers identified in the report Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

To obtain that history, the workflow uses fetch-depth: 0. It then looks for credential-like patterns and, in some cases, gathers nearby lines around AWS key IDs.

Those lines may contain useful context, such as a matching secret key or details about an account or service. The same collection steps can therefore expose more than a standalone key string.

The workflow sends the collected data to attacker-controlled infrastructure over plain HTTP. Because the transfer occurs from a CI runner, it can resemble routine build activity unless defenders inspect workflow changes and outbound network traffic.

For background on a previous GhostAction wave, see Cyber Security News’ GhostAction supply chain campaign report. The number reflects a campaign that has grown over time.

GitGuardian reported 772 affected repositories between August 31 and September 30, 2026. OpenSourceMalware’s later review recovered 790 through October 9, including repositories that may not remain publicly visible.

In a separate October 8 burst, Socket and StepSecurity reported activity across 346 repositories tied to two compromised accounts. These figures cover different periods and evidence sets, so they should not be added together.

That burst included repositories owned by the kitao and henrywoo accounts, as well as Uber’s uber/athenadriver. The activity reached active projects, forks, and repositories that had been dormant for years, suggesting automated discovery of repositories the compromised accounts could change.

The report says some workflows ran successfully, but it had not found malicious PyPI or crates.io releases linked to this latest burst as of October 9.

Why removing the workflow is not enough

A successful workflow run may expose credentials even if the file is later deleted. Removing it does not revoke a stolen GitHub token, invalidate cloud or publishing keys, or remove credentials from old commits.

Teams should preserve relevant workflow files, run logs, commits, and audit records, then revoke the account credentials that enabled the changes and rotate every secret the workflow could access. They should also check package releases, deployments, and cloud activity from the affected period.

For related context, Cyber Security News has covered GitHub Actions PyPI token theft and the financial risk of stolen AI service keys.

GitHub’s secure use guidance for Actions recommends least-privilege access, review of workflow code, and rotation of exposed secrets. Requiring approval for sensitive workflow changes and limiting runner network access can add further checks.

OpenSourceMalware also identified my-github[.]com, which resolves to the campaign’s current collection IP, as a high-priority indicator. The report says the domain is suspicious, but does not prove that the GhostAction operator registered it.

A similarly named GitLab domain is listed only as a watch item, not confirmed campaign infrastructure. Defenders should preserve that distinction when creating alerts.

items.title: Revolut Outage Disrupts Payments and Banking Services as Google Cloud Reports London Issues
items.summary: Revolut suffered a major service outage on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, disrupting payments, cash withdrawals, and access to its banking app. The digital bank said customer money and data remained safe while engineers worked to restore affected services. The disruption came as Google Cloud reported problems in its London region. Reuters reported that a person familiar with the matter linked Revolut’s outage to the Google Cloud disruption. Google said its engineering team was investigating an issue affecting europe-west2, its London cloud region. The reports did not establish the technical cause or provide a confirmed recovery time. Banking Services Face Widespread Disruption The outage affected everyday banking tasks rather than a single app feature. Revolut’s status page listed 28 services as partially unavailable, including account sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading and live support chat. Reuters also reported disruption to ATM withdrawals. For customers, that meant problems could extend beyond opening the app. An affected card payment could interrupt a purchase, while unavailable transfers or cash withdrawals could limit access to funds. Disruption to support chat also affected a channel customers would normally use to ask about payment failures or account access. “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” Revolut said. The company added that it had been working to fix the issue since identifying it that morning and apologized to affected customers. The reported connection to Google Cloud places the focus on service availability and cloud dependencies. However, neither the Reuters report nor Revolut’s quoted statement identified malware, ransomware or an intrusion as the cause. The available evidence supports reporting this as an outage, not a confirmed cyberattack or data breach. A banking service can become unavailable without customer records being stolen. Revolut’s statement addresses the safety of funds and data, while the service reports describe problems accessing banking functions. These are separate questions, and an investigation would need to establish what failed before assigning a more specific cause. Previous incidents show why the underlying failure matters. Cybersecurity News covered a Google Cloud outage linked to its API management system in June 2025. That incident involved a software failure affecting request processing across services. There is no evidence in the reports reviewed that Tuesday’s disruption shares that cause. The publication also reported Google Cloud’s accidental deletion of UniSuper’s private cloud account in 2024. Recovery involved rebuilding services and using backups held with another provider. That case offers a separate example of how cloud failures can disrupt financial services, rather than evidence explaining the current Revolut incident. At the stage described in the cited reports, Google was investigating, and Revolut was working to restore service. Neither report supplied a complete technical explanation or a confirmed time for full recovery. Any later update should distinguish restored functions from services that remain partly unavailable. For security and operations teams, the immediate issue is understanding the scope of the disruption without confusing downtime with compromise. The unanswered questions include which cloud component failed, how that failure affected Revolut’s services, and whether recovery measures restored all affected functions for affected customers. Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI, Then Accidentally Expose Their Own Attack Tools
items.summary: Hackers linked to AI-assisted attacks on South Korean banks left parts of their own infrastructure open, giving researchers a view of their tools and preparations. The exposed files showed a wider operation involving cryptocurrency theft tools, Linux attacks, and mobile security testing beyond the banking campaign. Public reporting cited in the investigation said the breaches exposed personal information belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions. Different organizations lost different types of data, including customer records and an outsourced developer’s personal details, rather than suffering one identical breach. Researchers from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the attack tools while investigating infrastructure linked to the actor, tracked as TAG-217. Their October 16 research report traced preparations back to August 2026. It described scripts and capabilities, not a newly named malware family, and showed how basic security mistakes exposed the operator’s work. Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI The campaign involved ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source framework for penetration testing. Such tools help authorized security teams find weaknesses, but attackers can use them against targets without permission. Earlier reporting on the AI-assisted bank breach campaign described exposed Claude Code sessions, ARTEX settings, and AI memory files that helped reveal the operator’s workflow. Public analysis dated October 7 linked the activity to Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Investigators suspected a Chinese-speaking operator, but language clues do not establish nationality or government backing. Recorded Future assessed that the broader activity likely reflected attempts to make money across several possible targets. The incidents also drew attention to systems outside core banking services. Network Infrastructure (Source – Recorded Future) Reporting on the South Korean security investigation described breaches affecting loan-agent and employee-support systems, showing why security reviews must cover connected business applications as well as customer banking platforms. These supporting services can still hold valuable personal and credit information. Exposed Files Reveal Earlier Preparations Open directories and other exposed evidence allowed Insikt Group to reconstruct activity from August 17–22. During that period, TAG-217 tested infrastructure for maintaining remote access and scanned internet-facing systems. Logs showed repeated connections between the actor’s own servers, but did not establish successful access to victims. By August 22, the operator had assembled tools targeting cryptocurrency mining operations using YiiMP. Their functions included trying default passwords, stealing wallet configuration and key files, keeping remote access, and sending Telegram alerts when credentials were captured. Other tools targeted known Linux weaknesses to gain higher access or extract protected password data. By September 5, the workspace included experiments involving iPhone weaknesses and changes to Android system software. Again, the available logs showed testing, not confirmed mobile compromises. By September 26, records covered target research, traffic routing, payload delivery, and checks involving payment processes, revealing a broader toolkit than the banking attacks alone suggested. TAG-217 also routed traffic through residential internet connections, likely to hide its source. As reporting on residential proxy network abuse explains, these services make traffic appear to come from ordinary household connections. The operator also maintained links between servers and copied AI working-memory files across its infrastructure. The exposed material demonstrates AI use, but it does not measure how much AI accelerated the attacks or prove that an autonomous agent completed every intrusion. Recorded Future emphasized this limit: the evidence shows the range of environments explored, rather than a confirmed success against every target represented in the toolkit. For defenders, the lesson is practical. Review internet-facing employee and partner applications, fix exposed weaknesses, and check that users can retrieve only authorized records. Monitor unusual sign-ins, repeated customer-record requests, unexpected remote access, and abnormal data transfers. Response automation should use clear approval limits, especially when blocking shared proxy addresses could affect legitimate customers. items.title: ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform That Uses Multiple Hacking Agents to Find Security Flaws
items.summary: ThreatBook has launched RedAgents, a cloud platform that brings several AI-powered penetration-testing agents together to assess an organization’s systems. Announced on October 16, 2026, the service is designed to help security teams find weaknesses in their own networks by running multiple automated tests within a defined, authorized scope. ThreatBook says the agents can work in parallel and show their findings and test logs in one place. The platform takes a different approach from relying on a single testing tool or provider. Each agent may look for different issues, so combining their results could give defenders a broader view of their exposure. The launch announcement describes RedAgents as a software-as-a-service platform for security operations teams, rather than a new malware family or a report on a specific intrusion. ThreatBook’s announcement also notes that the service brings together agents with different origins and capabilities. Those named at launch are Artex Pro, Cyber(YanJi), Yanxun and CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition. The company says teams can choose one agent or run several against the same approved target, then review results through a shared interface. ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform RedAgents acts as an aggregator: it connects multiple AI penetration-testing agents through one platform and can run them in parallel. A penetration test is an authorized review in which testers look for weaknesses in systems before malicious actors can exploit them. Running agents side by side may help uncover issues that a single tool misses, though the value of the results depends on how accurately the agents test and report. ThreatBook says the platform consolidates findings, test data and logs in a unified view. This could reduce the need for teams to move information between separate tools. The approach is similar to using multiple scanners or testing teams, but RedAgents is designed to coordinate AI agents as part of one assessment. For readers comparing different designs, Cybersecurity News has covered a multi-agent pentesting toolkit that assigns different testing tasks to specialist agents. The four named agents have distinct backgrounds. ThreatBook describes Artex Pro as the enterprise version of Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing agent. Cyber(YanJi) is a Python-based agent that searches for a route from a starting point to a defined goal. Yanxun is described as a system that coordinates specialist agents, while CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition is based on an AI-native testing tool that ThreatBook acquired in September 2026. These descriptions come from the company’s announcement and should be read as vendor claims, not as independent comparative test results. ThreatBook reports, for example, that Yanxun can coordinate several dozen agents and that Cyber(YanJi) solved 54 of 54 challenge problems during a validation event. The release does not provide a controlled, side-by-side benchmark showing how all four agents perform against the same targets. Scope and data controls Automated testing tools can cause disruption if they probe systems without permission or exceed an agreed scope. ThreatBook says RedAgents lets customers define an allowlist of approved targets and that agents must operate within those authorized limits. Organizations should still confirm the scope, timing, rate limits and test conditions before running any penetration test, especially on systems that support business operations. The company also says customer test data stays within the ThreatBook environment and is not sent to third-party agents. RedAgents supports Zero Data Retention, or ZDR, which ThreatBook says enables complete deletion of test data. Security teams should confirm how these controls work in practice, including retention periods, access permissions, logging and any contractual terms, before submitting sensitive environment details. The launch comes as more security products use AI agents to automate parts of testing. Other examples covered by Cybersecurity News include PentestCode’s AI testing agent and Xalgorix’s verification-focused platform . These products differ in how they are deployed and how they handle findings, so teams should compare scope controls, evidence quality and data handling rather than treating “AI pentesting” as one uniform category. The main promise of RedAgents is breadth: multiple agents may explore a target in different ways and give teams a combined view of possible weaknesses. That does not guarantee that every result is valid or that every vulnerability will be found. Security staff still need to review evidence, reproduce important findings safely and prioritize fixes based on business impact and exposure. ThreatBook says the platform can reduce false positives by combining agent results, but the announcement does not publish independent accuracy figures or a false-positive rate. It also does not identify a specific customer deployment, measured security outcome or external validation of the service. Those details will matter to organizations assessing whether the platform fits their testing process. For context, a separate Cybersecurity News report describes Apex’s black-box testing approach , which evaluates applications without source-code access. RedAgents’ stated distinction is not a single testing method but a central platform for selecting and coordinating several agents. ThreatBook says it plans to add more open-source agents over time, alongside the enterprise tools available at launch. The company’s announcement and RedAgents product blog provide further product details. RedAgents is available through the company’s website, where ThreatBook says organizations can request a trial. items.title: U.S. Government Bans DeepSeek AI and Orders Federal Agencies to Remove All Related Tools
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop buying DeepSeek products and remove related technology from their IT systems. The action covers products from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., its affiliates, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations. The notice was filed for public inspection on October 19, 2026, with publication scheduled for October 20. It creates a government supply chain restriction, not a nationwide ban on private use. Businesses and individuals are not prohibited from using DeepSeek by this order. U.S. Government Bans DeepSeek AI The DHS notice sets out two requirements. Federal civilian agencies must exclude DeepSeek and affiliate IT products and services from procurement. They must also remove DeepSeek and affiliate products, including covered third-party implementations, from agency technology systems. That second requirement makes the order broader than a block on new purchases. The third-party provision is especially important for security teams. An agency may use DeepSeek through another supplier rather than through an application carrying the DeepSeek name. A review limited to branded chat tools could therefore miss products covered by the removal requirement. Agencies need to establish what powers their existing AI services. The notice does not provide a public list of every affected third-party vendor or product. Suppliers and agency buyers will need to assess whether particular tools use DeepSeek implementations, rather than assuming that a different product name places them outside the order. Contract records and technical documentation can help support that review. For vendors serving civilian agencies, the order also raises a direct procurement question. They must understand whether their own AI features depend on technology that government customers must now exclude or remove. items.title: Meta glasses caught recording conversations without wake phrase
items.summary: Meta says it has resolved an issue after some Ray-Ban Meta owners reported that their glasses recorded conversations without the “Hey Meta” wake phrase. Users reported finding recordings and transcripts of conversations they did not knowingly save. Recording without anyone realizing raises privacy concerns for both the wearer and the people around them. The complaints surfaced on Reddit , where one owner described unexpected recordings occurring with three pairs of glasses. The owner said the behavior started after a firmware update and occurred even with Respond without Hey Meta disabled. They also reported that the glasses’ internal notification light sometimes activated during normal conversation. Other commenters described similar unexplained activations. As Android Authority reports , Meta says the problem has been fixed: “This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.” What’s missing is a public explanation of what caused it, how many people were affected, and what happened to the audio captured. This isn’t the first time we’ve reported on privacy concerns involving smart glasses. In June, we covered unreleased facial-recognition code found in Meta’s companion app . The code was not active, but the reporting raised concerns about how wearable cameras could eventually move from capturing people to identifying them without their knowledge. What owners can do According to the Reddit owner, Meta Support recommended disabling microphone and camera permissions, turning off Wear Detection , deleting voice history, and disabling automatic updates. Those steps would limit much of the gadget’s core functionality without explaining what went wrong. Until Meta provides a fuller explanation, here are a few precautions that make sense if you wish to keep using your smart glasses: Review your voice history. Look for interactions you do not recognize and delete unwanted recordings or transcripts. Meta says users can manage these logs through Settings . Check your voice-activation settings. The owner reporting the issue said Respond without Hey Meta was already disabled, so do not treat that setting alone as a guarantee against unintended activation. Keep the glasses and companion app updated. Although the user associated the behavior with an update, that is not a good reason to permanently abandon updates that may contain security and privacy fixes. Always ask before recording other people. Their privacy matters even when your glasses are working exactly as intended. Meta still owes users an explanation of what went wrong and what it has done to ensure it won’t happen again. Browse like no one’s watching. items.title: Hackers Exploit Palo Alto VPN Flaw to Bypass MFA and Steal Credentials From VMware Disks
items.summary: Ransomware operators are exploiting a Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect VPN flaw to bypass multi-factor authentication and enter corporate networks. In one investigated case, attackers reached VMware management systems and stole credentials directly from a domain controller’s virtual disk, avoiding security tools running inside the virtual machine. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed the activity in an October 19 threat brief update . Researchers linked exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 to Spikey Scorpius, also known as Qilin, and Tarnished Scorpius, also known as Inc. Separate public reporting connected exploitation to operators using Settra ransomware. Investigations ongoing since early June have covered healthcare, education, financial services, manufacturing, government, energy, and other sectors. The latest findings show how unauthorized VPN access can develop into credential theft, data theft, and ransomware deployment. GlobalProtect Flaw Bypasses MFA The vulnerability affects GlobalProtect portals and gateways in certain PAN-OS and Prisma Access deployments. Exposure requires authentication override cookies to be enabled alongside a vulnerable certificate setup. Palo Alto Networks rates the flaw High, with a CVSS score of 7.8 and its highest suggested response urgency. Panorama and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Authentication override cookies let previously authenticated users reconnect without repeating the full login process. According to Rapid7’s technical analysis , vulnerable devices decrypt these cookies but do not properly verify that a trusted system created them. If the cookie certificate is reused for a publicly exposed service, attackers can obtain its public key and forge a cookie. The gateway may accept that cookie as proof of authentication, allowing a VPN connection without the normal login and MFA checks. Cybersecurity News previously covered this GlobalProtect authentication bypass . After establishing access, attackers use remote monitoring and management tools to explore internal networks. They move between systems through Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block, then prepare tools for credential harvesting, data theft, and ransomware deployment. The most notable case involved a move from the compromised VPN gateway to VMware’s vCenter management appliance. Attackers then disabled the execInstalledOnly security control on ESXi hosts and used a custom tool to extract credentials offline from a domain controller’s VMDK virtual disk. Unit 42 did not name the tool or provide its implementation details. Reading credentials directly from the disk bypasses endpoint detection and response controls inside the affected virtual machine. The approach targets the infrastructure beneath the operating system rather than relying on a credential-stealing program running within it. Cybersecurity News has also reported on VMware attacks involving detached domain controller disks . Unit 42 also observed attackers combining this initial access with tools targeting Veeam backup infrastructure through CVE-2023-27532. That separate flaw can expose encrypted credentials stored in the backup configuration database, potentially opening access to backup hosts. Defenders should examine GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events linked to suspicious sources and client details. Reported indicators include 104.207.144[.]154 , 146.19.216[.]125 , device names GP-CLIENT and DESKTOP-GP01 , and host IDs aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55 . Earlier monitoring found that many probes did not establish full VPN sessions, making connection events important for investigation. Organizations should follow the Palo Alto Networks advisory and upgrade every affected portal and gateway. Temporary mitigations include disabling authentication override or generating a new certificate dedicated exclusively to override cookies. An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the

Man seeking love travels 2,000 km to meet an AI-generated woman
items.summary: A 49-year-old bricklayer sold his belongings before traveling 2,000 km by bus from his home in Brazil to meet “Jéssica,” an online influencer he had fallen for. Yet despite having a social media account with more than 300,000 followers, she never existed. Edimar Rocha Martins lives in Imperatriz, a city in northeastern Brazil. He says he struck up an online conversation with Jéssica Fazendeira, who supposedly lived near the southeastern city of Belo Horizonte. The AI persona promising love The online persona’s name, “Fazendeira,” loosely translates as “female farmer.” She described herself as living on a farm. Martins said that he had been talking with the persona online since 2020. He decided to visit her after she offered to pay for his trip and have him live on the farm with her, he said. The account’s operator disputes this, saying the character was created in 2025 and denying any private messages with him. A video posted on one of her online accounts (captured here by Brazilian news service Imirante) asked for a man to come and live with her and offered to fund the trip. The AI-generated farmer says, translated: I’m not joking, my intentions are serious. I want to meet someone who wants to build something real and beautiful with me. If you’re a simple man who likes peace and quiet and a calm life, then maybe we’d get along really well. After selling his possessions to fund the bus trip, Martins arrived in Belo Horizonte and began asking about the woman. Unable to find her, he approached a local radio station, where staff explained that she was an AI-generated character. Without enough money to return, he received food, support, and a bus ticket to Augustinópolis, in Tocantins, from the city’s migrant assistance service. He later returned to Imperatriz, where he stayed with relatives. The account’s operator hits back The account’s administrator posted a message through the AI character’s TikTok account denying any kind of scam. Translated, it said: This profile is pretty much abandoned, but I’ve come here to state the obvious. I’m made of artificial intelligence , and I’ve never talked to anyone on this profile. The aim was to get engagement for sales. I never spoke directly to anyone, much less brought anyone to Belo Horizonte. The operator told reporters that the character was created to attract viewers and promote products through affiliate sales. They said they did not know whether other people had reused the character’s content on other accounts. Another video shows messages people have reportedly sent the account, with the character explaining that it keeps telling viewers it’s an AI. It complains: And then it’s still my fault, right? These people are lost. In another video, where it is being interviewed by an AI-generated male character, the persona explains that it deactivated and then reactivated its account. It said: I was the first AI to get canceled for absolutely nothing. These are scripted responses published through a fictional character, rather than an AI independently defending itself. Police said they could not establish at that stage whether a crime had occurred. One outlet reported that Martins has been struggling with loneliness following his mother’s death. Videos published to the reactivated TikTok account are labeled as AI generated. It also links to an Instagram account with videos of the character, where videos carry similar labels. Those current labels don’t establish what Martins saw before his trip. Social media already encourages parasocial relationships, where viewers feel a personal connection with someone who doesn’t know them. AI-generated personas add another complication: The person viewers feel connected to may be entirely fictional. In our Face value report , 88% of adults surveyed said it’s becoming harder to tell what online content is genuinely human or real. The AI plot thickens June saw reports of a 72-year-old man who traveled 4,000 km from his home in Boa Vista to … Belo Horizonte. He visited after seeing a farm woman on a social network who was offering a job opportunity and perhaps something more. Unable to return home, he sought help from social workers. In August, 71-year-old Alberto da Costa traveled from Manaus to the same city after watching videos featuring the same woman, according to Itatiaia. He paid almost R$3,000 for a flight, then sought help from the outlet when he couldn’t afford to return home. The videos simulated personal conversations, giving viewers the impression that the woman was speaking directly to them. The account reportedly had nearly a million followers. The reporting doesn’t establish whether this woman was AI-generated or whether the account was connected to Jéssica’s. Nor does it establish that the men sent money to the account operators. But the costs can still be real: selling possessions, paying for travel, and finding yourself stranded far from home. Protect yourself and others The same advice applies here as to romance scams, but with some extras. Don’t send money or travel to see someone you’ve never met without independently checking who they are. Don’t rely on video calls alone. Scammers now use deepfake video calls to dupe victims live. And check whether you’re exchanging private messages or watching public videos that anyone can see. Look for information beyond the account itself. Search their name and profile pictures, and research where they say they work. Be cautious if their story doesn’t add up or they avoid questions about their identity. When you feel close to someone, questioning that connection can be difficult. Before sending money or booking travel, talk to a friend or family member and get their perspective. And if you’re worried about someone who may be in a similar situation, check in without judgment and offer to look through the account together. Images courtesy of Jam Press Something feel off? items.title: Detecting GitHound Enumeration via the GitHub API
items.summary: For many organizations, GitHub Enterprise serves as a central platform for software development, collaboration, and source code management. This makes it an increasingly valuable target for attackers seeking access to source code, sensitive information, credentials, and development infrastructure. Recent incidents demonstrate an increasing preference among attackers for targeting GitHub environments. In March 2026, the Trivy supply-chain attack involved stolen credentials being used to publish malicious releases and tamper with GitHub Actions. The compromise subsequently extended to Checkmarx’s GitHub environment, where attackers gained unauthorized repository access and distributed malicious code through developer tools and CI/CD . In May 2026, GitHub itself disclosed that an employee device had been compromised through a malicious VS Code extension, resulting in the exfiltration of internal repositories . In May 2026, a reported exposure of sensitive CISA information through a public GitHub repository highlighted how misconfigured access and unintended data disclosure can expose sensitive information. These incidents highlight the growing importance of protecting and monitoring code repositories. Tools such as GitHound , a BloodHound OpenGraph collector for GitHub released by SpecterOps earlier in 2026, can help defenders map a GitHub organization’s environment by identifying relationships between users, teams, repositories, and permissions that allows them to understand access relationships, identify excessive privileges, and uncover potential attack paths. However, the same capabilities can also be leveraged by adversaries to map an organization’s GitHub environment, discover accessible resources, and identify opportunities for further access. With this in mind, I took a closer look at GitHub Enterprise audit logs and weather they can be used to detect enumeration through the GitHub API. Running GitHound Against a GitHub Organization GitHound interacts directly with the GitHub API to collect information about an organization’s users, teams, repositories, and permissions. To do so, it requires a GitHub access token with the appropriate permissions to access the resources being queried. The scope of the collected data therefore depends on the token’s privileges. Step 1: Create a GitHub personal access token To authenticate GitHound, create a personal access token (PAT) on GitHub. Navigate to GitHub’s personal access token settings for your account. Select Tokens , then click Generate new token . Provide a descriptive name and set an appropriate expiration date. Configure the repository access and permissions required for the resources you intend to collect. Use the GitHub documentation to understand the available permissions. Generate the token and copy it immediately. Step 2: Run GitHound against the Organization The next step would be to download and run GitHound. Download the tool from the official SpecterOps repo . To run GitHound against your organization open a powershell session and run the following commands: Load the collector: . ./githound.ps1 GitHound module loading 2. items.summary_html:
For many organizations, GitHub Enterprise serves as a central platform for software development, collaboration, and source code management. This makes it an increasingly valuable target for attackers seeking access to source code, sensitive information, credentials, and development infrastructure.

Recent incidents demonstrate an increasing preference among attackers for targeting GitHub environments. In March 2026, the Trivy supply-chain attack involved stolen credentials being used to publish malicious releases and tamper with GitHub Actions. The compromise subsequently extended to Checkmarx’s GitHub environment, where attackers gained unauthorized repository access and distributed malicious code through developer tools and CI/CD. In May 2026, GitHub itself disclosed that an employee device had been compromised through a malicious VS Code extension, resulting in the exfiltration of internal repositories. In May 2026, a reported exposure of sensitive CISA information through a public GitHub repository highlighted how misconfigured access and unintended data disclosure can expose sensitive information. These incidents highlight the growing importance of protecting and monitoring code repositories.

Tools such as GitHound, a BloodHound OpenGraph collector for GitHub released by SpecterOps earlier in 2026, can help defenders map a GitHub organization’s environment by identifying relationships between users, teams, repositories, and permissions that allows them to understand access relationships, identify excessive privileges, and uncover potential attack paths. However, the same capabilities can also be leveraged by adversaries to map an organization’s GitHub environment, discover accessible resources, and identify opportunities for further access.

With this in mind, I took a closer look at GitHub Enterprise audit logs and weather they can be used to detect enumeration through the GitHub API.

Running GitHound Against a GitHub Organization

GitHound interacts directly with the GitHub API to collect information about an organization’s users, teams, repositories, and permissions. To do so, it requires a GitHub access token with the appropriate permissions to access the resources being queried. The scope of the collected data therefore depends on the token’s privileges.

Step 1: Create a GitHub personal access token

To authenticate GitHound, create a personal access token (PAT) on GitHub.

  1. Navigate to GitHub’s personal access token settings for your account.
  2. Select Tokens, then click Generate new token.
  3. Provide a descriptive name and set an appropriate expiration date.
  4. Configure the repository access and permissions required for the resources you intend to collect. Use the GitHub documentation to understand the available permissions.
  5. Generate the token and copy it immediately.
Step 2: Run GitHound against the Organization

The next step would be to download and run GitHound. Download the tool from the official SpecterOps repo.

To run GitHound against your organization open a powershell session and run the following commands:

  1. Load the collector:
. ./githound.ps1
GitHound module loading

2. Create a session with your Personal Access Token

$session = New-GitHubSession -OrganizationName "" -Token ""
GitHound session variable creation

3. Run the collection script

Invoke-GitHound -Session $session

or 

Invoke-GitHound -Session $session -CollectAll
GitHound executionGitHub Logging Configuration

As GitHound makes API requests to enumerate these resources, its activity will be visible in GitHub audit logs, providing an opportunity for defenders to investigate and detect potentially suspicious patterns of API usage. Before building a detection for GitHub API enumeration though, it is important to ensure that the relevant audit events are being collected.

  1. Sign in to GitHub with an enterprise owner account and navigate to Settings.
  2. Open Audit log and select Log streaming. For our tests we are selecting streaming to Azure Blob Storage to ingest the logs to Microsoft Sentinel via the GitHub data connector from Microsoft’s Content Hub.
  3. Create a new audit log stream and configure the destination where the logs will be sent.

4. In the Settings tab, enable the option to Enable API Request Events so that API activity is captured alongside other audit events.

5. Save the configuration and verify that events are arriving at the configured destination.

For detailed instructions refer to GitHub’s official documentation: Streaming the audit log for your enterprise.

Building the Detection

Sure enough, GitHound’s API activity is visible in the GitHub audit logs, providing an opportunity to detect the enumeration through Microsoft Sentinel.

GitHound enumeration activity

The query focuses on API routes commonly used to retrieve organizational information, including repositories, teams, permissions, and GitHub Actions configuration. It counts the distinct routes and URL paths accessed by an actor and compares these counts against predefined thresholds to identify potential enumeration activity. While this behavior is consistent with GitHound, the detection identifies an enumeration pattern rather than this specific tool.

let route_threshold = 10;
let url_path_threshold = 20;
let routes_of_intrest = dynamic([@'/graphql', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles/:role_id/teams', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/secrets', @'/organizations/:organization_id/custom-repository-roles', @'/organizations/:organization_id/repos', @'/organizations/:organization_id/secret-scanning/alerts', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles/:role_id/users', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions/self-hosted-runners', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/variables', @'/organizations/:organization_id', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions/workflow', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles', @'/organizations/:organization_id/teams']);
GitHubAuditLogsV3_CL
| where Action == "api.request"
| project-reorder UrlPath, Route, RequestMethod, QueryString, StatusCode, UserAgent
| where Route in~ (routes_of_intrest)
| summarize
    c = count(),
    RequestMethod = make_set(RequestMethod),
    StatusCode = make_set(StatusCode),
    Route = make_set(Route),
    UrlPath = make_set(UrlPath),
    UserAgent = make_set(UserAgent),
    User = make_set(User),
    OperationType = make_set(OperationType),
    Org = make_set(Org),
    OrgId = make_set(OrgId),
    ActorId = make_set(ActorId),
    ActorIsBot = make_set(ActorIsBot),
    ProgrammaticAccessType = make_set(ProgrammaticAccessType),
    TokenScopes = make_set(TokenScopes),
    Type = make_set(Type),
    Action = make_set(Action),
    Business = make_set(Business)
by Actor, TokenId
| extend RouteCount = array_length(Route)
| extend UrlPathCount = array_length(UrlPath)
| where RouteCount > route_threshold or UrlPathCount > url_path_threshold
GitHub API enumeration query resultsClosing Thoughts

GitHub API enumeration can provide attackers with valuable insight into an organization’s repositories, permissions, and development workflows, making API monitoring essential for protecting development environments.

In this blog post, we demonstrated how GitHound’s activity can be observed in GitHub audit logs and how we can detect the API enumeration pattern. By enabling API request logging and implementing this or similar detections, defenders can improve visibility across their GitHub Enterprise environment and identify suspicious activity at an early stage.

Detecting GitHound Enumeration via the GitHub API was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware
items.summary: Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases. The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the cloud provider, which blocked the malicious files within 94 minutes. OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba said the affected releases were v0.11.0, v0.12.0, v0.13.0, v0.14.0, and v0.15.0. He identified v0.10.0 as clean and announced a safe v0.16.0 release. That replacement is now available on the project’s official GitHub releases page , where it is marked as immutable, meaning its published release files cannot be changed. OVHcloud Supply Chain Attack According to Klaba’s account, the compromised files appeared at 14:47 and were detected and blocked at 16:21. OVHcloud’s initial checks found no other affected repository. Those findings limit the confirmed scope to the CLI project, rather than establishing a wider breach across the company’s GitHub organization or cloud platform. The attacker used an existing developer account to add a malicious binary to the software distributed through GitHub. This placed the threat inside a trusted download location, giving users little reason to suspect that a routine CLI download could expose local credentials. OVHcloud has not explained how the developer account was first compromised. The customer’s report raised concerns about release files being replaced with a “dirty build” of a later commit. In software builds, that label generally signals changes beyond the recorded source revision. The public issue listing identifies the report as issue #300, covering replaced assets for v0.13.0 through v0.15.0. OVHcloud’s warning named two additional affected versions. The customer also questioned the account behind the changes and asked whether release files should be locked against replacement. They said they had switched to building through the Go module proxy while seeking clarification. Their report was public because the repository lacked a private vulnerability reporting channel. Klaba described the added program as a binary whose job was to retrieve secrets from disk. He said its quality was poor but warned that it could still achieve its purpose. The available disclosure does not establish which files it searched, where collected data was sent, or how many users executed the malicious downloads. The CLI’s normal role makes this threat especially serious. OVHcloud documents the tool as a way to manage cloud services, account resources, and automated workflows. Its supported authentication methods include a local .ovh.conf file containing credentials, alongside environment variables for application keys, application secrets, and consumer keys. Those documented credential locations explain why a compromised administration tool can create risks beyond the downloaded program itself. However, they are not a confirmed list of this malware’s targets. Until OVHcloud publishes its technical findings, specific claims about stolen SSH keys, browser passwords, persistence, or attacker infrastructure would go beyond the evidence. The incident fits the broader pattern covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s reporting on trusted software updates used to steal developer and cloud credentials . Attackers can use stolen publishing access to turn familiar software delivery channels into routes for credential theft, without needing users to visit a fake website. OVHcloud urged users who downloaded the CLI during the incident to update it immediately or delete it. Klaba also advised affected users to change all secrets stored on disk. Rotation is important because replacing the malicious program does not cancel credentials that may already have been copied. Organizations investigating possible exposure should identify which machines downloaded and ran affected files, preserve available evidence, and review account activity tied to potentially exposed credentials. Their response should extend beyond OVHcloud credentials if other secrets were accessible on those machines. The company’s warning covers local secrets broadly, not only its own service keys. A related GhostAction GitHub credential theft campaign shows why repository access deserves close attention. That campaign used stolen accounts to introduce malicious workflows under trusted identities. No evidence currently links it to the OVHcloud incident. For OVHcloud users, the immediate priorities remain replacing affected downloads and renewing potentially exposed secrets while the company continues its malware investigation and publishes further technical findings.
