Zusätzlich konnte mithilfe eines Skripts eine Ereignis-Timeline auf Basis der extrahierten Binärdatei erstellt werden.

Skriptergebnisse der Binäranalyse Dynamische Analyse

Die statische Analyse kann gute Hinweise auf den Payload liefern. Mit einer dynamischen Analyse lassen sich diese Erkenntnisse jedoch überprüfen und bestätigen.

Dieser Schritt sollte nur in einer sauberen und isolierten Umgebung durchgeführt werden, da das Gerät beim Einstecken sofort mit der Ausführung beginnt und ein Sicherheitsrisiko darstellen kann.

Ein mögliches Setup für die dynamische Analyse könnte Folgendes umfassen:

  1. Eine isolierte virtuelle Maschine mit der Möglichkeit, das Gerät durchzureichen, oder einen dedizierten Opfer-Host
  2. Host-Monitoring zur Beobachtung von Prozesserzeugung und Befehlsausführung
  3. Protokollierung von Tastatureingaben oder Bildschirmaufzeichnung
  4. Netzwerküberwachung, sofern relevant

Durch den Vergleich des beobachteten Verhaltens mit der extrahierten Firmware lässt sich überprüfen, ob sich das Gerät wie erwartet verhält oder ob Teile der Logik verborgen, verschleiert oder nur unter bestimmten Bedingungen ausgelöst werden.

In unserem Fall konnte die Überwachung der Tastatureingaben mit einem Python-Skript die vom Gerät ausgeführte Abfolge von Aktionen nachvollziehen.

Ausgabe des Key-Monitoring-Skripts – Auszug

Das Testgerät ließ sich wie geplant auslesen und der Payload analysieren, der entwickelte Analyseablauf konnte damit erfolgreich validiert werden. Derselbe Prozess kann nun auf das während des Vorfalls identifizierte Gerät angewendet werden, um die darin verborgene Funktionalität offenzulegen.

Erkennung und Host-Analyse

Sobald klar ist, welche Inhalte auf dem Mikrocontroller gespeichert waren und welche Aktionen das Gerät auf angeschlossenen Systemen ausgelöst haben könnte, stellt sich die Frage, wie sich diese Aktivitäten in einer Untersuchung nachweisen lassen. Das ist besonders wichtig, wenn das physische USB-Gerät nicht mehr verfügbar ist und sich die Untersuchung vollständig auf hostbasierte Artefakte stützen muss.

In der Praxis gibt es zwei zentrale Ansatzpunkte. Zum einen kann das Gerät selbst anhand von USB-bezogenen Spuren auf dem System erkannt werden. Zum anderen lässt sich untersuchen, was auf dem Host nach dem Anschluss des Geräts passiert ist.

Erkennung

Erkennung und Threat Hunting können häufig mit den USB-Enumerierungsdaten beginnen. In unseren Tests wurde der Digispark mit den folgenden Kombinationen aus Hersteller- und Produkt-ID erkannt:

Plaintext
VID_16D0&PID_0753
VID_16C0&PID_27DB
VID_16D0&PID_0753
VID_16C0&PID_27DB

Vendor- und Geräteinformationen (Quelle)

Diese Kennungen dienen als guter Ausgangspunkt für die Suche über mehrere Systeme, insbesondere bei der Analyse historischer USB-Aktivitäten. Für sich allein sind sie jedoch weder ein verlässlicher Nachweis noch eine zuverlässige Erkennungsmethode. Ein wichtiger Punkt ist, dass sich VID und PID solcher Geräte ändern lassen. Ein Angreifer könnte das Gerät beispielsweise so konfigurieren, dass es sich als legitime Tastatur ausgibt und in der normalen Peripherieaktivität untergeht.

Trotzdem können bei einer Untersuchung beobachtete VID- und PID-Werte unbekannter oder verdächtiger USB-Geräte gegen öffentliche USB-Datenbanken wie Device Hunt geprüft werden, um die wahrscheinliche Hardware-Familie oder den Hersteller zu identifizieren.

Auf Windows-Systemen lassen sich diese Kennungen häufig aus mehreren Artefakten wiederherstellen, darunter Event Logs, Registry-Speicherorte und Setup-Logs.

QuelleSpeicherortDetailsEvent logMicrosoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP/ConfigurationEvent-IDs 400 und 410Log-DateiC:\Windows\inf\setupapi.dev.log und setupapi.dev.*.logRegistrySYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBUSB-Geräte-EnumerationsdatenRegistrySYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\HIDHID-bezogene Enumerationsdaten

Diese Quellen können hilfreiche Informationen liefern, etwa die erste und letzte bekannte Verbindungszeit, Hardwarekennungen und Device-Class-Informationen.

In Kombination zeigen diese Informationen, ob das verdächtige Gerät jemals angeschlossen war, wann es erkannt wurde und wie Windows es klassifiziert hat.

Host-Analyse

Wenn ein Digispark oder ein ähnliches HID-Angriffsgerät an einen Host angeschlossen wurde, sind USB-Artefakte nur ein Teil des Gesamtbildes. Sie können bestätigen, dass ein Gerät verbunden war, zeigen jedoch nicht direkt, welche Tastatureingaben gesendet oder welche Aktionen ausgeführt wurden. Um die Auswirkungen auf dem Host nachzuvollziehen, sollten daher weitere hostbasierte Artefakte überprüft werden.

Der erste Schritt besteht in der Regel darin, die Geräteverbindung über die USB-bezogenen Registry-Einträge zu bestätigen, insbesondere:

Plaintext
SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB
SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\HID
SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB
SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\HID

Registry-Informationen – SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB

Diese Quelle kann Details zum angeschlossenen Gerät liefern, darunter Kennungen und Zeitstempel, die bei der Rekonstruktion der Timeline helfen. Je nach Fall können auch die entsprechenden Enum\HID-Einträge relevant sein, insbesondere wenn das Gerät als Human Interface Device, etwa als Tastatur, erkannt wurde.

Anschließend sollten Artefakte für Benutzeraktivität geprüft werden, die Hinweise auf Befehle enthalten können, die durch die injizierten Tastatureingaben ausgelöst wurden. Ein hilfreiches Beispiel ist der Registry-Schlüssel RunMRU:

Plaintext
HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU
HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU

RunMRU-Registry-Schlüssel

Der RunMRU-Schlüssel speichert Befehle, die über den Windows-Ausführen-Dialog eingegeben wurden. Wenn der Digispark-Payload das Ausführen-Fenster geöffnet und von dort Befehle gestartet hat, kann dieser Schlüssel Hinweise darüber enthalten. Wenn das Gerät beispielsweise einen Befehl wie das Starten eines Browsers, das Öffnen von PowerShell oder das Starten eines Skripts über den Ausführen-Dialog ausgeführt hat, kann der Befehl möglicherweise noch aus diesem Artefakt rekonstruiert werden.

Zusätzlich zu RunMRU können je nach vermutetem Payload auch andere Host-Artefakte (z. B. PowerShell-Logs, Prefetch, Shortcut-Dateien) relevant sein.

Fazit

Der Digispark ist unauffällig, günstig und flexibel konfigurierbar. Das macht ihn zu einem attraktiven Werkzeug für HID-basierte Angriffe.

Aus forensischer Sicht bedeutet der fehlende austauschbare Speicher, dass für die Analyse direkter Zugriff auf den Mikrocontroller und zumindest grundlegende Hardwarekenntnisse erforderlich sind. Wie in diesem Beitrag gezeigt, lässt sich die Firmware jedoch mit vergleichsweise wenig Equipment und ohne großes Budget auslesen und analysieren.

Für Verteidiger ist dies eine wichtige Erinnerung daran, dass USB-Angriffe nicht auf kommerzielle Red-Team-Tools beschränkt sind. Selbst einfache Hobby-Hardware kann effektiv zweckentfremdet werden. Unbekannte USB-Geräte sollten daher grundsätzlich als potenziell bösartig betrachtet werden.

Empfehlungen

Um das Risiko durch manipulierte USB-Geräte zu verringern, empfehlen wir folgende Maßnahmen:

  • Endpoints gegen verdächtige Folgeaktivitäten härten und überwachen: Verbessern Sie die Sichtbarkeit auf Endpoints sowie das Monitoring von USB-Geräten, um unautorisierte oder verdächtige Aktivitäten mit Wechseldatenträgern besser zu erkennen, zu untersuchen und im Umfang zu bestimmen. Logging und Erkennung sollten Verhaltensweisen abdecken, die häufig mit HID-Injection in Verbindung stehen, etwa den Missbrauch von Win+R, die Ausführung von PowerShell, unerwartete Prozessstarts und andere anomale Aktivitäten, die scheinbar aus normaler Benutzereingabe stammen.
  • Physische Sicherheitsmaßnahmen in exponierten Bereichen stärken: Systeme an Orten wie Empfangsbereichen, gemeinsam genutzten Arbeitsplätzen, Besprechungsräumen oder Produktionsumgebungen sind stärker unautorisierten USB-Geräten und physischer Manipulation ausgesetzt. Wo möglich sollten Maßnahmen wie die Einschränkung des physischen Zugangs, das Verlegen sensibler Systeme, das Begrenzen des Zugangs zu USB-Ports und regelmäßige Inspektionen in Betracht gezogen werden, um Risiken zu reduzieren.
  • Unbekannte USB-Geräte standardmäßig als bösartig behandeln: Stärken Sie das Bewusstsein der Mitarbeitenden für die Risiken im Zusammenhang mit USB-Geräten und Wechseldatenträgern, um unsicheres Verhalten zu reduzieren und die zeitnahe Meldung verdächtiger Hardware oder Aktivitäten zu fördern. Mitarbeitende sollten geschult werden, niemals nicht vertrauenswürdige oder gefundene USB-Geräte anzuschließen, selbst wenn sie harmlos erscheinen, wie z. B. Speichersticks, Tastaturen, Adapter oder Entwicklungsboards.
  • Die Nutzung von USB-Geräten durch Device-Control-Richtlinien einschränken: Auch wenn Allowlisting auf Basis von PID/VID helfen kann, die Angriffsfläche zu verringern, ist es keine vollumfängliche Lösung, da diese Werte wie beschrieben verändert werden können. Organisationen sollten PID/VID-Filter daher als ergänzende Kontrolle betrachten und mit Monitoring, Endpoint-Sicherheit und einer strikten Autorisierung entfernbarer Peripheriegeräte kombinieren.
Anhänge

Das folgende Skript dient als einfaches Beispiel für die Aufzeichnung von Tastenanschlägen zu Monitoring- und Analysezwecken. Da es nur illustrativen Zwecken dient, kann die vollständige Funktionsfähigkeit nicht gewährleistet werden.

Python
import ctypes
from ctypes import wintypes
from datetime import datetime
import os
import time

if os.name != "nt":
    raise SystemExit("This script is for Windows only.")

# False: show only pressed events
# True: show pressed and released events
SHOW_RELEASED = False

user32 = ctypes.WinDLL("user32", use_last_error=True)

user32.GetAsyncKeyState.argtypes = [wintypes.INT]
user32.GetAsyncKeyState.restype = wintypes.SHORT

KEYS = {
    0x08: "BACKSPACE",
    0x09: "TAB",
    0x0D: "ENTER",
    0x14: "CAPS LOCK",
    0x1B: "ESCAPE",
    0x20: "SPACE",
    0x21: "PAGE UP",
    0x22: "PAGE DOWN",
    0x23: "END",
    0x24: "HOME",
    0x25: "LEFT ARROW",
    0x26: "UP ARROW",
    0x27: "RIGHT ARROW",
    0x28: "DOWN ARROW",
    0x2C: "PRINT SCREEN",
    0x2D: "INSERT",
    0x2E: "DELETE",
    0x5B: "LEFT WIN",
    0x5C: "RIGHT WIN",
    0x5D: "MENU",
    0x90: "NUM LOCK",
    0x91: "SCROLL LOCK",

    # Left/right modifier keys
    0xA0: "LEFT SHIFT",
    0xA1: "RIGHT SHIFT",
    0xA2: "LEFT CTRL",
    0xA3: "RIGHT CTRL",
    0xA4: "LEFT ALT",
    0xA5: "RIGHT ALT",

    # Common punctuation/OEM keys
    0xBA: ";",
    0xBB: "+",
    0xBC: ",",
    0xBD: "-",
    0xBE: ".",
    0xBF: "/",
    0xC0: "`",
    0xDB: "[",
    0xDC: "\\",
    0xDD: "]",
    0xDE: "'",
    0xE2: "OEM 102",
}

# Letters A-Z
for code in range(0x41, 0x5B):
    KEYS[code] = chr(code)

# Number row 0-9
for code in range(0x30, 0x3A):
    KEYS[code] = chr(code)

# Function keys F1-F24
for number in range(1, 25):
    KEYS[0x6F + number] = f"F{number}"

# Numpad
for number in range(10):
    KEYS[0x60 + number] = f"NUMPAD {number}"

KEYS.update(
    {
        0x6A: "NUMPAD *",
        0x6B: "NUMPAD +",
        0x6D: "NUMPAD -",
        0x6E: "NUMPAD .",
        0x6F: "NUMPAD /",
    }
)


def now() -> str:
    return datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3]


def is_down(virtual_key: int) -> bool:
    return bool(user32.GetAsyncKeyState(virtual_key) & 0x8000)


def pressed_modifiers() -> list[str]:
    modifiers = []

    if is_down(0xA2) or is_down(0xA3):
        modifiers.append("CTRL")

    if is_down(0xA4) or is_down(0xA5):
        modifiers.append("ALT")

    if is_down(0xA0) or is_down(0xA1):
        modifiers.append("SHIFT")

    if is_down(0x5B) or is_down(0x5C):
        modifiers.append("WIN")

    return modifiers


def main() -> None:
    states = {virtual_key: False for virtual_key in KEYS}

    modifier_keys = {
        "LEFT CTRL",
        "RIGHT CTRL",
        "LEFT ALT",
        "RIGHT ALT",
        "LEFT SHIFT",
        "RIGHT SHIFT",
        "LEFT WIN",
        "RIGHT WIN",
    }

    mode = "pressed and released" if SHOW_RELEASED else "pressed only"

    print("Visible Windows key monitor")
    print(f"Mode: {mode}")
    print("Nothing is written to disk.")
    print("Press CTRL+Q to stop.\n")

    try:
        while True:
            ctrl_down = is_down(0xA2) or is_down(0xA3)

            if ctrl_down and is_down(ord("Q")):
                break

            for virtual_key, key_name in KEYS.items():
                currently_down = is_down(virtual_key)
                previously_down = states[virtual_key]

                if currently_down and not previously_down:
                    if key_name in modifier_keys:
                        display_name = key_name
                    else:
                        modifiers = pressed_modifiers()
                        display_name = "+".join(modifiers + [key_name])

                    print(
                        f"[{now()}] PRESSED:  {display_name}",
                        flush=True,
                    )

                elif (
                    SHOW_RELEASED
                    and not currently_down
                    and previously_down
                ):
                    print(
                        f"[{now()}] RELEASED: {key_name}",
                        flush=True,
                    )

                states[virtual_key] = currently_down

            time.sleep(0.005)

    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass

    print("\nKey monitor stopped.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages to Steal Google Credentials
items.summary: Two websites are hosting fake Google Meet pages designed to steal Google account credentials and carry out phishing involving two-factor authentication (2FA), according to threat intelligence shared on October 20, 2026. The pages imitate a familiar meeting service to make a request for account details look more believable. The researcher also reported a serious security issue on an exposed /install page: it reveals database configuration information and a prefilled database password. The source does not disclose the password itself. Analysts say this case highlights a risk that goes beyond a lookalike sign-in page. If a user enters a password or verification code on a fake site, criminals may be able to use those details to try to access the account. The available report does not provide a full account of the page’s design, how victims reach it, or whether any accounts were confirmed stolen. Anurag (@Malwarehunterr) identified and noted the campaign in a post describing the two domains, the exposed installation page, and the related web paths. Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages Google Meet is commonly used for work meetings, classes, and personal calls, so a page that looks like a meeting link may not raise immediate concern. The two domains reported in this case are meet-google[.]cyou and qooglo[.]com . Their names resemble Google-related terms, but neither is the genuine meet.google.com domain. Users should check the complete website address before entering a password, even when the page uses familiar logos or meeting language. The researcher’s post describes the pages as designed to steal Google credentials and facilitate 2FA phishing. It does not spell out the exact steps in the sign-in process or explain whether the site relays authentication in real time. In general, a stolen password can put an account at risk; a captured verification code may add further danger if criminals use it quickly. Google advises users to choose stronger verification options, such as security keys or Google prompts, and says passkeys are designed to resist phishing. items.summary_html:
Two websites are hosting fake Google Meet pages designed to steal Google account credentials and carry out phishing involving two-factor authentication (2FA), according to threat intelligence shared on October 20, 2026.

The pages imitate a familiar meeting service to make a request for account details look more believable. The researcher also reported a serious security issue on an exposed /install page: it reveals database configuration information and a prefilled database password.

The source does not disclose the password itself. Analysts say this case highlights a risk that goes beyond a lookalike sign-in page. If a user enters a password or verification code on a fake site, criminals may be able to use those details to try to access the account.

The available report does not provide a full account of the page’s design, how victims reach it, or whether any accounts were confirmed stolen.

Anurag (@Malwarehunterr) identified and noted the campaign in a post describing the two domains, the exposed installation page, and the related web paths.

Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages

Google Meet is commonly used for work meetings, classes, and personal calls, so a page that looks like a meeting link may not raise immediate concern.

The two domains reported in this case are meet-google[.]cyou and qooglo[.]com. Their names resemble Google-related terms, but neither is the genuine meet.google.com domain.

Users should check the complete website address before entering a password, even when the page uses familiar logos or meeting language.

The researcher’s post describes the pages as designed to steal Google credentials and facilitate 2FA phishing. It does not spell out the exact steps in the sign-in process or explain whether the site relays authentication in real time.

In general, a stolen password can put an account at risk; a captured verification code may add further danger if criminals use it quickly.

Google advises users to choose stronger verification options, such as security keys or Google prompts, and says passkeys are designed to resist phishing.

Google Meet Phishing

Two domains hosting fake Google Meet pages designed to steal Google credentials and facilitate 2FA phishing.

Misconfiguration: An exposed /install page reveals database configuration and a prefilled DB password!

IOCs:

meet-google[.]cyou
qooglo[.]com… pic.twitter.com/u50nHZ2zME

— Anurag (@Malwarehunterr) October 19, 2026

This matters because an account can hold more than email. Depending on the user’s settings and connected services, access may expose documents, contacts, saved information, or business data.

A successful sign-in can also help a criminal send believable messages from the victim’s account. Google recommends reviewing recent security events and devices if a user suspects unauthorized access. For more background on how attackers can target Google sign-ins and authentication, readers can see this report on a Google account phishing kit.

Exposed installation page raises a separate concern

The reported /install page adds a second issue to the credential theft risk. According to the post, visiting that path exposes database configuration and a prefilled database password.

Such information may help an unauthorized visitor understand how a site’s backend is set up. The report does not say whether the exposed details were used to access the database, and the password value is not included in the source.

A misconfigured setup page should not be publicly available with sensitive information filled in. Site operators should restrict access to installation and setup routes, remove default or prefilled secrets, and review whether any credentials displayed on the page remain valid.

If they do, they should be changed and any systems using them checked. These are practical defensive steps based on the exposure described; the available report does not confirm what response the site owners have taken.

The report also lists web paths associated with the campaign: /meet, /assets/js/demo.js, /api/demo/sessions, /api/demo/sessions/{token}, and /api/demo/sessions/{token}/resend.

These paths may help defenders search relevant web logs, but a path alone does not prove that a system or user has been compromised. The source does not provide a sample file, malware name, IP address, or cryptographic hash.

Lookalike services remain a common theme in phishing. Cybersecurity News has previously reported on a Gmail phishing login flow that sought account details, and on fake Google Forms pages used to collect credentials.

A separate campaign used a fake Meet page to push a malicious command rather than simply request a password, as described in this Google Meet ClickFix report. Those reports describe different campaigns; they should not be treated as evidence that the same operators are behind this one.

Users should open Google Meet by typing its known address or using a trusted calendar invitation, rather than signing in through an unexpected page.

Check the full domain carefully: a padlock or HTTPS connection only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site belongs to Google. Do not enter a password or 2FA code after following an unfamiliar link.

Anyone who may have entered credentials should change the Google password through Google’s official account page, review recent security events, and remove unfamiliar devices or sessions.

If the password was reused elsewhere, change it on those services too. Google’s guidance explains how to secure a compromised account and review account activity. Organizations should also check sign-in logs for suspicious access and alert staff to the reported domains and paths.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- TypeIndicatorDomainmeet-google[.]cyouDomainqooglo[.]comWeb path/meetWeb path/installWeb path/assets/js/demo.jsAPI path/api/demo/sessionsAPI path/api/demo/sessions/{token}API path/api/demo/sessions/{token}/resend

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs.

items.title: Cybersecurity, AI, and Digital Sovereignty at the ICT Austria Industry Forum 2026
items.summary: How are cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and digital sovereignty connected? And what challenges does this pose for businesses? Managing Partner Marc Nimmerrichter addressed these questions at the ICT Austria Industry Forum 2026. The event brought together representatives from business, politics, academia, and technology to discuss key questions about Europe’s digital future. In his presentation, Marc used real-world examples to show how AI is changing vulnerability research and what new challenges this creates for cybersecurity. The capabilities that AI offers security experts are equally available to potential attackers, which changes the speed at which vulnerabilities can be discovered and exploited. Another focus was digital sovereignty and the question of how companies can assess their technological dependencies and remain able to act in the long term. Many thanks to ICT Austria for the invitation, the opportunity to share our experience, and the stimulating exchange! You can find more highlights from the event in ICT Austria’s photo gallery . Photos: (c) David Bohmann To learn how AI agents are changing the cybersecurity threat landscape, check out our blog post: The New Reality in Cybersecurity: AI Agents, Acceleration, and Asymmetry – Certitude Blog

items.title: Beyond Passwords: How Attackers Abuse Device Code Authentication
items.summary: By: Adriane Andaya, Cofense Phishing Defense Center The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has analyzed several emails that may look like ordinary spam to the untrained eye. Threat actors attempt to mimic routine corporate emails and blend into everyday inbox traffic. As aware of the common phishing tac tactics grows, threat actors are turning to techniques such as device code phishing. To understand how this technique works, it is important to understand what access codes are and how they differ from the common username-and-password method of authentication. Access codes are temporary codes that are entered instead of the users’ credentials on devices that are requesting authentication. While this method can simplify sign-ins, attackers can abuse it. If a victim completes the sign-in process, they may unknowingly authorize the threat actor’s session, which potentially grants access to the account and associated resources. Figure 1: Fake bid invitation email Cofense PDC analysts have handled several of these malicious emails that use subjects designed to capture the recipient’s interest. As illustrated in Figure 1, the email appears to be a regular bidding invitation, but when the recipient clicks on the link to view the project details, they’re redirected to a fake login page and prompted to enter their email. Microsoft branding is used to make the page appear more trustworthy. Figure 2: Syncfusion phishing login page from the embedded URL Figure 3: Spoofed Mimecast device enrollment page As shown in Figure 2, the threat actors leveraged familiar brands such as Syncfusion and Microsoft to give the phishing page an appearance of legitimacy. The attack then proceeds after the victim has entered their email address. As seen in Figure 3, a very convincing spoofed Mimecast page adds another layer of legitimacy, encouraging the victim to enroll their device under the guise of an IT policy. It is important to note that despite these familiar brands being used, the URL in the address bar does not match any of these brands’ registered domains. This mismatch should be an immediate red flag. By incorporating well-known brands, threat actors exploit familiarity to increase the likelihood of a successful phishing attempt. Figure 4: Access code generation Figure 5: Microsoft pop-up window Figure 4 shows that a code will be generated, and a button to “view the document” will be presented to the user, which opens a Microsoft window (Figure 5) prompting the user to enter the code to allow access. Microsoft warns that entering the code will grant the originating application or device access to the account without requiring the user’s password and may bypass the protection normally provided by MFA. The second warning advises users not to enter codes from unverified sources. If a code from an untrusted source has been entered, it must be treated as an account compromise, and you must immediately notify your IT department. You can also take these steps to prevent or minimize the account breach: Change the account password. Sign out of all active sessions or revoke existing sessions. Review recent account activity for suspicious or unauthorized access. Review authorized applications and remove any unfamiliar or suspicious entries. Re-verify registered security and MFA methods. Check for unauthorized account changes, including sent emails, deleted items, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, or other modified settings. This tactic targets decision-makers, management-level personnel, and key figures, but anyone can fall victim to this phishing campaign. It is crucial to verify any agreement, contract, or other related documents, especially if they are from an unfamiliar sender. In some cases, even familiar emails have been compromised and have been used to send emails that contain malicious URLs or attachments. To prevent your account from being compromised, you must check for any suspicious signs on the website you will be redirected to before entering any credentials. As the digital threat landscape continues to shift and threat actors exploit new attack vectors, practicing good cyber hygiene and staying informed about emerging threats remain essential. While no security measure can eliminate all risks, staying vigilant and adopting safe digital habits can go a long way toward keeping you and your credentials secure. However, as sophisticated tactics like device code phishing demonstrate, individual awareness alone is not enough. Organizations also need the ability to detect and respond to threats that slip past traditional security controls. Cofense combines real-world threat intelligence, AI-driven detection, and human expertise to help organizations identify and respond to these evolving phishing threats. Learn how Cofense can help strengthen your organization's phishing defenses: https://cofense.com/platform.

items.title: SBI Data Breach Claim – Hackers Allegedly Claim Access to 3.75 Lakh Users’ Database
items.summary: An unverified SBI data breach claim alleges that a threat actor named Siriusim posted customer records and banking documents online. The claimed dataset contains 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files, but those figures do not establish that 3.75 lakh unique customers were affected. CyberPulse reported the allegation on October 16, 2026. Its post described personal customer information, loan applications, supporting documents, account-opening forms and address details. The actor called it the first disclosure of the dataset. The authenticity, source and extent of the alleged exposure remain unverified. SBI Data Breach Claim According to India Today , Siriusim posted the claim on BreachForums and shared what it described as four sample customer records. The report said the material may include Know Your Customer (KYC) records, Aadhaar numbers and residential addresses. These details remain allegations rather than confirmed findings from an investigation. CSV files store information in rows and columns, while PDFs can hold forms and scanned documents. A row count alone cannot show how many people appear in a dataset. Multiple applications or duplicate entries could relate to the same person, and document totals do not prove separate victims. India Today reported on October 19 that SBI had not addressed the claims when its article was published. The outlet said it had requested comment and could not independently confirm the breach. It also remained unclear whether the material was newly exposed or recycled from earlier leaks. The available reports do not establish how the alleged records were obtained. Their source could not be traced to SBI itself, a subsidiary or a service provider handling banking applications. There is no verified evidence in these reports identifying an exploited flaw, stolen login or compromised server. That uncertainty matters because documents bearing a bank’s name do not, by themselves, establish access to its core banking systems. Any investigation would need to validate samples, identify their owner, and check the claimed records against system logs before drawing conclusions about the source or scale. If genuine, the records could support identity theft, loan fraud and targeted phishing. Criminals could use application details to make fake bank calls or messages sound convincing. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake SBI reward apps and fraudulent YONO deactivation alerts , both relevant examples of banking impersonation, not evidence connecting those campaigns to this claim. Customers should verify unexpected bank messages through official channels, avoid shared APK files, and never disclose passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords. SBI should assess the claim, preserve logs, and notify affected customers if an investigation confirms exposure. Until then, this remains an alleged data leak, not a confirmed compromise of accounts. items.title: One Hacker Uses AI Agents to Breach Over 100 Company Websites for Just $5,000
items.summary: A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites while spending an estimated $5,000 on AI tokens, according to a Reuters investigation in October. The operation shows how one person can direct software to carry out complex attacks with little ongoing human input. The targets included sites linked to Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, although the reported impact differed across those companies. After the campaign began on September 25, the agents attempted to compromise more than 1,200 websites, mainly online stores in the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at NorForge, uncovered the activity while searching for exposed Cairn installations, an open-source platform that coordinates AI agents. Around October 2, he found roughly two dozen installations apparently being used for malicious activity. How Cairn Automated the Attacks Cairn is a general-purpose problem-solving engine rather than a tool built only for hacking. In the attacks described in NorForge’s technical report , operators supplied a target and a goal, then agents searched for weaknesses and worked toward gaining access. The platform stores findings on a shared project board so its agents can use earlier discoveries to choose their next steps. That allows them to try different paths when an initial approach fails, instead of relying on a single fixed scan. NorForge tracked the largest Chinese-language activity cluster as AIA0001, linking it to 14 dashboards containing more than 1,100 attack projects. Its target pipeline used Microsoft’s Playwright browser automation tool to check that shopping sites could accept orders before passing them to Cairn. The task instructions focused on finding ways to run code without signing in, including SQL injection, unsafe file uploads, login bypasses and unsafe handling of stored objects. The apparent aim was lasting access to shopping and payment systems that could later generate money. NorForge confirmed one claimed breach by checking a reported address on a hardware vendor’s website and finding a live uploader webshell. This server-side script allowed files to be placed on the compromised site, creating a foothold for further attacks. According to the agent’s own account, that attack combined unauthorized write access to a memcached session store with unsafe PHP object deserialization and older Zend Framework components. The chain turned weaknesses in session storage and object processing into server access, rather than depending on one obvious entry point. In another case, agents moved beyond a company’s main application after failing to find a weakness. They searched related infrastructure, found an exposed control panel, and spent hours testing its handling of data before reporting that they could run commands on the server. Low Costs, Long Running Agents Successful AIA0001 projects took just under 23 hours on average, while one ran for more than five days. Across the observed campaigns, NorForge estimated success at around 10%, although goals and targets varied between operators. Fagerland estimated the main campaign consumed about $5,000 in tokens, or roughly $50 per successful intrusion. These figures are estimates, not confirmed billing records. NorForge separately put the average task cost near $5 when failed and early-ending attempts were included, warning that uncertainty was substantial. Worker names suggested a Claude Code setup using a DeepSeek model, but NorForge did not confirm the full model configuration. Chinese-language instructions also do not establish the operator’s nationality, and researchers found no obvious state-backed activity in the exposed panels. Related reporting on AI agents used to steal retail credit card data described a separate campaign involving Cairn and other tools. Another investigation into DeepSeek-powered credential theft showed attackers using agents to exploit exposed secrets and weak settings, rather than relying on new flaws. Deere told Reuters it took corrective action and found no indication that attackers accessed sensitive information. SharkNinja said the affected system was a separate product support site and that the threat had been contained. Cummins was investigating a possible attack on a third-party-run website. Reuters could not determine how much data, if any, was taken across the breaches. NorForge also found hundreds of exposed secrets in the open panels and said it was working with Reuters to notify victims. The exposure also affected legitimate security testers. NorForge found unsecured testing dashboards revealing customer information, showing that poorly protected AI tools create risk during authorized work. Defenders should patch public-facing applications, restrict access to admin panels, and watch for unexpected files in web directories. Security teams should also review suspicious web requests and isolate servers where webshells are found, then investigate for stolen data, further access, and other malware before restoring service. items.title: Claude AI Detects Hidden Crypto Miner While Building Temperature Monitor App on Mac
items.summary: An ordinary coding task led to an unexpected security discovery when Claude Code reportedly found a hidden cryptocurrency miner on a developer’s Mac. The AI assistant was building a temperature monitoring app when unusually high sensor readings prompted it to investigate CPU activity. It identified XMRig consuming about 1,175% CPU, described as roughly 12 cores of processing load. The developer, posting as u/UntilHEX on Reddit , said Claude checked running processes after reviewing raw sensor data. The discovery offered an explanation for the Mac’s poor performance. However, the account remains a user report supported by a screenshot, rather than a published forensic investigation. High CPU Usage Exposed the Hidden Miner According to the shared screenshot, Claude reported that the CPU had peaked at 112°C. “Your Mac is running a cryptominer that I didn’t put there,” the assistant warned. Those figures reflect the reported session and have not been independently verified through hardware logs or a separate examination. The screenshot identified /tmp/rigupdater as the miner’s running location and pool.hashvault.sh as its mining pool destination. These details provide useful leads for investigators examining this specific device. They do not establish how the software arrived, who installed it, or whether other systems were affected. XMRig is not inherently malicious. It is mining software with official macOS builds, including support for Apple Silicon. The security concern is its apparent use without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Finding the program alone would not prove an infection without examining its installation, configuration, and activity. LaunchAgent Reportedly Kept the Miner Running Claude also flagged a suspicious property list file inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ . The screenshot described a randomly named startup entry dated August 29 that ran a large encoded script through bash , with KeepAlive enabled. Claude said the entry was already present before its development work began. Apple’s LaunchAgent documentation explains that user agents run within a logged-in user’s session. The KeepAlive setting can tell launchd to keep a job running. That makes the startup entry important because stopping a process without disabling its launcher may allow it to return. LaunchAgents themselves are legitimate macOS features, not automatic proof of malware. The screenshot also raised concern about credentials available on the Mac, including its GitHub login. That warning describes possible exposure, not confirmed theft. The public evidence does not show that passwords, access tokens, source code, or other files were stolen. The infection route and full scope remain unknown. Claude initially said it had not killed or removed anything. Instead, it requested permission to stop the startup item and miner, then move files into quarantine. UntilHEX later said the assistant performed cleanup, although one file required manual deletion because of an access issue. The behavior resembles techniques seen in other Mac threats, without proving a connection. Cyber Security News previously covered fake CAPTCHA attacks that install a backdoor and XMRig . That campaign used a LaunchAgent and could combine mining with password theft, showing why removing a miner alone may leave risks behind. Separate reporting on CrashStealer’s abuse of Apple crash-reporting branding also documented LaunchAgent persistence. Neither campaign has been linked to UntilHEX’s Mac. Their relevance is the shared use of trusted operating system features to keep unwanted software running. For affected users, the practical lesson is to investigate unexplained heat and sustained CPU load, review persistence, and check account exposure. Suspected compromise warrants isolation and password changes from a clean device. Claude’s discovery was useful, but the reported cleanup does not establish that every threat was removed. An ordinary coding task led to an unexpected security discovery when Claude Code reportedly found a hidden cryptocurrency miner on a developer’s Mac. The AI assistant was building a temperature monitoring app when unusually high sensor readings prompted it to investigate CPU activity. It identified XMRig consuming about 1,175% CPU, described as roughly 12 cores of processing load.

The developer, posting as u/UntilHEX on Reddit, said Claude checked running processes after reviewing raw sensor data. The discovery offered an explanation for the Mac’s poor performance. However, the account remains a user report supported by a screenshot, rather than a published forensic investigation.

High CPU Usage Exposed the Hidden Miner

According to the shared screenshot, Claude reported that the CPU had peaked at 112°C. “Your Mac is running a cryptominer that I didn’t put there,” the assistant warned. Those figures reflect the reported session and have not been independently verified through hardware logs or a separate examination.

The screenshot identified /tmp/rigupdater as the miner’s running location and pool.hashvault.sh as its mining pool destination. These details provide useful leads for investigators examining this specific device. They do not establish how the software arrived, who installed it, or whether other systems were affected.

XMRig is not inherently malicious. It is mining software with official macOS builds, including support for Apple Silicon. The security concern is its apparent use without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Finding the program alone would not prove an infection without examining its installation, configuration, and activity.

LaunchAgent Reportedly Kept the Miner Running

Claude also flagged a suspicious property list file inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/. The screenshot described a randomly named startup entry dated August 29 that ran a large encoded script through bash, with KeepAlive enabled. Claude said the entry was already present before its development work began.

Apple’s LaunchAgent documentation explains that user agents run within a logged-in user’s session. The KeepAlive setting can tell launchd to keep a job running. That makes the startup entry important because stopping a process without disabling its launcher may allow it to return. LaunchAgents themselves are legitimate macOS features, not automatic proof of malware.

The screenshot also raised concern about credentials available on the Mac, including its GitHub login. That warning describes possible exposure, not confirmed theft. The public evidence does not show that passwords, access tokens, source code, or other files were stolen. The infection route and full scope remain unknown.

Claude initially said it had not killed or removed anything. Instead, it requested permission to stop the startup item and miner, then move files into quarantine. UntilHEX later said the assistant performed cleanup, although one file required manual deletion because of an access issue.

The behavior resembles techniques seen in other Mac threats, without proving a connection. Cyber Security News previously covered fake CAPTCHA attacks that install a backdoor and XMRig. That campaign used a LaunchAgent and could combine mining with password theft, showing why removing a miner alone may leave risks behind.

Separate reporting on CrashStealer’s abuse of Apple crash-reporting branding also documented LaunchAgent persistence. Neither campaign has been linked to UntilHEX’s Mac. Their relevance is the shared use of trusted operating system features to keep unwanted software running.

For affected users, the practical lesson is to investigate unexplained heat and sustained CPU load, review persistence, and check account exposure. Suspected compromise warrants isolation and password changes from a clean device. Claude’s discovery was useful, but the reported cleanup does not establish that every threat was removed.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The post Claude AI Detects Hidden Crypto Miner While Building Temperature Monitor App on Mac appeared first on Cyber Security News.

items.title: introducing The CISO Game
items.summary: There is no flight simulator for the CISO's chair. So I made one. The CISO Game is free, takes about 40 minutes, and gives you three years in the hot seat. The Standardised Staples cyber security team debate an investment decision Pilots don't meet their first crisis in the air. They meet it in a simulator, again and again, until the right response is a habit rather than a guess. Cyber security leaders and Chief Information Security Officers have no such luxury. Most of us met our first serious incident live: a board watching, a budget already spent, and advice arriving from every direction at once. You learn a great deal very quickly. You also learn it at the company's expense. That gap has bothered me for a long time, and not only for CISOs. Boards are asked to oversee cyber risk without ever having made the trade-offs themselves. Security professionals move from technical roles into leadership and discover that the job is mostly about relationships, resources and judgement. Students learn about threats and controls in the abstract, without seeing how they collide inside a real organisation. In practice, technical idealism then clashes with commercial reality. You can't learn this from a textbook or an exam, so I made a game anyone can play. It's called The CISO Game , and you can play it now at cisogame.mattpalmer.net (Source) . Welcome to Standardised Staples Standardised Staples is a fictional, mid-sized staple manufacturer with manufacturing, retail and services divisions. Its intranet looks like it was built some time ago, and so do its security controls. You are its new Chief Information Security Officer. Your job is to get the company ready for the future we all know is coming, without running out of money, losing the board, or losing the company. In doing this, you'll work with a wide range of characters all of whom have different goals and needs. What you actually do The game runs for three years, played as twelve quarters. Each quarter you are briefed on a rising threat and hear from four advisors. Each argues for their own corner: technology, people, governance and insurance, or saving money. None of them knows what attack is coming. You decide where to spend a limited budget and your team's limited time to improve your cyber security posture. An attack arrives and is tested against your controls. If it gets through, you run the response against the clock: contain, remove the attacker, recover, and keep people informed throughout. The most serious incidents end in a press conference, where you brief the CEO before facing journalists who have an uncanny knack of finding your weakest areas. Along the way, the game models the things that are easy to forget when you're drawing up a strategy. Controls you neglect wear down over time. Colleagues and stakeholders seek to influence your decisions. Insurance can soften a loss, but has limitations. A team whose advice you ignore gets less done. And every time you ask the board for more money or people, you spend some of their goodwill, whether they say yes or not. The game ends when you are fired, when the company goes into administration, or when you survive all twelve quarters. Survivors get one of four outcomes, from Demoted to Promoted to the Board. Everyone gets a written performance review. Why a game? Last year I wrote about why compulsory CBTs and phishing tests keep failing . You can force people to tick boxes, but you can't force people to learn. People learn when they are engaged, and when their decisions have consequences they can see. A game gives you both. You make a call, you see what happens, and you try again with a different approach. Over a few games the lessons that matter most become hard to miss: there is never enough money or time to do everything, advice conflicts, attacks get through even good defences, and how you respond matters as much as what you bought. There is uncertainty in it, just as there is in real life. Strong controls make an attack much less likely to succeed, but never impossible, and weak ones don't guarantee a breach. Each game draws its scenarios and attacks afresh, so no two are the same. You won't find the rules and numbers published anywhere, and that is deliberate. A real CISO has to judge risk without knowing the odds. It's about developing professional judgement, not calculation. Built on real frameworks It's a game, but it isn't made up from scratch. The eleven control areas you invest in are groupings of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 . Every attack is described in FAIR terms, with losses split between the direct cost and the fines, lost customers and reputational damage that follow. Incident response follows the containment, eradication and recovery steps of NIST SP 800-61. These provide a vocabulary and a structure, not a compliance test. The game simplifies a great deal so it can be played in under an hour: a year passes in about ten minutes, and the characters are deliberate caricatures. It is a game, not professional advice. Play it together The game can be played on your own, but some of the best conversations come from playing it as a group. Anyone with an account can host a group game for a class, a seminar or a team, in the room or online. Players join with a three-word code, and up to 40 teams or individuals can take part. Every game in the group gets the same scenarios, the same attacks and the same luck. So when one team survives an attack that sinks another, the difference came from the decisions they made. That is where the discussion starts, and at the end of each year, everyone sees a scoreboard of how each team is doing. If you sit on a board, why not play it as a board or with your executive team, with an advisor or your own CISO as facilitator? If you teach, there is a guide for educators . Why 'Standardised Staples'? Standardised Staples is not based on any individual company. It draws heavily on my early experience working with a regional development agency as an IT Advisor to industrial and manufacturing companies in the north of England. Whilst most of my career has been spent as a CISO in global financial services, I feel an affinity for companies that make a physical product efficiently and at scale, often at narrow margins, and yet still manage to innovate and reinvent themselves. They are impressively serious about what they do, and yet can also be vulnerable to shocks. They are the companies that the world we live in was built on. They are the sort of company that would really benefit from good security leadership, yet might struggle to obtain it. Standardised Staples is such a company. How it was made I designed the game and built it with Anthropic's Claude Code. Each character in the game is unique, and much of what they say to you is written by Claude as you play, in response to your decisions and the events that unfold. The scores are always calculated by the game itself, never by the AI. Each scenario is based around incidents that really happen. All the scenarios and incidents in the game are ones I have dealt with in practice. The game runs to about 25,000 lines of TypeScript, React, CSS and SQL: roughly 17,400 for the game itself, 6,100 for tests and 850 for tools such as the simulator. Development ran over a week: 198 code commits, 77 pull requests and 276 design decisions so far. Over 400,000 simulated games were played by bots to calibrate the game mechanics. The pre-launch balance review alone played 164,000 (41 variants of a strategy, 4,000 games each), with further runs of 20,000 games for close calls. No personal data is needed, and you don't need an account to play. Every game also leaves an anonymous record of choices, which over time should tell us something useful about how these decisions are made. Your turn Give it 40 minutes. See whether you make it to the Board. And you don't? We learn far more from our failures than from our wins! Play the CISO Game at cisogame.mattpalmer.net . References Available at: https://cisogame.mattpalmer.net (Accessed: 20 October 2026). Incidentally by Matt Palmer

There is no flight simulator for the CISO's chair. So I made one.

The CISO Game is free, takes about 40 minutes, and gives you three years in the hot seat.

The Standardised Staples cyber security team debate an investment decision

Pilots don't meet their first crisis in the air. They meet it in a simulator, again and again, until the right response is a habit rather than a guess.

Cyber security leaders and Chief Information Security Officers have no such luxury. Most of us met our first serious incident live: a board watching, a budget already spent, and advice arriving from every direction at once. You learn a great deal very quickly. You also learn it at the company's expense.

That gap has bothered me for a long time, and not only for CISOs. Boards are asked to oversee cyber risk without ever having made the trade-offs themselves. Security professionals move from technical roles into leadership and discover that the job is mostly about relationships, resources and judgement. Students learn about threats and controls in the abstract, without seeing how they collide inside a real organisation. In practice, technical idealism then clashes with commercial reality.

You can't learn this from a textbook or an exam, so I made a game anyone can play. It's called The CISO Game, and you can play it now at cisogame.mattpalmer.net (Source).

Welcome to Standardised Staples

Standardised Staples is a fictional, mid-sized staple manufacturer with manufacturing, retail and services divisions. Its intranet looks like it was built some time ago, and so do its security controls.

You are its new Chief Information Security Officer. Your job is to get the company ready for the future we all know is coming, without running out of money, losing the board, or losing the company.

In doing this, you'll work with a wide range of characters all of whom have different goals and needs.

What you actually do

The game runs for three years, played as twelve quarters. Each quarter you are briefed on a rising threat and hear from four advisors. Each argues for their own corner: technology, people, governance and insurance, or saving money. None of them knows what attack is coming.

You decide where to spend a limited budget and your team's limited time to improve your cyber security posture. An attack arrives and is tested against your controls.

If it gets through, you run the response against the clock: contain, remove the attacker, recover, and keep people informed throughout. The most serious incidents end in a press conference, where you brief the CEO before facing journalists who have an uncanny knack of finding your weakest areas.

Along the way, the game models the things that are easy to forget when you're drawing up a strategy. Controls you neglect wear down over time. Colleagues and stakeholders seek to influence your decisions. Insurance can soften a loss, but has limitations. A team whose advice you ignore gets less done. And every time you ask the board for more money or people, you spend some of their goodwill, whether they say yes or not.

The game ends when you are fired, when the company goes into administration, or when you survive all twelve quarters. Survivors get one of four outcomes, from Demoted to Promoted to the Board. Everyone gets a written performance review.

Why a game?

Last year I wrote about why compulsory CBTs and phishing tests keep failing. You can force people to tick boxes, but you can't force people to learn. People learn when they are engaged, and when their decisions have consequences they can see.

A game gives you both. You make a call, you see what happens, and you try again with a different approach. Over a few games the lessons that matter most become hard to miss: there is never enough money or time to do everything, advice conflicts, attacks get through even good defences, and how you respond matters as much as what you bought.

There is uncertainty in it, just as there is in real life. Strong controls make an attack much less likely to succeed, but never impossible, and weak ones don't guarantee a breach. Each game draws its scenarios and attacks afresh, so no two are the same.

You won't find the rules and numbers published anywhere, and that is deliberate. A real CISO has to judge risk without knowing the odds. It's about developing professional judgement, not calculation.

Built on real frameworks

It's a game, but it isn't made up from scratch. The eleven control areas you invest in are groupings of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Every attack is described in FAIR terms, with losses split between the direct cost and the fines, lost customers and reputational damage that follow. Incident response follows the containment, eradication and recovery steps of NIST SP 800-61.

These provide a vocabulary and a structure, not a compliance test. The game simplifies a great deal so it can be played in under an hour: a year passes in about ten minutes, and the characters are deliberate caricatures. It is a game, not professional advice.

Play it together

The game can be played on your own, but some of the best conversations come from playing it as a group.

Anyone with an account can host a group game for a class, a seminar or a team, in the room or online. Players join with a three-word code, and up to 40 teams or individuals can take part. Every game in the group gets the same scenarios, the same attacks and the same luck. So when one team survives an attack that sinks another, the difference came from the decisions they made. That is where the discussion starts, and at the end of each year, everyone sees a scoreboard of how each team is doing.

If you sit on a board, why not play it as a board or with your executive team, with an advisor or your own CISO as facilitator?

If you teach, there is a guide for educators.

Why 'Standardised Staples'?

Standardised Staples is not based on any individual company. It draws heavily on my early experience working with a regional development agency as an IT Advisor to industrial and manufacturing companies in the north of England. Whilst most of my career has been spent as a CISO in global financial services, I feel an affinity for companies that make a physical product efficiently and at scale, often at narrow margins, and yet still manage to innovate and reinvent themselves. They are impressively serious about what they do, and yet can also be vulnerable to shocks. They are the companies that the world we live in was built on. They are the sort of company that would really benefit from good security leadership, yet might struggle to obtain it. Standardised Staples is such a company.

How it was made

I designed the game and built it with Anthropic's Claude Code. Each character in the game is unique, and much of what they say to you is written by Claude as you play, in response to your decisions and the events that unfold. The scores are always calculated by the game itself, never by the AI.

Each scenario is based around incidents that really happen. All the scenarios and incidents in the game are ones I have dealt with in practice.

The game runs to about 25,000 lines of TypeScript, React, CSS and SQL: roughly 17,400 for the game itself, 6,100 for tests and 850 for tools such as the simulator. Development ran over a week: 198 code commits, 77 pull requests and 276 design decisions so far.

Over 400,000 simulated games were played by bots to calibrate the game mechanics. The pre-launch balance review alone played 164,000 (41 variants of a strategy, 4,000 games each), with further runs of 20,000 games for close calls.

No personal data is needed, and you don't need an account to play.

Every game also leaves an anonymous record of choices, which over time should tell us something useful about how these decisions are made.

Give it 40 minutes. See whether you make it to the Board.

items.title: Kubernetes Extension Pack release for Podman Desktop
items.summary: Kubernetes Extension Pack for Podman Desktop Release! 🎉 This Kubernetes Extension Pack release includes Kubernetes Dashboard v0.6.0, Kubernetes Contexts v0.3.0, and Kreate v0.4.0. The new releases have been added to the catalog. If automatic extension updates are enabled (the default), Podman Desktop updates already installed extensions automatically. If you have not installed the extensions, open the Extensions > Catalog page, search for the Kubernetes Extension Pack or for Kubernetes Dashboard, Kubernetes Contexts, and Kreate, and install them. note Podman Desktop is moving Kubernetes dashboard and context management from core into extensions so they can evolve and release independently of the desktop app. The Kubernetes Extension Pack remains available in Podman Desktop's catalog, making the full set easy to install while letting you choose individual extensions. The Kubernetes Dashboard extension also exposes Kubernetes resource data through an API that other extensions can use. Installing either Kubernetes Dashboard or Kubernetes Contexts disables the corresponding feature in core. The built-in features will not evolve and will be removed in a future release, so we recommend switching to the extensions for new features. These extensions now include: Apply YAML : Apply Kubernetes YAML from a dedicated page in Kubernetes Dashboard. Container logs : View logs of terminated containers, unfollow the log stream, and see the configured tail line count in the terminal. Deployment scaling : Scale Deployments directly from the UI. Resource tables and details : Choose visible columns on all resource tables, see more information on the pod page, and view Internal IP on the nodes list. Collapsible navigation : Sidebar grouped into collapsible sections with icons, including a new Access Control section. New resource views : DaemonSets, StatefulSets, ReplicaSets, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, Endpoints, EndpointSlices, NetworkPolicies, IngressClasses, HTTPRoutes, Gateways, GatewayClasses, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, PodDisruptionBudgets, PriorityClasses, RuntimeClasses, Leases, HorizontalPodAutoscalers, MutatingWebhookConfigurations, and ValidatingWebhookConfigurations. Lazy resource loading : Resources are watched on demand as you navigate. Extension API : Other extensions can access Kubernetes resource data, and data from the Discovery API. Context deletion confirmation : Kubernetes Contexts now always asks for confirmation before deleting a context. Kreate : Create namespaces, Jobs, and CronJobs, and select any Kubernetes resource type based on the Discovery API. Release details ​ Apply YAML ​ Kubernetes Dashboard now includes a dedicated Apply YAML page. Open it from the Apply YAML button on resource list pages to apply manifests to your cluster without leaving Podman Desktop. You can apply YAML in two ways: select a .yaml or .yml file from disk, or write custom YAML from scratch in the built-in editor. Choose the Kubernetes context to apply to, then run the apply action. The dashboard creates new resources on the cluster. If an existing resource uses a supported built-in Kubernetes API, it is updated with a strategic merge patch ( Content-Type: application/strategic-merge-patch+json ). That patch type is not supported for CustomResourceDefinition APIs, so existing custom resources are not updated. When the apply completes, you get a summary of how many resources were applied and of which kinds. You can still patch an existing resource from the YAML tab on its details page, including custom resources the dashboard shows such as Gateways. That path uses a strategic merge patch for built-in APIs and server-side apply for kinds provided by a CustomResourceDefinition, which the API server accepts for those APIs. Container logs ​ The Logs tab on a pod details page now makes it easier to inspect container output, including containers that have already stopped. You can open logs for a container that is no longer running. Terminated containers stay in the container list, marked as not running, so you can still read their previous output. Previous logs also works for restarted containers, so you can inspect the output from the previous instance. Uncheck Stream logs to stop following the live stream and scroll through the captured lines at your own pace. The Stream logs option is only shown for running containers. The line count you set is passed through to the terminal scrollback, so the terminal keeps the number of lines you requested. Deployment scaling ​ You can now scale a Deployment from the Deployments list, without opening kubectl or editing YAML. Change the replica count in place on the Deployments list or details page, so you can add capacity or scale down without leaving the overview of status and conditions. The change is applied only after you confirm it. Scaling updates the Kubernetes Deployment scale subresource. That matters when your RBAC allows patching deployments/scale but not the Deployment itself. Resource tables and details ​ Resource lists now let you choose which columns to show and in which order, so each table can match the information you actually use. Hide columns you do not need, bring the ones you care about forward, and reset to the default layout when you want a clean slate. This uses the same column editing as other Podman Desktop tables, and it is available on every resource table, not only Pods. The pod details page also shows more of the workload context, and the Nodes list includes an Internal IP column so you can find a node's cluster address without leaving the dashboard. Collapsible navigation ​ The sidebar is grouped into collapsible sections, so the many new resource types stay organized instead of filling a long flat list. Resources are grouped under Compute, Config, Network, Storage, and a new Access Control section for RBAC. Collapse the areas you are not using to keep the sidebar scannable. The dashboard remembers which sections you left open, and expands a section when you open a resource that belongs to it. For example, opening a Service from the dashboard expands Network even if that section was collapsed. New resource views ​ Kubernetes Dashboard now covers many more resource kinds, so you can inspect more of the cluster without switching to kubectl. Compute: DaemonSets, StatefulSets, and ReplicaSets. Storage: PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses. Network: Endpoints, EndpointSlices, NetworkPolicies, IngressClasses, HTTPRoutes, Gateways, and GatewayClasses. Config: ServiceAccounts, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, PodDisruptionBudgets, PriorityClasses, RuntimeClasses, Leases, HorizontalPodAutoscalers, MutatingWebhookConfigurations, and ValidatingWebhookConfigurations. Access Control: Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, and ClusterRoleBindings. Lazy resource loading ​ The dashboard no longer watches every resource kind as soon as you connect. It starts watching a kind when you open that resource's page. Common resources such as Pods, Deployments, and Services are still watched immediately, so the dashboard overview can show live counts. The many new kinds, such as Roles, Gateways, StorageClasses, and many more, wait until you visit them. That keeps startup faster and reduces load on the API server. Extension API ​ Other Podman Desktop extensions can now use the Kubernetes Dashboard API instead of opening their own connection to the cluster. They can subscribe to live resource data, context health, and permissions from the dashboard's existing watches. Kubernetes Contexts uses that subscriber for the state of each context, instead of watching the cluster on its own. They can also call the Kubernetes Discovery API to learn which API groups and kinds are served by the cluster. That is how Kreate can offer any resource type the cluster knows about, not only a hardcoded list. Extensions that use this API need the @podman-desktop/kubernetes-dashboard-extension-api npm package. Context deletion confirmation ​ Kubernetes Contexts now asks you to confirm before deleting a context, so a context is not removed from your kubeconfig by accident. Confirmation is required for every delete, not only the current context. If you delete the context you are using, the dialog also warns that you will need to switch to another one. Kreate ​ Kreate can create more kinds of resources, including kinds that are not supported by the kubectl create command. You can now also create a Namespace, Job, or CronJob, as with kubectl create . You can also pick any other kind the cluster advertises through the Discovery API, including custom resources such as those from an installed operator. The YAML template will contain the apiVersion and kind fields, and documentation will be provided for the resource fields from the cluster OpenAPI spec. Community meeting ​ If you would like to discuss any of the new features, issues, or other topics, join us at the monthly community meeting on the fourth Thursday of each month . See the meeting details . Final notes ​ The complete list of issues fixed in this release is available for Dashboard , Contexts and Kreate .
