Resource lists now let you choose which columns to show and in which order, so each table can match the information you actually use.

Hide columns you do not need, bring the ones you care about forward, and reset to the default layout when you want a clean slate. This uses the same column editing as other Podman Desktop tables, and it is available on every resource table, not only Pods.

The pod details page also shows more of the workload context, and the Nodes list includes an Internal IP column so you can find a node's cluster address without leaving the dashboard.

Collapsible navigation​

The sidebar is grouped into collapsible sections, so the many new resource types stay organized instead of filling a long flat list.

Resources are grouped under Compute, Config, Network, Storage, and a new Access Control section for RBAC. Collapse the areas you are not using to keep the sidebar scannable. The dashboard remembers which sections you left open, and expands a section when you open a resource that belongs to it. For example, opening a Service from the dashboard expands Network even if that section was collapsed.

New resource views​

Kubernetes Dashboard now covers many more resource kinds, so you can inspect more of the cluster without switching to kubectl.

Compute: DaemonSets, StatefulSets, and ReplicaSets.

Storage: PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses.

Network: Endpoints, EndpointSlices, NetworkPolicies, IngressClasses, HTTPRoutes, Gateways, and GatewayClasses.

Config: ServiceAccounts, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, PodDisruptionBudgets, PriorityClasses, RuntimeClasses, Leases, HorizontalPodAutoscalers, MutatingWebhookConfigurations, and ValidatingWebhookConfigurations.

Access Control: Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, and ClusterRoleBindings.

Lazy resource loading​

The dashboard no longer watches every resource kind as soon as you connect. It starts watching a kind when you open that resource's page.

Common resources such as Pods, Deployments, and Services are still watched immediately, so the dashboard overview can show live counts. The many new kinds, such as Roles, Gateways, StorageClasses, and many more, wait until you visit them. That keeps startup faster and reduces load on the API server.

Extension API​

Other Podman Desktop extensions can now use the Kubernetes Dashboard API instead of opening their own connection to the cluster.

They can subscribe to live resource data, context health, and permissions from the dashboard's existing watches. Kubernetes Contexts uses that subscriber for the state of each context, instead of watching the cluster on its own.

They can also call the Kubernetes Discovery API to learn which API groups and kinds are served by the cluster. That is how Kreate can offer any resource type the cluster knows about, not only a hardcoded list.

Extensions that use this API need the @podman-desktop/kubernetes-dashboard-extension-api npm package.

Context deletion confirmation​

Kubernetes Contexts now asks you to confirm before deleting a context, so a context is not removed from your kubeconfig by accident.

Confirmation is required for every delete, not only the current context. If you delete the context you are using, the dialog also warns that you will need to switch to another one.

Kreate​

Kreate can create more kinds of resources, including kinds that are not supported by the kubectl create command.

You can now also create a Namespace, Job, or CronJob, as with kubectl create.

You can also pick any other kind the cluster advertises through the Discovery API, including custom resources such as those from an installed operator. The YAML template will contain the apiVersion and kind fields, and documentation will be provided for the resource fields from the cluster OpenAPI spec.

Community meeting​

If you would like to discuss any of the new features, issues, or other topics, join us at the monthly community meeting on the fourth Thursday of each month. See the meeting details.

Final notes​

The complete list of issues fixed in this release is available for Dashboard, Contexts and Kreate.

items.title: SaaS access governance: Does access end when employees leave?
items.summary: Cybersecurity Awareness Month encourages organizations to examine the controls behind everyday security habits. Training helps employees spot phishing and use strong authentication but does not resolve gaps in systems that govern access. Many organizations manage employee access through an identity provider (IdP) and single sign-on (SSO). However, not every AI or SaaS application connects to those systems. Other access paths, including shared credentials and OAuth connections, may require separate controls, especially when they provide access to company-owned resources that outlive an individual account. Employees join companies, change roles, and leave every day. Contractors, seasonal employees, and business partners use many of the same applications. Each transition can change what access a person has or should have. Consider a contractor who connects an AI application to company documents during a project. When the engagement ends months later, IT disables the contractor’s account in the IdP. But who revokes the application’s OAuth access? Who transfers ownership of connected files? Who verifies the connection is no longer active? If those steps rely on a spreadsheet or a message to an application owner, that is an access governance gap. According to 1Password’s 2025 Access-Trust Gap Report , 38% of employees have successfully accessed a former employer’s account. This finding reminds us that access can outlive the role it was created for, accruing cybersecurity and non-compliance costs. This October, security awareness should include the systems behind employee behavior. Effective SaaS governance helps IT discover applications and access paths across connected data sources. It governs access beyond SSO and creates repeatable workflows for onboarding, role changes, and offboarding. Why employee access persists after people leave or change roles When an employee leaves, IT may disable their primary account and assume the process is complete but work rarely happens in one system. A former employee may still have an account in a project management tool, customer relationship management system, file-sharing platform, or AI application. If those tools are not connected to single sign-on (SSO), disabling the central account does not remove access. Personal accounts, shared credentials, and OAuth connections can create additional paths back to company data. OAuth connections allow a third-party application to access company resources, and those permissions can persist until someone revokes them. Role changes create a different version of the same problem. An employee moves from sales to marketing and receives access to new systems, but keeps permissions from their previous role. A contractor finishes a project but retains access to the workspace where the work took place. In each case, the access remains because one system recorded the transition while a different team managed the permissions. Often with these scenarios, no one sees the full picture of what a person accesses, who owns it, or when it should end. Access governance closes that gap by connecting the employee event to every application and resource involved. 5 SaaS governance best practices for employee access 1. Discover the applications and access employees use Governing access starts with visibility. IT and security teams need to know which applications, accounts, credentials, files, and integrations teams use for work. That inventory should include applications outside SSO, OAuth connections and the permissions they grant, shared credentials, personal accounts used for work, and SaaS or AI applications adopted without formal approval. IT needs to have visibility in order to change or revoke unnecessary access. 2. Connect access workflows to employee lifecycle events Onboarding, role changes, contractor end dates, and terminations should trigger defined access workflows. Connect these events to provisioning and deprovisioning processes with clear ownership across HR, IT, security, managers, and application teams. Automate repeatable actions where supported, and define an exception process for applications that require manual review. Record when each action is complete, and escalate anything that fails, remains unresolved, or requires an application owner to intervene. 3. Apply least privilege when roles change Access should reflect a person’s current responsibilities, not their history with the company. When an employee changes teams or roles, remove permissions associated with their previous work and review access to sensitive systems. Check privileged access, transfer ownership of files and workflows, and document the changes for future access reviews. A role change is an access event, even when the employee remains trusted. This review reduces accumulated permissions and makes it easier to identify access that no longer has a business justification. 4. Govern newly adopted SaaS and AI tools Employees adopt new AI and SaaS applications every day, often without IT approval. These tools can access company data, create new integrations, and introduce access outside SSO. IT and security teams need visibility into what those tools can access, along with a clear process for requesting and approving them. AI program managers should be able to introduce useful tools without creating an unmanaged exception to the organization’s security process. A governance process for new SaaS and AI applications should connect discovery with data-use policies, third-party connection reviews, and an owner for every approved application. It should also give employees and teams a clear way to request, approve, and remove access. AI tools should be governed as part of the broader SaaS environment, not treated as a separate category with separate visibility and controls. 5. Verify access removal after offboarding Offboarding is complete when the organization can show that it removed access from every relevant system. That review may include applications outside SSO, active sessions where supported, OAuth and other third-party connections, shared credentials, files and workflows, application ownership, and licenses or paid seats. Require evidence of completion and maintain a review trail. Use a second reviewer for higher-risk departures or users with privileged access. IT teams should also test the offboarding process regularly. A scheduled test can reveal gaps in application coverage, unclear ownership, or failed automation before those gaps affect a real departure. Together, these practices make access governance part of the employee lifecycle rather than a task someone remembers at the end of it. For any departure, IT teams should be able to name what access existed, who closed it, and when. How 1Password SaaS Manager supports employee access governance 1Password SaaS Manager helps IT teams close access gaps across the employee lifecycle. It streamlines onboarding and offboarding across the SaaS environment by connecting HR and identity systems to automatically provision and deprovision applications, including apps outside SSO. Through 400+ supported integrations, teams can automate provisioning, deprovisioning, access requests, and access reviews. Depending on the integration, workflows can also support actions such as OAuth token revocation, license removal, and ownership transfer. SaaS Manager also discovers managed and unmanaged SaaS and AI applications, including shadow IT and AI tools employees adopt without IT approval. It can even surface OAuth connections and the permissions they grant, helping IT and security teams review and revoke access outside SSO. It inventories applications, accounts, licenses, and contracts, and supports access reviews and license management so IT and security teams can govern the tools employees use. For IT teams, security awareness starts with visibility into employee access. Cybersecurity Awareness Month is a useful moment to review the applications, accounts, and workflows that need to change when people join, move, or leave. Want to learn more? Learn how SaaS Manager identifies onboarding and offboarding gaps and automates employee access and app management beyond SSO. Explore the solution

items.title: Launching post-quantum safe passkeys
items.summary: Passkeys make authentication safer by resisting phishing attacks and eliminating shared secrets like passwords that attackers can steal from a website to access your accounts. By removing the secrets from servers, they reduce the risk of data breaches. However, advances in quantum computing threaten to increase the risk of those data breaches yet again by breaking the cryptography passkeys currently use. As another step in our Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) migration , 1Password is adding support for ML-DSA passkeys in order to preserve their benefits over the long term. By supporting this algorithm early, we signal websites to start supporting ML-DSA passkeys. This helps protect our customers' credentials against future attackers. Why now? We’ve talked about quantum computers and passkeys before, back in 2023 to be precise. Back then, a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) seemed far off, so why are we rolling out quantum-safe passkeys only three years later? Well, because things changed and research has accelerated. We’ve been closely monitoring the research to ensure we act well ahead of any concerning developments. Back in 2023, governments were mandating a migration to PQC algorithms by 2035, and the estimated amount of qubits estimated to be required to break elliptic curve digital signatures was around 13 million physical qubits. Now, in 2026, improvements in error correction and recent research reduce that estimate to only 26,000 physical qubits . This is still far from the latest largest quantum computer at 6,100 physical qubits , though the gap has shrunk enough for us to start migrating . NIST standardized the post-quantum safe signature algorithm, ML-DSA , in 2024. The IETF standardized ML-DSA’s encoding in COSE in RFC 9964 in May of 2026. COSE is the format that WebAuthn/CTAP2 uses to transfer the passkey back to the website. This means that the stage is set for ML-DSA passkey adoption. Given all these advances and 1Password’s ongoing PQC migration, we decided to roll out ML-DSA passkeys as early as possible. By doing so, we can protect as many of our customers' online accounts as possible. Are my existing passkeys safe? Yes. Supporting ML-DSA is precautionary. Since passkeys are generally long-lived, we want our customers to have the most secure passkeys available early on so they stay secure as long as possible. That’s why we’re providing support now rather than later. But your existing passkeys are still safe because no CRQC currently exists. This support is early, earlier than most websites in fact. With this launch, we expect to see that change soon. We’re engaged in the W3C and the FIDO Alliance to develop a way to update existing passkeys seamlessly. So you don’t need to worry about updating passkeys now or in the future. We’ll take care of it for you! Automatically improving the security of all of our customers’ passkeys is yet another reason why we’re so excited about them. Try ML-DSA Passkeys Today! Starting on version 8.12.44, 1Password will support using the post-quantum safe algorithm, ML-DSA, for passkeys. This doesn’t mean that your passkeys are now all going to be made with ML-DSA going forward. Remember that both sides have to understand the same algorithm, so we will only create these keys for websites that support ML-DSA for passkeys. You can test it yourself at webauthn.io . Open Advanced settings, select an ML-DSA variant under Registration settings, then create a passkey and authenticate with it. Passkey authentication works on all supported platforms, but as of now, creating an ML-DSA passkey isn’t supported on iOS or through the native macOS autofill extension. Thanks to Matt Miller for adding ML-DSA support to webauthn.io , the best WebAuthn test website there is! Our goal is to make this transition as seamless as possible, so we do all the hard work to keep you safe online, and you don’t even have to worry about it. Start using passkeys with 1Password today 1Password is helping prepare passkeys for the future of cryptography. Start using passkeys with 1Password today, and let us handle the hard work of keeping your authentication secure as cryptographic standards evolve. Get started with 1Password
